docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
KOR-ee, from the greek Κόρη, the queen of the underworld, daughter of Zeus and Demeter. Kore is a numerical tool to study the flows inside rapidly rotating planets and stars, or any rotating fluid enclosed in a near-spherical container.

Kore solves the linearized equations of a rotating fluid whose density may vary with radius (the anelastic approximation), with an equation for the entropy and, optionally, an imposed magnetic field. The fluid fills a spherical shell or a full sphere. Kore assumes that every quantity oscillates in time at a single complex frequency. It can either find this frequency, as the eigenvalue of a free oscillation mode (for example the inertial modes of a rotating fluid, in which the Coriolis force is the main restoring force), or impose it, to compute the response to an external forcing such as a tide.

Kore uses a spectral method with Gegenbauer (ultraspherical) polynomials in radius. Unlike traditional Chebyshev collocation, this gives sparse matrices, which need much less memory. This makes it possible to study flows at extremely small viscosities (small Ekman numbers).

To start, see Installation and Getting started. The user guide then takes the features one by one, and Combining features shows which of them work together.

Kore is free for everyone to use, with no restrictions. Too often in the scientific literature the numerical methods used are presented with enough detail to guarantee reproducibility, but only in principle. Without access to the actual implementation of those methods, which would require a significant amount of work and time to develop, readers are left effectively without the possibility to reproduce or verify the results presented. This leads to very slow scientific progress. We share our code to avoid this.

If this code is useful for your research, we invite you to cite the relevant papers (coming soon) and hope that you can also contribute to the project.

docs.title: Anelastic equations
docs.text: kore solves the linear anelastic equations in the form of Lantz (1992) and Braginsky & Roberts (1995), "LBR", for small perturbations of a background whose density varies with radius. This page gives those equations, what the approximation drops, how kore makes them dimensionless, and where they hold. The Boussinesq equations are a special case. How the code discretizes the equations is on Numerical method, and the terms that a differential rotation adds are derived on Differential rotation.

docs.title: Background
docs.text:
The background is at rest in the frame rotating at \(\Omega\), spherically symmetric and hydrostatic: density \(\rho_0(r)\), pressure \(p_0(r)\), temperature \(T_0(r)\), gravity \(-g(r)\thinspace\hat{\mathbf r}\) with \(dp_0/dr = -\rho_0 g\), and specific entropy \(s_0(r)\). Its entropy gradient sets the buoyancy frequency,

\[ N^2 = \frac{g\thinspace \alpha T_0}{c_p}\frac{ds_0}{dr}, \]

with \(\alpha\) the thermal expansion coefficient and \(c_p\) the specific heat at constant pressure. The kinematic viscosity \(\nu(r)\) and the thermal diffusivity \(\kappa(r)\) are radial profiles. Background model explains how to choose all of these.

docs.title: The equations
docs.text:
For a perturbation with velocity \(\mathbf u\) and specific entropy \(s'\), the linear LBR equations are

\[ abla\cdot( ho_0\mathbf u) = 0, \] \[ \partial_t\mathbf u + 2 hinspace\mathbf\Omega imes\mathbf u = - abla\Pi + g hinspace rac{\alpha T_0 s'}{c_p} hinspace\hat{\mathbf r} + rac{1}{ ho_0} abla\cdot\left( ho_0 u hinspace\mathsf S ight), \] \[ ho_0 T_0\left(\partial_t s' + u_r rac{ds_0}{dr} ight) = abla\cdot\left(\kappa hinspace ho_0 T_0 abla s' ight), \]

with the reduced pressure \(\Pi = p'/ ho_0 + \Phi'\) (\(\Phi'\) the perturbation of the gravitational potential) and the rate-of-strain tensor without its trace,

\[ \mathsf S = abla\mathbf u + ( abla\mathbf u)^{\mathsf T} - frac{2}{3}( abla\cdot\mathbf u) hinspace\mathsf I . \]

The momentum equation is per unit mass. The flow is not solenoidal: \( abla\cdot\mathbf u = -u_r hinspace d\ln ho_0/dr\). The viscous force is the divergence of the full stress \( ho_0 u hinspace\mathsf S\), with the terms that come from \(d\ln ho_0/dr\), from \(d u/dr\) and from \( abla\cdot\mathbf u\). Any \( u(r)\) is allowed. The bulk viscosity is zero. The heat flux is a diffusion of entropy.

What is dropped. Starting from the linearised compressible equations about the same background, LBR drops two things (Brown et al. 2012; Vasil et al. 2013):

  1. The acoustic part of \(\partial_t ho'\) in the mass equation. This removes sound.
  2. The entropy part of \(\partial_t ho'\) in the mass equation, together with the force \((N^2/g)(p'/ ho_0) hinspace\hat{\mathbf r}\) in the momentum equation. That force is the buoyancy of the density \(p'/c^2\) that the pressure perturbation induces, in the part of the stratification that is not adiabatic. These two terms must be dropped together.

The second step treats the background as adiabatic wherever the entropy gradient only corrects a term that is already there. The entropy gradient is kept in the heat equation, where it is the source of \(s'\) and gives gravity waves their restoring force. The Coriolis force, the self-gravity (absorbed into \(\Pi\)) and the viscous force are not approximated.

Energy. Multiply the momentum equation by \( ho_0\mathbf u^*\) and integrate. The pressure does no work inside the fluid, although \( abla\cdot\mathbf u eq 0\), because \( abla\Pi\) is a gradient acting on the solenoidal \( ho_0\mathbf u\): it only works through walls that move. The Coriolis force does no work, and the viscous force only dissipates, for any \( u(r)\). This holds only because the two terms of item 2 are dropped together: an anelastic set that keeps the force but drops the mass term makes the pressure do work (Brown et al. 2012). The full balance is under Energy balance.

docs.title: Non-dimensionalization
docs.text:
kore assumes \(\alpha T_0 = 1\) and uses \(p_0\) in place of \( ho_0 T_0\), both exact for an ideal gas of uniform composition. Each quantity is then a scale times a dimensionless variable:

quantity scale dimensionless variable length \(L\), the radius of the outer wall (r_out star radii) \(r\), with \(r = 1\) at the outer wall time \( au\) \(t\) velocity \(L/ au\) \(\mathbf u\) reduced pressure \(L^2/ au^2\) \(\Pi\) entropy perturbation and background entropy \(c_p\) \(s\), \(S\) gravity \(g_{\mathrm{ref}}\) the profile \(g(r)\) of the structure viscosity and thermal diffusivity \( u_{\mathrm{ref}}\), \(\kappa_{\mathrm{ref}}\) the profiles \( u(r)\), \(\kappa(r)\) of diffusivity density and pressure any \( ho_0\), \(p_0\)

The equations are linear in \(\mathbf u\) and \(s\), and contain \( ho_0\) only through \(d\ln ho_0/dr\) and \(p_0\) only through its shape, so the scales of the velocity, of \( ho_0\) and of \(p_0\) do not matter. The solar structures have \(g = 1\) at the surface, so that \(g_{\mathrm{ref}}\) is the surface gravity; \( u_{\mathrm{ref}}\) and \(\kappa_{\mathrm{ref}}\) are the values where the diffusivity profiles are 1 (the convection zone for 'solar_rz' and 'step').

Insert these in the equations, multiply the momentum equation by \( au^2/L\) and the heat equation by \( au/c_p\):

\[ abla\cdot( ho_0\mathbf u) = 0, \] \[ \partial_t\mathbf u + 2 hinspace\mathrm{Gaspard} hinspace\hat{\mathbf z} imes\mathbf u = - abla\Pi + \mathrm{Beyonce} hinspace g hinspace s hinspace\hat{\mathbf r} + \mathrm{ViscosD} hinspace rac{1}{ ho_0} abla\cdot\left( ho_0 u hinspace\mathsf S ight), \] \[ p_0\left(\partial_t s + u_r rac{dS}{dr} ight) = \mathrm{ThermaD} hinspace abla\cdot\left(\kappa hinspace p_0 abla s ight). \]

These are the equations kore solves. \(dS/dr\) is the background entropy gradient over \(c_p\), and \(g\), \( u\) and \(\kappa\) are dimensionless profiles, set by the parameters structure, stratification and diffusivity (Background model). Four numbers carry the scales:

parameter definition meaning Gaspard \(\Omega au\) rotation rate of the frame Beyonce \(g_{\mathrm{ref}} hinspace au^2/L\) gravity ViscosD \( u_{\mathrm{ref}} hinspace au/L^2\) viscosity; the Ekman number when \( au = 1/\Omega\) ThermaD \(\kappa_{\mathrm{ref}} hinspace au/L^2\) thermal diffusivity

The buoyancy frequency is

\[ N^2 = \mathrm{Beyonce} hinspace g hinspace rac{dS}{dr} \]

in units of \(1/ au^2\).

Eigenvalues. Fields go as \(e^{im\phi + \lambda t}\), with \(\lambda = \sigma - i\omega\): \(\sigma\) is the growth rate and \(\omega\) the frequency, in units of \(1/ au\) in the rotating frame; \(\omega > 0\) is prograde. Forced runs (forcing > 0) solve at \(\lambda = i hinspace\)forcing_frequency.

docs.title: The time scale
docs.text:
par.timescale and par.set_scales() set the four parameters from the Ekman number Ek \(= u_{\mathrm{ref}}/(\Omega L^2)\) and Etherm \(= \kappa_{\mathrm{ref}}/(\Omega L^2)\):

timescale \( au\) Gaspard ViscosD ThermaD Beyonce 'rotation' \(1/\Omega\) 1 Ek Etherm 0 'viscous' \(L^2/ u_{\mathrm{ref}}\) 1/Ek 1 Etherm/Ek 0 'free fall' \(\sqrt{L/g_{\mathrm{ref}}}\) 0 0 0 1

set_scales() resets all four, so set the ones it leaves at 0 after calling it (Beyonce with 'rotation'). The parameter files of the examples use 'rotation', and bin/units.py sets the parameters from physical values for that choice (Background model).

Ratios of the parameters do not depend on \( au\):

  • the Ekman number \(E = \mathrm{ViscosD}/\mathrm{Gaspard} = u_{\mathrm{ref}}/(\Omega L^2)\);
  • the Prandtl number \(Pr = \mathrm{ViscosD}/\mathrm{ThermaD} = u_{\mathrm{ref}}/\kappa_{\mathrm{ref}}\);
  • the buoyancy frequency over the rotation rate, \(N/\Omega = \sqrt{\mathrm{Beyonce} hinspace g hinspace dS/dr} hinspace/\mathrm{Gaspard}\);
  • for convection, the Rayleigh number of an entropy drop \(\Delta S\) across the shell (inner minus outer wall), \(Ra = \mathrm{Beyonce} hinspace\Delta S/(\mathrm{ViscosD} hinspace\mathrm{ThermaD}) = g_{\mathrm{ref}}L^3\Delta S/( u_{\mathrm{ref}}\kappa_{\mathrm{ref}})\);
  • the frequency over the rotation rate, \(\omega/\Omega = -\mathrm{Im} hinspace\lambda/\mathrm{Gaspard}\).

docs.title: The Boussinesq case
docs.text: With structure = 'Boussinesq' (\( ho_0 = p_0 = 1\), \(g = r\)) and diffusivity = 'uniform', the equations are the Boussinesq equations: \( abla\cdot\mathbf u = 0\), the viscous force is \(\mathrm{ViscosD} hinspace abla^2\mathbf u\), the diffusion is \(\mathrm{ThermaD} hinspace abla^2 s\), and the buoyancy is \(\mathrm{Beyonce} hinspace r hinspace s hinspace\hat{\mathbf r}\), with \(s\) in place of the temperature perturbation. With stratification 'linear' (\(dS/dr = r\)), \(N^2 = \mathrm{Beyonce} hinspace r^2\).

docs.title: Without thermal diffusion
docs.text:
With ThermaD = 0 the heat equation loses its diffusion term,

\[ p_0\left(\partial_t s + u_r\frac{dS}{dr}\right) = 0 : \]

the entropy perturbation is only carried by the flow, and the motion is adiabatic. This is the limit for modes whose periods are short compared with the time of thermal diffusion. The equation is then first order in \(r\), so it takes no thermal boundary conditions: bci_thermal and bco_thermal are not used. The rows kore builds in that case are on Numerical method, and what to watch for in such runs is in Background model.

docs.title: Composition
docs.text:
A fluid can also be stratified by its composition, as a star by the helium and heavier elements that settle below its convection zone, or a planet's core by its light elements. With compositional = 1 kore solves for the perturbation \(c\) of a second scalar, the composition, beside the entropy or without it. The flow carries \(c\) across the background gradient \(dC/dr\), \(c\) diffuses with its own diffusivity, and it changes the density, so it has its own buoyancy. Its equation is that of the entropy with \( ho_0\) in place of \(p_0\), the conservation of a mass fraction:

\[ ho_0\left(\partial_t c + u_r rac{dC}{dr} ight) = \mathrm{CompoD} hinspace abla\cdot\left(D hinspace ho_0 abla c ight), \]

and the momentum equation gains the force \(\mathrm{BeyonceC} hinspace g hinspace c hinspace\hat{\mathbf r}\) beside \(\mathrm{Beyonce} hinspace g hinspace s hinspace\hat{\mathbf r}\). \(c\) measures the deficit of density that the composition makes at a given pressure and entropy, relative to \( ho_0\): like \(s\), a larger \(c\) is lighter. The buoyancy frequency then has two parts,

\[ N^2 = \mathrm{Beyonce} hinspace g hinspace rac{dS}{dr} + \mathrm{BeyonceC} hinspace g hinspace rac{dC}{dr}, \]

and each can have its own sign: a stable composition gradient under an unstable entropy gradient, or the reverse, is the double-diffusive case. \(D\) is the profile of the diffusivity of the composition (diffusivity), and two numbers carry its scales:

parameter definition meaning BeyonceC \(g_{\mathrm{ref}} hinspace au^2/L\), for \(c\) a relative density buoyancy of the composition CompoD \(D_{\mathrm{ref}} hinspace au/L^2\) diffusivity of the composition

set_scales() sets CompoD from Ecomp \(= D_{\mathrm{ref}}/(\Omega L^2)\) as it sets ThermaD from Etherm, and BeyonceC to 0, so set BeyonceC after calling it. The composition takes the wall conditions of the entropy, a fixed composition (\(c = 0\)) or no flux (\(\partial_r c = 0\)). With CompoD = 0 it is only carried by the flow, as the entropy with ThermaD = 0: its equation is then of first order and takes no wall conditions. With a differential rotation it gains the advection \(i hinspace m hinspace\mathrm{Gaspard} hinspace\Delta\Omega hinspace c\) inside the bracket; the background composition is spherical, so nothing in it plays the part of the thermal wind.

With 'Boussinesq' and diffusivity = 'uniform' the equation is \(\partial_t c + u_r hinspace dC/dr = \mathrm{CompoD} hinspace abla^2 c\).

docs.title: Differential rotation
docs.text:
With a differential rotation \(\Omega(r,\theta) = \Omega_{\rm ref}\left[1 + \Delta\Omega(r,\theta)\right]\), kore solves in the frame rotating at \(\Omega_{\rm ref}\), where the background is a steady azimuthal flow,

\[ \mathbf{U}_0 = \mathrm{Gaspard}\thinspace\Delta\Omega\thinspace r\sin\theta\thinspace\hat{\mathbf{e}}_\phi . \]

The perturbation is advected and sheared by this flow. In the momentum equation this adds

\[ \mathrm{Gaspard}\left[\Delta\Omega\thinspace (i\thinspace m\thinspace \mathbf{u} + 2\hat{\mathbf{z}}\times\mathbf{u}) + r\sin\theta\thinspace (\mathbf{u}\cdot\nabla\Delta\Omega)\thinspace \hat{\mathbf{e}}_\phi\right] \]

to the left side: the advection by the local rotation and its Coriolis force, and the transport of angular momentum by the perturbation across the shear. The heat equation gains, inside the bracket multiplied by \(p_0\),

\[ i\thinspace m\thinspace\mathrm{Gaspard}\thinspace\Delta\Omega\thinspace s + u_r\thinspace \frac{\partial S_{tw}}{\partial r} + \frac{u_\theta}{r}\thinspace \frac{\partial S_{tw}}{\partial\theta}. \]

The first term is the advection of \(s\) by \(\mathbf U_0\). The other two are the advection, by the perturbation, of a latitudinal background entropy \(S_{tw}(r,\theta)\): either the thermal wind that balances \(\Omega(r,\theta)\) (the latitudinal entropy a differentially rotating star needs to be in equilibrium; Bekki, Cameron & Gizon 2022) or prescribed. In a convection zone these terms act at the same order as the momentum terms. The background is fixed: nothing maintains or evolves \(\Omega\) and \(S_{tw}\) against diffusion, and \(\rho_0\), \(T_0\) and \(g\) stay spherical unless centrifugal = 1 flattens the body (Centrifugal deformation). Differential rotation derives these terms and their spectral form.

docs.title: Energy balance
docs.text:
kore's fields are complex amplitudes: a physical field is the amplitude times \(e^{im\phi + \lambda t}\), plus the complex conjugate. The product of two such fields, averaged over \(\phi\) (or, for \(m = 0\), over a period of a forced response), is \(2\thinspace\mathrm{Re}\) of the product of their amplitudes. kore writes every energy and power this way: the kinetic energy

\[ K = \int\rho_0\lvert\mathbf u\rvert^2\thinspace dV , \]

the mean of \(\int\tfrac12\rho_0\thinspace\mathbf u_{\rm phys}^2\thinspace dV\), and the power of a force \(\mathbf F\) per unit mass,

\[ W[\mathbf F] = 2\thinspace\mathrm{Re}\int\rho_0\thinspace\mathbf u^*\cdot\mathbf F\thinspace dV . \]

docs.title: Kinetic energy
docs.text:
Take the momentum equation with \(\partial_t = \lambda = \sigma - i\omega\), multiply it by \(2 ho_0\mathbf u^*\), integrate over the fluid and keep the real part:

\[ 2\sigma K = W_ u + W_b + W_c + W_\Omega + W_p , \]

with, term by term:

  • Coriolis. \(\mathbf u^*\cdot(\hat{\mathbf z} imes\mathbf u)\) is imaginary: the Coriolis force does no work.

  • Pressure. Since \( abla\cdot( ho_0\mathbf u) = 0\), the power of \(- abla\Pi\) is a flux through the walls,

    \[ W_p = -2 hinspace\mathrm{Re}\oint ho_0 hinspace\Pi hinspace u_r^* hinspace(\hat{\mathbf r}\cdot\mathbf n) hinspace dA , \]

    with \(\mathbf n\) the outward normal of the fluid (\(-\hat{\mathbf r}\) at the inner wall). It is zero when \(u_r = 0\) at the walls (bco, bci = 0 or 1), and not when the walls move radially (the tidal forcing 14) or with bco = 2.

  • Viscosity. With the stress \( oldsymbol\sigma = \mathrm{ViscosD} hinspace ho_0 u hinspace\mathsf S\), an integration by parts splits the power of the viscous force into the work of the stress at the walls and the dissipation:

    \[ W_ u = 2 hinspace\mathrm{Re}\int\mathbf u^*\cdot( abla\cdot oldsymbol\sigma) hinspace dV = W_ u^{ m wall} - D_ u , \qquad W_ u^{ m wall} = 2 hinspace\mathrm{Re}\oint\mathbf u^*\cdot oldsymbol\sigma\cdot\mathbf n hinspace dA , \] \[ D_ u = 2 hinspace\mathrm{Re}\int oldsymbol\sigma: abla\mathbf u^* hinspace dV = \int 4 hinspace\mathrm{ViscosD} hinspace ho_0 u hinspace\mathsf e_d:\mathsf e_d^* hinspace dV \geq 0 , \]

    with \(\mathsf e = frac12[ abla\mathbf u + ( abla\mathbf u)^{\mathsf T}]\) the rate of strain and \(\mathsf e_d = \mathsf e - frac13( abla\cdot\mathbf u) hinspace\mathsf I\) its deviatoric part: \(\mathsf S = 2\mathsf e_d\), and \( oldsymbol\sigma\) is symmetric and traceless, so that \( oldsymbol\sigma: abla\mathbf u^* = oldsymbol\sigma:\mathsf e_d^*\). The physical dissipation is \(\int 2 ho u hinspace\mathsf e_d:\mathsf e_d hinspace dV\), and the factor 4 is its mean in the convention above. \(W_ u^{ m wall}\) is zero on a no-slip wall at rest and on an impenetrable stress-free wall, unless a force acts on the fluid at that wall: a drag (Drag at the outer wall) or the push of the background field's current sheet (Magnetic field equations).

  • Buoyancy. \(W_b = 2 hinspace\mathrm{Beyonce} hinspace\mathrm{Re}\int ho_0 hinspace g hinspace s hinspace u_r^* hinspace dV\), the energy exchanged with the entropy perturbation, and with compositional = 1 \(W_c = 2 hinspace\mathrm{BeyonceC} hinspace\mathrm{Re}\int ho_0 hinspace g hinspace c hinspace u_r^* hinspace dV\), the energy exchanged with the composition.

  • Differential rotation. Of the terms of Differential rotation, the advection \(i m hinspace\mathrm{Gaspard} hinspace\Delta\Omega hinspace\mathbf u\) and the Coriolis force of \(\Delta\Omega\) do no work. The last one does:

    \[ W_\Omega = -2 hinspace\mathrm{Gaspard} hinspace\mathrm{Re}\int ho_0 hinspace r\sin heta hinspace u_\phi^* hinspace(\mathbf u\cdot abla\Delta\Omega) hinspace dV , \]

    the Reynolds stress of the perturbation acting on the shear. \(W_\Omega > 0\) is energy that the perturbation takes from the background flow.

With a magnetic field the Lorentz force adds its power (Magnetic field). The imaginary part of the same equation is the frequency balance: \(2 hinspace\mathrm{Im}(\lambda) hinspace K\) against the imaginary parts of the same integrals, where the Coriolis force now enters.

docs.title: Entropy
docs.text:
Multiply the heat equation by \(2s^*\), integrate and keep the real part:

\[ 2\sigma T = W_{ m adv} - D_{ m th} + W_{\Omega, m th} , \qquad T = \int p_0\lvert s vert^2 hinspace dV , \]

with the advection by the background gradient \(W_{ m adv} = -2 hinspace\mathrm{Re}\int p_0 hinspace rac{dS}{dr} hinspace u_r s^* hinspace dV\), the diffusion \(D_{ m th} = 2 hinspace\mathrm{ThermaD}\int\kappa p_0\lvert abla s vert^2 hinspace dV\) (the wall term vanishes for both thermal conditions, \(s = 0\) or \(\partial_r s = 0\)), and, with a differential rotation, \(W_{\Omega, m th} = -2 hinspace\mathrm{Re}\int p_0 hinspace s^*\left[i m hinspace\mathrm{Gaspard} hinspace\Delta\Omega hinspace s + \mathbf u\cdot abla S_{tw} ight]dV\).

\(T\) is not an energy, and this budget closes on its own: the buoyancy work \(W_b\) is only in the kinetic budget. The two combine into a total energy with the available potential energy, in the convention above \(\int ho_0 hinspace\mathrm{Beyonce} hinspace g hinspace\lvert s vert^2/(dS/dr) hinspace dV\): without diffusion its rate of change is \(-W_b\). It is positive only where the stratification is stable, and kore does not form it.

The composition has the same budget with \( ho_0\) in place of \(p_0\): \(2\sigma C = W_{ m adv,c} - D_{ m c}\), with \(C = \int ho_0\lvert c vert^2 hinspace dV\), \(W_{ m adv,c} = -2 hinspace\mathrm{Re}\int ho_0 hinspace rac{dC}{dr} hinspace u_r c^* hinspace dV\) and \(D_{ m c} = 2 hinspace\mathrm{CompoD}\int D ho_0\lvert abla c vert^2 hinspace dV\). The advection by a differential rotation only enters its imaginary part.

docs.title: A forced, periodic response
docs.text:
A forced run has \(\lambda = i hinspace\)forcing_frequency, so \(\sigma = 0\), and the kinetic budget reads

\[ P_{ m in} \equiv W_p + W_ u^{ m wall} = D_ u - W_b - W_c - W_\Omega : \]

the power that the moving walls put into the flow is dissipated by viscosity, handed to the entropy perturbation or to the composition, or given to the differential rotation. With a uniform rotation and no buoyancy, \(P_{ m in} = D_ u\). With a differential rotation \(W_\Omega\) has either sign, so the power the forcing puts in and the heat the viscosity releases can differ. Tidal forcing explains which of these quantities a tidal study needs, and Numerical method how spin_doctor computes them.

docs.title: Where the approximation holds
docs.text:
• Sound-proof: \(\max(\lvert\lambda\rvert^2, 4\Omega^2) \ll c^2k^2\) for a mode of wavenumber \(k\), with \(c\) the sound speed. It fails for p modes and near a surface where \(c\to 0\).
  • Nearly adiabatic over the scale \(\ell\) of the motion: \(N^2\ell/g \ll 1\), the relative size of the dropped terms of item 2. In kore's units this is \(\lvert dS/dr\rvert\thinspace\ell \ll 1\). Their effect on frequencies is smaller, and for \(N \gg \omega\) it does not grow with \(N\), so a strongly stratified radiative zone is not a problem in itself. The case where it fails is that of low-order g modes with frequencies near \(N\).
  • A possible background: hydrostatic, and with \(N^2 < g/H_\rho\) (\(H_\rho\) the density scale height), since \(g/c^2 = -d\ln\rho_0/dr - N^2/g\) must be positive. In kore's units this is \(dS/dr < -d\ln\rho_0/dr\). kore never uses \(c\), so it cannot detect a background that breaks this: check it when choosing structure and stratification separately.

docs.title: Background model
docs.text:
kore computes small perturbations of a steady background state. You describe that background in the parameter file, in seven independent parts:

part parameter what it sets structure structure density, pressure and gravity as functions of radius stratification stratification the radial entropy gradient (only with thermal = 1) diffusivity diffusivity how viscosity and thermal diffusivity vary with radius composition comp_stratification the gradient of a second scalar, the composition (only with compositional = 1) rotation diff_rot, diff_rot_type uniform or differential rotation shape centrifugal, centrifugal_shape a sphere, or a body flattened by its rotation flow bgflow a steady axisymmetric flow, see Background flow

The equations where these enter are on Anelastic equations.

docs.title: Units
docs.text:
kore works with dimensionless quantities (Non-dimensionalization). The unit of length is the radius of the outer wall. The parameter r_out (default 1) gives that radius as a fraction of the stellar radius; the solar profiles below are written in terms of this fractional stellar radius, called \(x\).

The helper module bin/units.py converts physical values into kore's parameters, using \(1/\Omega\) as the time unit. In a parameter file, after setting r_out:

import units
units.set_physical(par, frame_nHz=456.0, nu=1e12, kappa=1e12)   # sets Gaspard, Beyonce, ViscosD, ThermaD, diff_rot_frame
units.set_target(par, omega=-271.2, sigma=-33.2)                 # sets the solver target from a frequency and a damping rate in nHz

set_physical takes the viscosity and thermal diffusivity in cm²/s, and uses the solar radius and surface gravity unless you pass radius and gsurf (in cgs units). Running python3 bin/units.py in a run directory prints the computed eigenvalues as frequency and damping rate in nHz.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
The background of the smooth Sun example (examples/smooth_sun/parameters.py), a full sphere with the observed solar rotation:

par.thermal        = 1
par.r_out          = 0.985                 # outer wall in solar radii
par.structure      = 'model S hydrostatic'
par.stratification = 'solar_rz'            # a radiative interior below a slightly subadiabatic convection zone
par.solar_rz_delta_cz = -4e-7
par.diffusivity    = 'solar_rz'            # viscosity and diffusivity drop to visc0, therm0 below 0.70 R☉
par.visc0, par.therm0 = 0.01, 0.04
par.diff_rot       = 1
par.diff_rot_type  = 'tabulated'           # rotation rate read from a table
par.diff_rot_file  = 'bin/jsoc_hmi_2010_2026.npz'
par.diff_rot_nmax  = 4
par.thermal_wind   = 2                     # with its exact thermal wind
par.thermal_wind_radial = 0
units.set_physical(par, frame_nHz=456.0, nu=1e12, kappa=1e12)

The default bin/parameters.py uses structure = 'Wu 2005' and stratification = 'top hat' with uniform rotation. Getting started uses an incompressible fluid ('Boussinesq', thermal = 0).

docs.title: Structure
docs.text:
structure sets the density, pressure and gravity. It has no default.

structure description parameters 'model S hydrostatic' the Sun: a smooth fit to the density of solar Model S, with gravity and pressure consistent with it. Recommended for solar work structure_deg (30) 'Wu 2005' a polytrope-like density \(\rho_0 = (1 - x^2)^2\) (Wu 2005) needs r_out < 1, so that the density is not zero at the wall 'Boussinesq' uniform density: the Boussinesq (incompressible) equations – '8-term fit' legacy solar fit, kept to reproduce old runs – 'old model S prototype' legacy solar fit, kept to reproduce old runs solar_density_deg, solar_density_window, solar_density_sun_deg
  • Only the shape of the density and pressure profiles matters, not their overall scale.
  • 'model S hydrostatic' matches Model S to within about 1 % at the default degree 30. Use structure_deg = 50 to compare closely with work that uses Model S itself; this needs a slightly higher lmax.

docs.title: Stratification
docs.text:
With thermal = 1, stratification sets the background entropy gradient \(dS/dr\), which controls buoyancy. A positive gradient is stable (radiative), zero is neutral (convective). There is no default.

stratification profile parameters 'top hat' a stable layer between two smooth steps aux1…aux5: position and width of each step, then the amplitude 'odd top hat' the same, but well behaved at the centre of a full sphere aux1…aux5 'solar_rz' the solar radiative interior of Mukhopadhyay et al. 2025b (below) solar_rz_* 'linear' proportional to \(r\) – 'inverse square' proportional to \(1/r^2\) (conduction between the walls) needs ricb > 0 'two zone' a nearly neutral inner zone below a stable outer zone two_zone = [transition radius, width] ([0.7, 0.1]) 'user' your own expression (below) stratification_profile, stratification_param
  • In a full sphere the gradient must go to zero smoothly at the centre. Use 'odd top hat' rather than 'top hat' unless the first step is far from the centre.
  • In a shell without thermal diffusion, keep the gradient zero at the inner wall (see ThermaD = 0).
  • 'odd top hat' with aux1…aux5 = 0, 0.03, 0.68, 0.06, 2.6 approximates the entropy gradient of solar Model S.

'solar_rz'. A stable radiative interior joined to a convection zone at about 0.7 solar radii, following Mukhopadhyay et al. (2025b) and Bekki et al. (2024):

\[ \frac{dS}{dr} = \frac{A}{4}\left[1 - \mathrm{erf}\frac{x - x_1}{d}\right]\left[1 - \mathrm{erf}\frac{x - x_2}{d}\right]\mathrm{erf}\frac{x}{w_0} + \delta(x)\thinspace \frac{d\ln p_0}{dr}\thinspace \frac{1}{2}\left[1 + \mathrm{erf}\frac{x - x_{OS}}{d_{OS}}\right]. \]

The first term is the radiative interior, the second the convection zone. The parameters and their defaults:

parameter meaning default solar_rz_dSdr amplitude \(A\) of the radiative gradient 2.615 solar_rz_steps \([x_1, x_2, d]\), the steps that shape it [0.61, 0.68, 0.04] solar_rz_core \(w_0\), makes the profile smooth at the centre 0.05 solar_rz_os \([x_{OS}, d_{OS}]\), base and width of the convection zone [0.70, 0.04] solar_rz_delta_cz superadiabaticity \(\delta\) of the convection zone (negative is stable) 0 solar_rz_delta_sf \(\delta\) just below the surface 0

A slightly negative solar_rz_delta_cz, such as the \(-4\times10^{-7}\) of the smooth Sun example, noticeably changes the frequencies of the high-frequency retrograde modes.

docs.title: Diffusivity
docs.text:
The viscosity is ViscosD times a radial profile, and the thermal diffusivity is ThermaD times another. diffusivity chooses those profiles (and the composition's, with comp0 in place of therm0).

diffusivity profile parameters 'uniform' (default) constant – 'step' visc0, therm0 below radius aux3, 1 above, joined by a smooth step of width aux4 visc0, therm0, aux3, aux4 'solar_rz' visc0, therm0 in the radiative interior, 1 in the convection zone (Mukhopadhyay et al. 2025b) visc0, therm0, solar_rz_os 'user' your own expressions (below) diffusivity_profiles, diffusivity_param
  • With 'step' and 'solar_rz', ViscosD and ThermaD are the values in the outer (convective) layer.
  • visc_pow, therm_pow and comp_pow (default 0) multiply the profile by a power of the density. With 1, the dynamic diffusivities (density times diffusivity) follow the profile instead of the kinematic ones.
  • Convective forcing uses only the turbulent part of the viscosity, above a floor rsf_nu_floor.

docs.title: ThermaD = 0
docs.text:
ThermaD = 0 turns thermal diffusion off: the motion is adiabatic and the thermal boundary conditions are not used. It works with every structure, stratification and rotation profile. Things to know:

  • Prefer ThermaD = 0 to a very small ThermaD. A very small diffusivity creates thin thermal boundary layers at the walls that need much more radial resolution. The eigenvalues approach the ThermaD = 0 ones smoothly anyway.
  • Keep the entropy gradient zero at the inner wall. Otherwise spurious modes appear there. They move when you change N, and spin_doctor flags them. If the gradient must reach the wall, ask for one or two more eigenvalues (nev), since the spurious modes take some of the slots.
  • With differential rotation, expect many spurious eigenvalues with near-zero damping. They come from the entropy being carried by the rotation without diffusion. They change with lmax and fail the ℓ-convergence check of spin_doctor; discard them. Keep the solver target away from that band.
  • Check convergence in N. Runs without diffusion usually need more radial resolution.
  • Forced runs. Without diffusion, the entropy is only carried by the flow. If the forcing frequency, seen from the rotating fluid, is zero somewhere in the domain, the problem has no well-behaved solution and kore stops (Combining features).

docs.title: Composition
docs.text:
A fluid can be stratified by composition as well as by entropy: helium below the convection zone of a star, or light elements in a planet's core. With compositional = 1 kore adds a second scalar, the composition, that is carried by the flow, diffuses, and adds its own buoyancy. It can be used alone (thermal = 0) or together with the entropy, for a double-diffusive fluid. Its equation is on Anelastic equations.

par.compositional = 1
par.comp_stratification = 'linear'      # background gradient proportional to r
par.BeyonceC = 10.                      # strength of its buoyancy; set after set_scales()
par.CompoD = 1e-3                       # its diffusivity
par.bci_compositional = 0               # at each wall, 0: fixed composition, 1: no flux
par.bco_compositional = 0

comp_stratification takes the values 'linear', 'inverse square', 'two zone' (with comp_two_zone) and 'user' (with comp_stratification_profile), as for the entropy. It has no default. BeyonceC sets the strength of the compositional buoyancy.

  • A higher composition is lighter, as for the entropy: the layer is stable where BeyonceC times the gradient is positive.
  • CompoD = 0 turns its diffusion off; the advice of ThermaD = 0 then applies to it.
  • units.set_physical(par, ..., D=...), with \(D\) in cm²/s, also sets CompoD and BeyonceC.
  • The composition works with nearly every other feature. The tidal forcing 1 needs compositional = 0 (Combining features).
  • Its results are in composition.dat (Output files).

docs.title: Rotation
docs.text:
With diff_rot = 0 (the default) the fluid rotates uniformly with the frame. With diff_rot = 1 it rotates differentially, at

\[ \Omega(r,\theta) = \Omega_{\rm ref}\left[1 + \Delta\Omega(r,\theta)\right], \]

where \(\Omega_{\rm ref}\) is the rotation rate of the frame and \(\Delta\Omega\) the relative departure from it. kore expands \(\Delta\Omega\) in even Legendre polynomials in latitude, so the rotation is always symmetric about the equator. Eigenvalues are given in the frame rotating at \(\Omega_{\rm ref}\).

With thermal = 1, the background also includes the latitudinal entropy variation that balances the differential rotation, the thermal wind (see below).

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
parameter default meaning diff_rot 0 1 turns on differential rotation diff_rot_type 'Y20' the profile, see below diff_rot_ampl 1.0 a factor that multiplies \(\Delta\Omega\) diff_rot_param 0.0 shape parameter of some profiles diff_rot_term_amp [1.0]*9 factors on each Legendre term; e.g. [1, 1, 0] drops the third term diff_rot_profiles {} 'user': one expression per Legendre degree (below) diff_rot_frame 456.0 'solar_P4', 'tabulated': frame rotation rate in nHz diff_rot_solar [464, -76, -50, 433.5, 0.71, 0.045] 'solar_P4': coefficients of the fit below diff_rot_file '' 'tabulated': the table file, absolute or relative to the run directory diff_rot_nmax 8 'tabulated', 'ferraro': highest Legendre degree kept (even) diff_rot_F 'psi' 'ferraro': the rotation as a function of the magnetic flux function diff_rot_rdeg, diff_rot_window, diff_rot_sun_deg 24, None, 60 'tabulated': settings of the radial fit thermal_wind 1 the thermal wind, see below thermal_wind_radial 1 0 drops the radial advection of the thermal-wind entropy thermal_wind_amplitude 1.0 a factor on the thermal-wind entropy dSdtheta 0.0 thermal_wind = 3: the prescribed latitudinal entropy gradient

If diff_rot is used with physical units ('solar', 'solar_P4', 'tabulated'), compute ViscosD, ThermaD and Beyonce for the frame rate: 435 nHz for 'solar', diff_rot_frame for the other two. units.set_physical does this.

docs.title: Profiles
docs.text:
Below, \(a\) is diff_rot_ampl and \(p\) is diff_rot_param.

diff_rot_type rotation notes 'rigid' uniform offset \(a\) for tests: the exact answer is known 'Y20' \(a\thinspace P_2(\cos\theta)\), latitudinal only use ricb > 0 'Y20-wall-bounded' the same, vanishing at both walls use ricb > 0 'shellular' \(a\thinspace (r^p - 1)\), radial only Baruteau & Rieutord 2013 'shellular_boussinesq' radial only, proportional to \(1 - r^2\) Mirouh et al. 2016; use with thermal_wind = 0, 'Boussinesq' and 'linear' 'cylindrical' \(a\thinspace r^2\sin^2\theta\), constant on cylinders Baruteau & Rieutord 2013 'conical' \(a\sin^2\theta\), constant on cones Guenel et al. 2016; use ricb > 0 'solar' an older helioseismic fit, relative to 435 nHz less accurate than 'solar_P4' or 'tabulated' 'solar_P4' a fit of the solar rotation, see below Mukhopadhyay et al. 2026 'tabulated' read from a table of observations see below 'user' your own expressions see below 'ferraro' constant along the field lines of a poloidal magnetic field needs magnetic = 1 (Magnetic field)

'solar_P4'. A uniformly rotating radiative zone, joined at the tachocline (radius \(r_{tc}\), width \(d_{tc}\)) to a convection zone whose rotation depends only on latitude:

\[ \frac{\Omega}{2\pi} = \Omega_{RZ} + \tfrac12\left[\Omega_{CZ}(\theta) - \Omega_{RZ}\right]\left[1 + \mathrm{erf}\thinspace \frac{x - r_{tc}}{d_{tc}}\right], \qquad \Omega_{CZ} = c_0 + c_2\cos^2\theta + c_4\cos^4\theta , \]

with diff_rot_solar = [\(c_0\), \(c_2\), \(c_4\), \(\Omega_{RZ}\), \(r_{tc}\), \(d_{tc}\)], rates in nHz and radii in solar radii.

'tabulated'. The rotation rate comes from an .npz file with the arrays ome[θ, r] (nHz), r (solar radii) and theta (radians). bin/jsoc_hmi_2010_2026.npz is the mean solar rotation measured by HMI from 2010 to 2026, and tests/diff_rot/ls_to_tabulated.py converts the Larson & Schou (2018) table to this format. kore expands the table up to Legendre degree diff_rot_nmax and prints how well the expansion fits the table: check that line. Near the surface at high latitude the solar profile needs a degree of about 12 for good accuracy.

'user'. diff_rot_profiles gives the radial shape of each even Legendre degree as an expression (below). For example, the cylindrical profile written by hand:

par.diff_rot_type     = 'user'
par.diff_rot_profiles = {0: '(2/3)*r**2', 2: '-(2/3)*r**2'}
par.diff_rot_ampl     = -0.25

docs.title: Thermal wind
docs.text:
In a stratified fluid, differential rotation must be balanced by a latitudinal variation of the background entropy, the thermal wind. With thermal = 1, thermal_wind chooses how kore treats it:

thermal_wind background entropy 0 no thermal wind; the rotation only carries the entropy perturbation (as in Mirouh et al. 2016) 1 (default) the thermal wind to first order in the differential rotation 2 the exact thermal wind; the eigenvalues then do not depend on the choice of frame 3 a prescribed latitudinal entropy gradient, dSdtheta (as in Bekki et al. 2024)
  • Options 1 and 2 need a non-zero Beyonce. set_scales() with timescale = 'rotation' sets Beyonce = 0, so set it after calling set_scales().
  • thermal_wind_radial = 0 drops one term of the thermal wind, as Bekki et al. 2022 and Mukhopadhyay et al. 2025 do. Keeping it is more consistent, but use 0 to compare with those papers.
  • With a magnetic field, the thermal wind ignores the force of the background field (Magnetic field).

docs.title: Resolution and cost
docs.text:
• Differential rotation couples spherical-harmonic degrees that uniform rotation keeps separate, so the matrices are larger and the runs slower. The cost grows with the highest Legendre degree of the rotation, so keep diff_rot_nmax as low as the problem allows.
  • In a full sphere, some profiles are not smooth at the centre ('Y20', 'conical', most 'shellular'). submatrices.py prints a warning for each.
  • Modes that reach into a radiative interior have short radial wavelengths and can need N of 700 or more. See Solver for the memory this takes.
  • Check every solution with spin_doctor, as for any run.

docs.title: Centrifugal deformation
docs.text:
A rotating star or planet is flattened at the poles. With centrifugal = 1, kore gives the background this shape: the walls and the surfaces of constant density become oblate spheroids, and every term of the equations feels it. kore keeps its spherical grid and solves in coordinates that follow the flattened surfaces. The equations are on Centrifugal deformation.

The deformation is accurate to first order in the flattening, which is enough for most stars and planets. 'spheroid' treats a uniform-density body exactly, at any flattening.

docs.title: Flattening
docs.text:
parameter default meaning centrifugal 0 1 flattens the body centrifugal_shape 'clairaut' how the flattening varies with radius (below) centrifugal_q 0.0 the ratio of centrifugal to gravitational acceleration at the equator centrifugal_f None the flattening of the outer wall, (equatorial − polar radius) / equatorial radius centrifugal_profile, centrifugal_param 'user': the flattening as an expression (below) centrifugal_shape flattening set by 'clairaut' the hydrostatic shape of the chosen structure centrifugal_q or centrifugal_f 'uniform' the same at every radius centrifugal_f 'user' any profile centrifugal_profile 'spheroid' the same at every radius, exact at any flattening centrifugal_f
  • 'spheroid' suits a uniform-density fluid in a fast-rotating or rigid container, such as a planetary core inside a rigid mantle. It needs 'Boussinesq', uniform diffusivities and no differential rotation. A negative flattening gives an elongated body.
  • submatrices.py prints the flattening at the walls, and warns above 0.1, where the first-order treatment becomes inaccurate.

Typical values:

body centrifugal_q surface flattening Earth 3.5e-3 3.4e-3 (core-mantle boundary: 2.5e-3) Jupiter 0.089 0.065 Saturn 0.155 0.098 Sun 2e-5 8e-6

A Jupiter-like body:

par.structure         = 'Wu 2005'
par.r_out             = 0.99
par.centrifugal       = 1
par.centrifugal_shape = 'clairaut'
par.centrifugal_q     = 0.089

The Earth's core, whose shape is set by the whole planet, so give the flattening of the core-mantle boundary directly:

par.structure         = 'Boussinesq'
par.centrifugal       = 1
par.centrifugal_shape = 'uniform'
par.centrifugal_f     = 2.5e-3

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
• The deformation works with buoyancy, viscosity, thermal and compositional diffusion, differential rotation, the drag at the outer wall and a magnetic field (insulating walls or a conducting inner core), in shells and full spheres.
  • It does not work with forced runs, walls of zero radial stress (bci or bco = 2), the rotating solids, thin conducting layers, a resolved mantle or a background flow. kore stops and says why (Combining features).
  • A viscous flow in a full sphere with m ≠ 0 needs rpower_v of at least 4; kore stops and says so.
  • With the thermal wind, the background entropy ignores the flattening. submatrices.py warns about this.
  • In spin_doctor, the total energy budget closes only approximately (to second order in the flattening), except with 'spheroid'.

docs.title: User profiles
docs.text:
The 'user' options take a numpy expression as a string. It may use r (kore's radius), x (the stellar radius with a solar structure, otherwise equal to r), p (the matching ..._param parameter), and the usual functions: sin, cos, tan, arcsin, arccos, arctan, sinh, cosh, tanh, exp, log, log10, sqrt, abs, sign, pi, where, minimum, maximum, erf, erfc. For example:

par.stratification = 'user'
par.stratification_profile = '2.5*exp(-((r - 0.75)/0.06)**2)'
par.diffusivity = 'user'
par.diffusivity_profiles = {'nu': '0.01 + 0.99*0.5*(1 + tanh((x - 0.70)/0.015))', 'kappa': '1'}

In a full sphere, profiles must be smooth at the centre; submatrices.py warns if they are not (Regularity at the centre). Expressions must not contain #.

docs.title: Checks
docs.text: kore checks the background before building anything, and stops with an explanation if something cannot work: an unknown type, a parameter name from an older version of kore (the message gives the new name), or a combination that is not supported. submatrices.py also warns about any parameter name it does not recognize, so a misspelled name is not silently ignored.

docs.title: Benchmarks
docs.text:
kore reproduces published eigenvalues of differentially rotating fluids, from an incompressible fluid to the solar convection zone with a radiative interior. This page gives the set-up of each benchmark, the script that runs it, and the result.

benchmark physics result Baruteau & Rieutord 2013 incompressible, shellular and cylindrical rotation reproduced Guenel et al. 2016 incompressible, conical rotation reproduced, including an unstable mode Mirouh et al. 2016 Boussinesq, stably stratified, shellular rotation reproduced Mukhopadhyay et al. 2025a solar convection zone, observed rotation, thermal wind reproduced, including an unstable mode Bekki et al. 2024 onset of the high-latitude instability reproduced Mukhopadhyay et al. 2025b solar convection zone with a radiative interior reproduced, except two high-latitude modes

The scripts are in tests/diff_rot/. Each one builds a run directory with a copy of bin/ and its own parameters.py, runs submatrices.py and assemble.py, and solves near the published eigenvalue. Getting started runs one of these benchmarks, fig. 10 of Baruteau & Rieutord, step by step.

Conventions. kore's eigenvalue is \(\lambda = \sigma - i\omega\), with \(\sigma\) the growth rate and \(\omega\) the frequency in the frame rotating at \(\Omega_{\rm ref}\) (Anelastic equations). The three fluid-dynamics papers give frequencies in the inertial frame, which are \(\mathrm{Im}\thinspace\lambda - m\) in kore's units. The solar papers give frequencies and growth rates in nHz, in the frame rotating at 456 nHz, with negative frequencies for retrograde modes.

docs.title: Incompressible and Boussinesq fluids
docs.text:
These three papers use a viscous fluid in a spherical shell with stress-free walls. Their Ekman number is \(E = \nu/(\Omega_{\rm ref}R^2)\), which is ViscosD with timescale = 'rotation'. The common settings are

par.timescale = 'rotation'; par.set_scales()
par.structure = 'Boussinesq'                 # uniform density
par.bci = par.bco = 0                        # stress-free
par.diff_rot = 1; par.thermal_wind = 0
par.ricb = 0.35                              # their η, unless stated
par.ViscosD = 1e-8                           # their E

tests/diff_rot/lit_bench.py WORKDIR CASE builds and solves one published mode; lit_bench.py WORKDIR list prints the cases (br*, gu*, mi*). The runs take minutes; the largest needs about 26 GB of memory.

docs.title: Baruteau & Rieutord 2013
docs.text:
JFM 719, 47. Shellular rotation \(\Omega = \Omega_{\rm ref}(r/R)^\sigma\), with \(\Omega_{\rm ref}\) the surface rate, and cylindrical rotation \(\Omega = \Omega_{\rm ref}(1 + \varepsilon s^2)\), with \(\Omega_{\rm ref}\) the rate on the axis:

par.thermal = 0
par.diff_rot_type = 'shellular';   par.diff_rot_param = -0.5   # σ: ΔΩ = r^σ - 1
par.diff_rot_type = 'cylindrical'; par.diff_rot_ampl = -0.4    # ε: ΔΩ = ε r² sin²θ

Result. For the 12 modes compared, the frequencies agree to about \(10^{-4}\) and the damping rates to about 1 %, once kore's resolution is sufficient. Two modes differ more: one in a cluster of modes that does not settle with resolution, and an unstable mode whose growth rate is a few percent lower. Two modes at the smallest Ekman numbers need too much memory and were not computed.

docs.title: Guenel et al. 2016
docs.text:
A&A 589, A22. Conical rotation \(\Omega = \Omega_{\rm ref}(1 + \varepsilon\sin^2\theta)\), in the frame rotating at the pole:

par.thermal = 0
par.diff_rot_type = 'conical'; par.diff_rot_ampl = -0.25      # ε
par.ricb = 0.71

Result. For the 7 modes compared, the frequencies agree to about \(10^{-4}\) and six damping or growth rates to about 1 %, including an unstable mode with a corotation layer. The seventh sits in a cluster of modes and is a few percent off in damping rate.

docs.title: Mirouh et al. 2016
docs.text:
JFM 800, 213. A stably stratified Boussinesq fluid with \(N^2\) uniform, \(g = r\), the temperature fixed at both walls, and the rotation \(\Omega = \Omega_{\rm ref}\left[1 + \tfrac{N^2}{2}(1 - r^2)\right]\):

par.thermal = 1; par.stratification = 'linear'               # dS/dr = r, so the buoyancy frequency is N² r² with g = r
par.bci_thermal = par.bco_thermal = 0
par.Beyonce = 1.5                                            # their N²
par.ThermaD = 1e-7                                           # their E/P
par.diff_rot_type = 'shellular_boussinesq'; par.diff_rot_ampl = 1.5   # N² again

thermal_wind = 0 is required: their background is balanced by centrifugal buoyancy, which kore does not carry.

Result. Of the 14 modes, 13 are identified. Their frequencies agree to about \(10^{-4}\), and most damping or growth rates to about 1 %. One mode at the smallest Ekman number needs more memory than was available, and a growing mode in a dense cluster of modes is not identified.

docs.title: The Sun
docs.text: These papers solve the fully compressible equations about solar Model S, whereas kore is anelastic. The common set-up: the Model S density, viscosity and thermal diffusivity of \(10^{12}\) cm² s⁻¹, an adiabatic convection zone, stress-free walls, a frame rotating at 456 nHz, and their rotation profile. "With the thermal wind" means thermal_wind = 2 with thermal_wind_radial = 0, as in the papers.

docs.title: Mukhopadhyay et al. 2025a
docs.text:
A&A, arXiv 2501.16797. The convection zone, 0.71–0.985 R☉, with their tabulated rotation, the file data/diff_rot.npz of their data set (doi:10.17617/3.NP26AI):

import units
par.timescale = 'rotation'; par.set_scales()
par.structure = 'old model S prototype'                  # the Model S density
par.r_out = 0.985; par.ricb = 0.71/0.985
par.thermal = 1
par.stratification = 'odd top hat'                       # with aux5 = 0: dS/dr = 0
par.aux1, par.aux2, par.aux3, par.aux4, par.aux5 = 0.0, 0.1, 0.68, 0.06, 0.0
par.bci = par.bco = 0; par.bci_thermal = par.bco_thermal = 1
par.diff_rot = 1; par.diff_rot_type = 'tabulated'; par.diff_rot_file = 'diff_rot.npz'
par.diff_rot_nmax = 12
par.thermal_wind = 2; par.thermal_wind_radial = 0
units.set_physical(par, frame_nHz=456.0, nu=1e12, kappa=1e12)   # Gaspard, Beyonce, ViscosD, ThermaD, diff_rot_frame
par.N = 64; par.lmax = par.m + 63

tests/diff_rot/mk_bekki.py NAME m=… symm=… file=… builds this run for any \(m\) and symmetry, and solve_bekki.py NAME FREQ GROWTH solves it near a frequency and growth rate in nHz. run_bekki.py DIFF_ROT_NPZ runs the five modes below (about a minute each, one core).

Result. For the \(m = 3\) Rossby modes, the \(m = 3\) columnar mode, the \(m = 10\) high-frequency retrograde mode and the unstable \(m = 1\) high-latitude mode, kore agrees with the compressible results to within 0.2 nHz in frequency and 0.4 nHz in growth rate. This needs the thermal wind: without it, the frequencies are off by up to about 10 nHz and the high-latitude mode is stable.

docs.title: Bekki et al. 2024
docs.text:
The high-latitude mode of the previous set-up becomes baroclinically unstable when the poles are warm enough. With thermal_wind = 3 the latitudinal entropy gradient is prescribed, \(\partial_\theta S_{tw}\) = dSdtheta \(\sin 2\theta\), with dSdtheta \(= \Delta_\theta s/c_p\) (negative: warm poles):

tests/diff_rot/mk_bekki.py RUN tw=3 ds=-1000 file=diff_rot.npz m=1 symm=-1
tests/diff_rot/solve_bekki.py RUN -93 5

with ds = \(\Delta_\theta s\) in erg g⁻¹ K⁻¹.

Result. The \(m = 1\) high-latitude mode becomes unstable at a latitudinal entropy difference of about 400 to 550 erg g⁻¹ K⁻¹, depending on the rotation profile used; the published value is about 500. The radial shear in the lower convection zone sets the onset.

docs.title: Mukhopadhyay et al. 2025b
docs.text:
A&A 708, A253. The convection zone extended down to 0.5 R☉ with their stably stratified, rigidly rotating radiative interior:

par.ricb = 0.5/0.985
par.solar_density_window = 'sun'                                # one Model S fit over the whole Sun
par.stratification = 'solar_rz'; par.diffusivity = 'solar_rz'   # their eqs. (8)-(10)
par.visc0, par.therm0 = 0.01, 0.04                              # ν and κ below 0.70 R☉, relative to the convection zone
par.diff_rot_type = 'solar_P4'                                  # their eqs. (5)-(6)
par.bci_thermal = 1; par.bco_thermal = 0                        # zero entropy flux at the bottom, s = 0 at the top
par.N = 128

the rest as above. tests/diff_rot/mk_rz.py NAME rin=0.5 m=… symm=… builds it for any inner radius rin (in R☉, 0 for the full sphere). tests/diff_rot/solar_checks.py DIFF_ROT_NPZ runs the modes of both Mukhopadhyay papers, with and without the thermal wind (about 40 minutes on one core).

Result. Without the thermal wind, all the convection-zone and mixed modes that can be identified agree with the paper to about 0.1 nHz. With the thermal wind they are a few nHz off, which suggests that the paper's runs with a radiative interior had no latitudinal entropy gradient. The paper's two high-latitude modes are not matched.

docs.title: Background flow equations
docs.text: This page gives the background flow of bgflow = 1 (Background flow), the terms it adds to the perturbation equations, how they become rows, what happens at the walls, the powers that spin_doctor reports, and the Newton's method that gives the nonlinear flow of turning walls. They hold for any density, in a shell or a full sphere, with the entropy, the composition and the magnetic field (bin/bgflow.py).

docs.title: The background
docs.text:
The background is written as the perturbations are (Numerical method), with a poloidal and a toroidal scalar for each degree, so that it carries no mass across a sphere whatever its scalars:

\[ \mathbf U = \mathrm{Ro} hinspace G\sum_n\left[ rac{1}{ ho_0} abla imes abla imes( ho_0 P_n Y_n hinspace\mathbf r) + abla imes(T_n Y_n hinspace\mathbf r) ight], \qquad S_U = \mathrm{Ro}\sum_n\sigma_n Y_n, \qquad C_U = \mathrm{Ro}\sum_n\gamma_n Y_n , \]

with \(Y_n\) the Legendre polynomial of degree \(n\) in \(\cos heta\), \(\mathrm{Ro}\) = bgflow_Ro, \(G\) = Gaspard (1 when Gaspard = 0), and \( abla\cdot( ho_0\mathbf U) = 0\). \(S_U\) and \(C_U\) are the entropy and the composition that the flow brought about in the run that made it. With \(\lambda_1 = (\ln ho_0)'\) and a prime for \(d/dr\), the components are

\[ U_r = \mathrm{Ro} hinspace G\sum_n rac{n(n+1)P_n}{r}Y_n, \qquad U_ heta = \mathrm{Ro} hinspace G\sum_n\left(P_n' + rac{P_n}{r} + \lambda_1 P_n ight)\partial_ heta Y_n, \qquad U_\phi = -\mathrm{Ro} hinspace G\sum_n T_n hinspace\partial_ heta Y_n . \]

\(T_1 = r\) is a rotation at the rate \(\mathrm{Ro} hinspace G\), and at Ro = 1 \(T_1 = (f_0 - f_2/5) hinspace r\), \(T_3 = f_2 hinspace r/5\) is the differential rotation \(\Delta\Omega = f_0 + f_2 Y_2\) of diff_rot. The poloidal scalars make the meridional circulation. The vorticity \( oldsymbol\Omega_U = abla imes\mathbf U\) follows degree by degree: \(\Omega_\phi = \mathrm{Ro} hinspace G\left[(rs_n)'/r - n(n+1)P_n/r^2 ight]\partial_ heta Y_n\) from \(P_n\), with \(s_n = P_n' + P_n/r + \lambda_1 P_n\), and \(\Omega_r = \mathrm{Ro} hinspace G hinspace n(n+1)T_n Y_n/r\), \(\Omega_ heta = \mathrm{Ro} hinspace G hinspace(rT_n)' hinspace\partial_ heta Y_n/r\) from \(T_n\).

Like the perturbations, the background is symmetric about the equator: \(P_n\), \(\sigma_n\), \(\gamma_n\) of even \(n\) and \(T_n\) of odd \(n\).

docs.title: The terms
docs.text:
The perturbation equations, linearised about \(\mathbf U\), \(S_U\) and \(C_U\), gain the advection of the perturbation by the background and of the background by the perturbation. The momentum equation gains

\[ (\mathbf U\cdot abla)\mathbf u + (\mathbf u\cdot abla)\mathbf U = abla(\mathbf U\cdot\mathbf u) - \mathbf U imes oldsymbol\omega - \mathbf u imes oldsymbol\Omega_U , \qquad oldsymbol\omega = abla imes\mathbf u , \]

on the side of the inertia; the gradient joins the pressure and leaves the rows, which take the curl and the double curl of the equation. The heat and the composition equations gain

\[ p_0\left(\mathbf U\cdot abla s + \mathbf u\cdot abla S_U ight), \qquad ho_0\left(\mathbf U\cdot abla c + \mathbf u\cdot abla C_U ight) \]

on the side of \(\partial_t\), and the induction equation gains \( abla imes(\mathbf U imes\mathbf b)\) on the side of the induction. The background itself is held fixed: what keeps \(\mathbf U\), \(S_U\) and \(C_U\) steady (the walls, the buoyancy of \(S_U\) and \(C_U\), the advection of \(\mathbf U\) by itself) belongs to the equations of the background, not to those of the perturbation.

docs.title: Rows and implementation
docs.text:
This section says how the terms become radial operators and where they sit in the matrices. It matters only to change or extend the code.

  • Angular couplings. The background vectors are polynomials in \(\cos heta\) times \(\hat{\mathbf r}\), \(\sin heta hinspace\hat{ oldsymbol heta}\) or \(\sin heta hinspace\hat{ oldsymbol\phi}\), and their products with the perturbation are sparse matrices over the degrees, built exactly with the recurrence algebra of angular.py, as for a background field (Magnetic field equations): a degree \(n\) of \(\mathbf U\) couples the degree \(l\) of a row to \(l'\) with \(\lvert l - l' vert \le n + 1\). bgflow.build writes each term as a sum of radial monomials times these matrices, in kore's rows: \(r^5 ho_0\) and \(r^3 ho_0\) times \(\hat{\mathbf r}\cdot abla imes abla imes\) and \(\hat{\mathbf r}\cdot abla imes\) of the momentum equation (sections u, v), \(r^2\) times the heat and composition equations (h, c), and the rows f, g of the induction.

  • Labels and profile codes. A monomial \(r^p hinspace w_B^{(j)} hinspace X^{(d)}\) of a row is the label {row}{q}w{B}{n}{j}[lho{k} | pss0 | dns0]_D{d}, with \(q\) the power of the row minus \(p\), \(w_B\) a profile code of degree \(n\) and its \(j\)-th derivative, lho{k} a factor \((\ln ho_0)^{(k)}\), pss0 and dns0 a factor \(p_0\) or \( ho_0\), and \(X^{(d)}\) the \(d\)-th derivative of the unknown. For example v2wt10_D1 is \(r hinspace\mathrm{Ro} hinspace G hinspace T_1 P_l'\) in the rows of \(T_l\), times its angular coefficient. The profile codes, per degree \(n\) (one character, 0–9 then a–z: degrees up to 35), are

    code profile wq \(\mathrm{Ro} hinspace G hinspace n(n+1)P_n/r\) ws \(\mathrm{Ro} hinspace G\left(P_n' + P_n/r + \lambda_1 P_n ight)\) wt \(\mathrm{Ro} hinspace G hinspace T_n\) wh, wd \(\mathrm{Ro} hinspace p_0\sigma_n\), \(\mathrm{Ro} hinspace p_0\sigma_n'\) (without \(p_0\) where the heat rows are divided by it) wc, we \(\mathrm{Ro} hinspace ho_0\gamma_n\), \(\mathrm{Ro} hinspace ho_0\gamma_n'\) (without \( ho_0\) where the rows of the composition are divided by it)

  • Assembly. assemble.bgflow_blocks places the blocks of each row degree for every \(\Delta l\) up to the largest degree of the background plus one, in the rows u, v (columns \(P\), \(T\)), h (\(s\), \(P\), \(T\)), c (\(c\), \(P\), \(T\)) and f, g (columns of the field). operators.background_flow returns each block as the sum of the angular coefficients times the radial operators, divided by \(\mathcal L^3\) of the row as every operator.

  • Without diffusion. With ThermaD = 0 the heat rows are \(r^2( ext{eq})/p_0\) in the \(C^{(1)}\) basis, as with the thermal wind (Differential rotation): \(\mathbf u\cdot abla S_U\) holds \(u_ heta\), which holds \(P_l'\), and \(\mathbf U\cdot abla s\) holds \(U_ heta\partial_ heta s/r\). With CompoD = 0 the rows of the composition are \(r^2( ext{eq})/ ho_0\) in \(C^{(1)}\) in the same way.
  • Inviscid runs (ViscosD = 0, full sphere). The terms hold \(P_l'''\) in the rows u and \(P_l''\) in the rows v, so these rows are in \(C^{(3)}\) and \(C^{(2)}\) and are \(r^5 ho_0^2\) and \(r^3 ho_0\) times the equations, as with a magnetic field.
  • Full sphere. Each scalar has the parity \((-1)^n\) of its degree, and the codes wq, ws, wd, we the opposite one. An expression is evaluated at \(\lvert r vert\) with that parity and interpolated at the Chebyshev–Lobatto points of \([-1, 1]\) (of \([r_i, 1]\) in a shell), so that a scalar that vanishes at the wall vanishes there to round-off. A scalar of degree \(n\) is smooth at the centre if it goes as \(r^n\) times a series in \(r^2\); submatrices.py warns for each one that does not (Regularity at the centre).

docs.title: The walls
docs.text:
kore's walls are impenetrable, so the background must not cross them: \(P_n = 0\) at each wall, which submatrices.py checks to \(10^{-10}\) of the largest \(\lvert P_n\rvert\), \(\lvert T_n\rvert\). A conducting solid at a wall (an inner core, a thin conducting layer, a resolved mantle) carries its field along as a solid body, so the background must turn rigidly there: \(P_n = P_n' = 0\), and \(T_n = 0\) for \(n \neq 1\). The solid then turns with the fluid at the wall, at

\[ \Omega_w = \mathrm{Ro}\thinspace G\thinspace\frac{T_1(r_w)}{r_w} \]

relative to the frame, and the equation of its field gains the advection by that rotation, \(-i\thinspace m\thinspace \Omega_w\thinspace\mathbf b\) (bgflow.rigid_rate, added as for a differential rotation). The Bessel inner core and spin_doctor's energies of the solids use the frequency in the frame of the solid.

With a background field \(\mathbf B_0\) the linear problem also assumes that the field is steady under the background flow. bgflow.steadiness reports

\[ \max\lvert\nabla\times(\mathbf U\times\mathbf B_0)\rvert\thinspace r \Big/ \left(\max\lvert\mathbf U\rvert\max\lvert\mathbf B_0\rvert\right) \]

on a grid of the fluid (with the flow of a differential rotation added), and warns above \(10^{-7}\), or stops with ferraro_policy = 'refuse'. A rotation about the axis keeps an axisymmetric field steady when the rotation rate is constant along the field lines (Magnetic field equations), so a rigid rotation keeps any of them.

docs.title: Energy budgets
docs.text:
spin_doctor adds the background's terms to the budgets of Energy balance, computed on a grid of Gauss–Legendre points in \(\cos heta\) that makes the angular products exact (utils4pp.bgflow_setup):

\[ W_\mathrm{bg} = -2 hinspace\mathrm{Re}\int ho_0 hinspace\mathbf u^*\cdot\left[(\mathbf U\cdot abla)\mathbf u + (\mathbf u\cdot abla)\mathbf U ight] dV , \]

its imaginary part, and the enstrophy term of the same force. The part of \((\mathbf U\cdot abla)\mathbf u\) has no real part, \(\mathrm{Re}\int ho_0 hinspace\mathbf u^*\cdot(\mathbf U\cdot abla)\mathbf u hinspace dV = frac12\int ho_0 hinspace\mathbf U\cdot abla\lvert\mathbf u vert^2 hinspace dV = 0\), since \( abla\cdot( ho_0\mathbf U) = 0\) and \(\mathbf U\) runs along the walls: \(W_\mathrm{bg}\) is the power that the perturbation draws from the shear of the background through \((\mathbf u\cdot abla)\mathbf U\). In the same way \(\mathbf r imes[(\mathbf U\cdot abla)\mathbf u + (\mathbf u\cdot abla)\mathbf U] = (\mathbf U\cdot abla)(\mathbf r imes\mathbf u) + (\mathbf u\cdot abla)(\mathbf r imes\mathbf U)\), whose integral with \( ho_0\) is a flux through the walls, zero when neither flow crosses them: the background puts no torque in the fluid, and the budget of its angular momentum (resid𝐋, axial and equatorial) holds as without it. The heat and composition budgets gain

\[ W_\mathrm{bg}^{s} = -2 hinspace\mathrm{Re}\int p_0 hinspace s^*\left(\mathbf U\cdot abla s + \mathbf u\cdot abla S_U ight) dV , \qquad W_\mathrm{bg}^{c} = -2 hinspace\mathrm{Re}\int ho_0 hinspace c^*\left(\mathbf U\cdot abla c + \mathbf u\cdot abla C_U ight) dV . \]

The force is computed with its gradient \( abla(\mathbf U\cdot\mathbf u)\), so that the pressure that spin_doctor derives from the momentum equation, and its power at the walls, are the physical ones. The columns are in Output files.

docs.title: Newton's method
docs.text:
The nonlinear flow of turning walls is the steady solution of the full axisymmetric equations, in which the flow also carries itself and its entropy and composition along. bgflow.py finds it with kore's own matrices. For \(m = 0\) the fields of a forced run are \(\mathbf x + \mathrm{c.c.} = 2\mathbf x\), so the steady problem reads

\[ A\mathbf x + \tfrac12 B(2\mathbf x)\thinspace\mathbf x = \mathbf b , \]

with \(A\mathbf x = \mathbf b\) the linear problem of forcing 12 and \(B(\mathbf V)\) the matrix of the terms of a background \(\mathbf V\). \(B(\mathbf V)\mathbf w\) is linear and symmetric in its two flows, so \(B(2\mathbf x)\) is also the Jacobian of the quadratic term, and a Newton step is

\[ \left(A + B_k\right)\mathbf x_{k+1} = \mathbf b + \tfrac12 B_k\thinspace\mathbf x_k, \qquad B_k = B(2\mathbf x_k), \]

with every degree of \(\mathbf x_k\) in \(B_k\). \(B_k\) is the matrix of a run with bgflow = 1 and the background \(2\mathbf x_k\) minus that of the same run at bgflow_Ro = 0, so that both have the same rows and bases. Ro rises from 0 in steps of at most 0.15, each starting from the flow of the last step with its part of order \(\mathrm{Ro}^2\) scaled to the new Ro, and the iterations of a step stop when one moves \(\mathbf x\) by less than \(10^{-9}\) of itself. The matrices of \(m = 0\) couple every degree of the background with every other, so the solves are dense. At Ek \(10^{-3}\) and Ro 1 (the example), each step takes three or four iterations, the change squaring at each, and the flow differs from Ro times the linear flow by 6%.

docs.title: The file
docs.text:
bgflow.py nmax [nonlinear] writes bgflow.npz:

key content nP, P; nT, T the degrees \(n \le\) nmax and the Chebyshev coefficients of \(P_n\), \(T_n\) per unit Ro, one row per degree, on \([r_i, 1]\) (on \([-1, 1]\), of parity \((-1)^n\), in a full sphere) nS, S; nC, C the same for \(\sigma_n\) and \(\gamma_n\), with thermal = 1 and compositional = 1 ricb the radius of the inner wall rho_r, rho the density at 8 radii: the poloidal flow is that density's wall, ratio the wall that turned ('inner' or 'outer'), and the rate of the other relative to it Ro for a nonlinear flow, the Ro it holds at

P and T are the scalars of the run's flow divided by the rate of the wall in units of \(1/\tau\), and \(\sigma_n\), \(\gamma_n\) those of its entropy and composition divided by that rate over \(G\).

docs.title: Background flow
docs.text:
With bgflow = 1 the fluid carries a steady, axisymmetric background flow, and kore computes the waves and instabilities on top of it. Differential rotation (diff_rot = 1, Background model) is the special case of a purely azimuthal flow. A background flow can also circulate in the meridional plane (up along the axis and back near the walls, or the reverse), and its rotation can have shapes that diff_rot cannot describe.

The main use is the flow driven by turning walls, computed by kore itself in a Spherical Couette flow run. You can also give the flow as expressions of the radius.

docs.title: What it adds
docs.text:
The background flow carries the perturbations and is distorted by them. kore adds both effects to the momentum, heat, composition and induction equations. The background may also have its own entropy and composition, which the perturbation flow then carries too.

The background flow is written as

\[ \mathbf U = \mathrm{Ro} hinspace\mathrm{Gaspard}\sum_n\left[ ho_0^{-1} abla imes abla imes( ho_0 P_n Y_n hinspace\mathbf r) + abla imes(T_n Y_n hinspace\mathbf r) ight], \]

where \(Y_n\) is the Legendre polynomial of degree \(n\) in \(\cos heta\), \(P_n(r)\) and \(T_n(r)\) are the poloidal and toroidal radial functions, and Ro = bgflow_Ro is the strength of the flow relative to the rotation rate of the frame. The equations are in Background flow equations.

The background flow must:

  • be symmetric about the equator;
  • not cross the walls;
  • turn rigidly at a conducting solid (a conducting inner core, thin conducting layer or resolved mantle), so that the solid can turn with the fluid.

It works with any structure, in a shell or a full sphere, with differential rotation, a magnetic field, conducting solids, the constant drag at the outer wall, the forcings and the free decay. It does not work with the centrifugal deformation, the rotating solids or the topographic drag.

With a magnetic field, the background field is in general not steady under the background flow. submatrices.py prints how far it is from steady and warns when the mismatch is significant: the linear problem assumes that something maintains the background.

docs.title: A background from turning walls
docs.text:
Run a Spherical Couette flow (forcing 12), then, in its folder,

python3 bin/bgflow.py 12

This writes bgflow.npz, holding the flow up to Legendre degree 12, normalized to Ro = 1. Copy it to the folder of the run that uses it, and set bgflow = 1 and the Ro you want. A maximum degree of about 12 is usually enough; thinner boundary layers, at lower Ekman numbers, need more.

This linear flow is accurate only for small Ro. At larger Ro the flow carries its own momentum, which the linear equations leave out. With

python3 bin/bgflow.py 12 nonlinear

kore solves the full steady equations of the axisymmetric flow at the Ro of the run (forcing_amplitude_icb over Gaspard) by Newton's method (Background flow equations). The file is then valid only at that Ro, and a run that reads it must set bgflow_Ro to that value.

The file also records the density, ricb and which wall turned, and kore stops if a run reads it with incompatible parameters. With thermal = 1 or compositional = 1 it also holds the background entropy and composition that the flow produced. bgflow.py does not support runs with a magnetic field.

docs.title: Example: waves on the flow of an inner core that turns
docs.text:
The flow of Spherical Couette flow at Ek \(10^{-3}\), nonlinear at Ro = 1 (the inner core turning at twice the rate of the frame), and the waves of \(m = 2\) on it. First the flow: write in bin/parameters.py

from params_default import default_params

par = default_params()

par.timescale = 'rotation'
par.Ek = 1e-3
par.set_scales()

par.structure = 'Boussinesq'
par.ricb = 0.35
par.bci = 1
par.bco = 1

par.m = 0
par.symm = 1
par.N = 48
par.lmax = 31
par.ncpus = 2

par.forcing = 12
par.forcing_frequency = 0.0
par.forcing_amplitude_icb = 1.0
par.forcing_amplitude_cmb = 0.0

and run

./bin/submatrices.py 2
mpiexec -n 2 ./bin/assemble.py
mpiexec -n 2 ./bin/solve.py
python3 bin/bgflow.py 12 nonlinear

Then, in a new folder with that bgflow.npz, use the same parameters with

par.m = 2
par.lmax = 29
par.forcing = 0
par.itau = 1.0

par.bgflow = 1
par.bgflow_Ro = 1.0

and run submatrices.py, assemble.py, solve.py and spin_doctor.py. The eigenvalue nearest \(1i\) is \(-0.1818 + 1.1437i\) with the flow, compared with \(-0.2687 + 0.9803i\) without it. The example takes a couple of minutes, most of it in Newton's method.

docs.title: A background from expressions
docs.text:
With bgflow_profiles the background is given as numpy expressions of r (and ricb), one per radial function and degree, normalized to Ro = 1:

par.bgflow = 1
par.bgflow_Ro = 0.3
par.bgflow_profiles = {'P2': '0.2*(r-ricb)**2*(1-r)**2',   # a meridional cell in each hemisphere
                       'T1': '0.5*r',                      # a rotation
                       'T3': '(r-ricb)*(1-r)*r',            # and its shear
                       'S2': '0.05*(r-ricb)*(1-r)'}         # an entropy of degree 2 (thermal = 1)

Each key is a letter and a degree: P and T for the poloidal and toroidal flow, S for the entropy, C for the composition. Poloidal, entropy and composition terms take even degrees, toroidal terms odd degrees. In this example the flow does not cross the walls and turns rigidly there, so the walls may be conducting. In a full sphere the expressions must be smooth at the centre (Regularity at the centre).

docs.title: Resolution
docs.text:
A background flow can make the waves much harder to resolve than in a fluid at rest:

  • The flow strains the waves. A meridional circulation can squeeze the waves into thin layers, for instance at the centre of a full sphere, and the radial resolution N must be raised until the spin_doctor residuals are small.
  • Without diffusion, the flow creates ever finer structure. Without thermal or compositional diffusion, or without viscosity, the background carries the perturbation along its streamlines with nothing to smooth it. This gives a band of frequencies where modes do not converge. Put the target outside that band, and keep only the modes that stay put when N and lmax are raised. For forced runs without diffusion kore stops in such cases (Combining features).

As with any run, compare two resolutions and check spin_doctor's residuals (Numerical method).

docs.title: Output
docs.text: spin_doctor.py adds the power exchanged with the background flow to the budgets: in flow.dat the power that the perturbation draws from the background, Wbg (columns 46–48), and in thermal.dat and composition.dat the work of its advection (column 8). A growing mode takes its energy from there. params.dat records bgflow and bgflow_Ro, and the expressions or the name of the file (Output files).

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: parameter meaning bgflow 1 for a background flow bgflow_Ro its strength Ro, relative to the rotation rate of the frame; a nonlinear file is valid only at its own Ro bgflow_file the file of the background, 'bgflow.npz' by default, read when bgflow_profiles is empty bgflow_profiles the background as expressions, {'P2': '...', 'T1': '...', ...}, normalized to Ro = 1; no # in them

docs.title: Centrifugal deformation equations
docs.text: This page gives the mathematics behind centrifugal = 1, for readers who want to check the code or extend it: the coordinates that follow the level surfaces, the equations in them and their rows, the magnetic field, the dissipative terms, the differential rotation, the exact spheroid, the flattening of each shape, the effective gravity, the energy budgets, the plots, the accuracy, and the checks. How to set up a run is on Background model. The code is in bin/centrifugal.py, the checks in tests/centrifugal/.

docs.title: Coordinates that follow the level surfaces
docs.text:
kore's flow conserves mass exactly only when the density depends on the radius alone. In a flattened body the density is constant on spheroids, so rather than give every profile a part that depends on latitude, kore maps the body onto a reference space in which the level surfaces are spheres.

A point \( oldsymbol\alpha\) of the reference space, at radius \(r\) and colatitude \( heta\), is at \(\mathbf X = oldsymbol\alpha + oldsymbol\xi\) in the body, with

\[ oldsymbol\xi = \varepsilon(r) hinspace abla\left( frac12 r^2P_2(\cos heta) ight) = \varepsilon(r) hinspace r\left[P_2 hinspace\hat{\mathbf r} + frac12 rac{dP_2}{d heta} hinspace\hat{ oldsymbol heta} ight], \qquad \varepsilon = - frac23 f , \]

where \(f(r)\) is the flattening of the level surface \(r\), positive for an oblate body. At first order that surface is at the distance \(r(1 + \varepsilon P_2)\) from the centre: its flattening is \(f\) and its volume that of the sphere of radius \(r\). In Cartesian components \( oldsymbol\xi = \varepsilon(r) hinspace(-\alpha_x/2, -\alpha_y/2, \alpha_z)\), an axisymmetric stretch at each radius, so the map is smooth at the centre when \(\varepsilon\) is even and smooth in \(r\); a purely radial \( oldsymbol\xi\) would not be. Every background profile is a function of \(r\), and the walls are the level surfaces \(r\) = ricb and \(r = 1\).

With the deformation gradient \(\mathsf F = \partial\mathbf X/\partial oldsymbol\alpha = \mathsf I + abla oldsymbol\xi\) and \(J = \det\mathsf F\), kore's poloidal and toroidal scalars describe the flow carried back to the reference space,

\[ \mathbf w = J hinspace\mathsf F^{-1}\mathbf u . \]

This transform keeps what kore's formulation relies on. Mass: \( abla_\alpha\cdot( ho_0\mathbf w) = J hinspace abla_X\cdot( ho_0\mathbf u)\), so the exact \( abla\cdot( ho_0\mathbf w) = 0\) of kore's scalars is exact mass conservation in the body. Walls: \(\mathbf u\cdot\mathbf n\) is proportional to \(w_r\) on a level surface, and \(\mathbf u = 0\) where \(\mathbf w = 0\), so the impenetrable and no-slip rows are unchanged.

docs.title: Equations
docs.text:
kore removes the pressure by taking curls of the momentum equation. In the reference space this works when the equation is written with covariant components, \(\mathsf F^{\mathsf T}\) times it: the pressure force stays a gradient, \(\mathsf F^{\mathsf T} abla_X\Pi = abla_\alpha\Pi\). So does the buoyancy, which acts along the gradient of the effective potential, constant on the level surfaces. The dimensionless equations of Anelastic equations become

\[ \mathsf M hinspace\partial_t\mathbf w + 2 hinspace\mathrm{Gaspard} hinspace ilde{\mathbf z} imes\mathbf w = - abla\Pi + \mathrm{Beyonce} hinspace g_{ m eff} hinspace s hinspace\hat{\mathbf r} + \dots , \qquad \mathsf M = rac{\mathsf F^{\mathsf T}\mathsf F}{J}, \quad ilde{\mathbf z} = \mathsf F^{-1}\hat{\mathbf z}, \] \[ p_0\left(J hinspace\partial_t s + w_r rac{dS}{dr} ight) = \dots , \]

with the dots the viscous force and the thermal diffusion, which take covariant forms too (Dissipative terms). Three terms of the ideal fluid change: the inertia gains the metric \(\mathsf M\), the Coriolis force turns with the map (\(\mathsf F^{\mathsf T}(\hat{\mathbf z} imes\mathsf F\mathbf w)/J = ilde{\mathbf z} imes\mathbf w\)), and the rate of change of the entropy gains \(J\). The advection keeps its form, \(\mathbf u\cdot abla_X S = w_r S'/J\), and the buoyancy takes the effective gravity \(g_{ m eff}\) (below).

At first order. With \(\eta = r\varepsilon'\) and \(w_z = \hat{\mathbf z}\cdot\mathbf w\),

\[ (\mathsf M - \mathsf I) hinspace\mathbf w = \varepsilon\left(3w_z\hat{\mathbf z} - \mathbf w ight) + \eta\left[ frac32\cos heta\left(w_z\hat{\mathbf r} + w_r\hat{\mathbf z} ight) - w_r\hat{\mathbf r} - P_2 hinspace\mathbf w ight], \] \[ ( ilde{\mathbf z} - \hat{\mathbf z}) imes\mathbf w = -\varepsilon hinspace\hat{\mathbf z} imes\mathbf w - \eta\left[ frac32\cos^2 heta hinspace\hat{\mathbf z} imes\mathbf w - frac12\cos heta hinspace\hat{\mathbf r} imes\mathbf w ight], \] \[ J - 1 = \eta hinspace P_2 . \]

A uniform flattening has \(\eta = 0\): the map is then a linear stretch, and \(J = 1\) at this order.

docs.title: Rows
docs.text:
The new terms have the form of the force of a differential rotation, so kore builds them with the same tools. Each one multiplies the components of \(\mathbf w\) by polynomials in \(\cos\theta\) of degree 2 at most, with the radial factor \(\varepsilon\) or \(\eta\); kore builds their couplings with the recurrence algebra of bin/angular.py and projects them on its rows as it does the force (Spectral form), without the terms that come from the shear of the rotation.

  • Selection rules. A degree \(l\) couples to \(l\) and \(l \pm 2\) of the same kind (poloidal to poloidal, toroidal to toroidal, entropy to entropy), and to \(l \pm 1\) and \(l \pm 3\) of the other kind (poloidal to toroidal).
  • Matrices. \(A\) gains \(2\thinspace\mathrm{Gaspard}\thinspace(\tilde{\mathbf z} - \hat{\mathbf z})\times\mathbf w\) in the momentum rows. \(B\) gains \(-(\mathsf M - \mathsf I)\thinspace\mathbf w\) in the momentum rows and \((J - 1)\thinspace s = \eta P_2\thinspace s\) in the heat rows, with the signs of the inertia and of the entropy. The poloidal–toroidal couplings of the inertia are imaginary, so \(B\) is complex.
  • Radial operators. Their labels are those of the differential rotation with the profile code of \(\varepsilon\) (ce0) or \(\eta\) (ce1) in place of that of \(\Delta\Omega\), and that of \(r\varepsilon'\) (ce1) or \(r\eta'\) (ce2) for the derivative terms (centrifugal.MOMENTUM).
