docs.title: Spherical Couette flow
docs.text: Forcing 12 turns the walls steadily about the rotation axis, each at its own rate, and kore returns the steady flow they drive through the viscosity of the fluid: the spherical Couette flow. An inner core that turns slightly faster or slower than the mantle drives such a flow, as do the spheres of a laboratory experiment.

docs.title: What it imposes
docs.text:
The outer wall turns at the rate forcing_amplitude_cmb and the inner wall at forcing_amplitude_icb, relative to the rotating frame. A wall that turns must be no-slip (bco or bci = 1), so that the fluid next to it turns with it. A wall at rest may also be stress-free (bco or bci = 0); the fluid then slips along it, held back only by a drag if there is one (Drag at the outer wall).

The equations are linear, so the flow is proportional to the rates. This is the limit of small differences in rotation.

Requirements:

  • forcing_frequency = 0, m = 0 and symm = 1 (for walls that turn back and forth, see Libration);
  • a viscous fluid (ViscosD > 0);
  • with buoyancy, its diffusion (ThermaD > 0 with thermal = 1, CompoD > 0 with compositional = 1).

In a full sphere (ricb = 0) only the outer wall can turn, and the fluid simply turns with it. Any structure, differential rotation, a background flow and a magnetic field work; with a field, a conducting inner core or mantle turns with its wall (Magnetic field).

docs.title: Example: an inner core that turns
docs.text:
Write in bin/parameters.py

from params_default import default_params

par = default_params()

par.timescale = 'rotation'
par.Ek = 1e-4
par.set_scales()                  # Gaspard = 1, ViscosD = Ek

# incompressible fluid between an inner core and the mantle, no-slip walls
par.structure = 'Boussinesq'
par.ricb = 0.35
par.bci = 1
par.bco = 1

# axisymmetric and equatorially symmetric
par.m = 0
par.symm = 1

par.N = 96
par.lmax = 191
par.ncpus = 2

# the inner core turns steadily, the mantle with the frame
par.forcing = 12
par.forcing_frequency = 0.0
par.forcing_amplitude_icb = 1.0
par.forcing_amplitude_cmb = 0.0

and run

./bin/submatrices.py 2
mpiexec -n 2 ./bin/assemble.py
mpiexec -n 2 ./bin/solve.py
./bin/spin_doctor.py 2

It takes a few seconds.

The figure shows the angular velocity of the fluid relative to that of the inner core, in the northern hemisphere. Fast rotation makes the flow nearly uniform along the rotation axis, so away from the walls the fluid turns in coaxial cylinders. Outside the tangent cylinder (the cylinder that touches the equator of the inner core) each cylinder of fluid meets only the mantle, and turns with it: here, not at all. Inside, each cylinder is held between the thin boundary layers on the inner core and on the mantle, and turns at a rate in between: about half the rate of the inner core near the axis, faster towards the tangent cylinder. At very small Ekman numbers this approaches the solution of Proudman (1956),

\[ \frac{\omega}{\Omega_{IC}} = \frac{(1 - s^2)^{1/4}}{(1 - s^2)^{1/4} + (1 - s^2/r_i^2)^{1/4}}, \qquad s < r_i , \]

with \(s\) the distance from the axis and \(r_i\) the inner radius, and zero outside the tangent cylinder. A thin shear layer on the tangent cylinder, the Stewartson layer, smooths the jump between the two regions.

docs.title: Reading the output
docs.text:
The flow is in flow.npy (Output files); its imaginary part is zero, since the flow is steady. For m = 0 the angular velocity is

\[ \omega = \frac{u_\phi}{r\sin\theta} = \frac{2}{r}\sum_l T_l(r)\thinspace P_l'(\cos\theta) , \]

with the toroidal coefficients \(T_l(r)\), as on Thermal forcing.

spin_doctor checks the energy and angular momentum budgets. The power that the turning walls put in (P_in) is dissipated by viscosity, and by Ohmic losses with a field. Columns 31 and 33 of flow.dat are the viscous torques on the mantle and on the inner core, and 35 and 37 the magnetic ones (Output files). In the steady state the torques on the two solids cancel. When the fluid turns rigidly (both walls at the same rate, or a full sphere), nothing is sheared and the budget residuals compare round-off errors; they can then be close to 1 and should be ignored.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
parameter meaning forcing 12 forcing_frequency 0 forcing_amplitude_cmb the rotation rate of the outer wall, relative to the frame forcing_amplitude_icb the rotation rate of the inner wall (0 in a full sphere) m, symm 0, 1 bci, bco 1 for a wall that turns; 0 or 1 for a wall at rest

The flow can also be used as the background of other runs, to study its waves and instabilities (Background flow).

docs.title: Derivation tools
docs.text:
Kore builds its matrices block by block. A block couples a row of degree \(l'\) to a column of degree \(l = l' + \Delta l\), and it is a sum of radial operators (Chebyshev/Gegenbauer matrices, built by submatrices.py) times coefficients that depend on \(l\) and \(m\) (in operators.py and diff_rot.py). A spherically symmetric background couples each degree only to itself. Two backgrounds in kore depend on latitude, so they couple different degrees:

  • an imposed magnetic field \(\mathbf{B}_0\) (Magnetic field; equations: Magnetic field equations), part A of this page;
  • a differential rotation \(\Delta\Omega(r, heta)\) (Differential rotation), part B.

For each, this page explains why the coefficients are computed the way they are (motivation), the mathematics (method), which file and function does each step (implementation), how the result is checked and how far the checks reach (verification), and how to run the tools yourself (worked examples).

background where kore gets the coefficients how they were obtained how they are checked magnetic field closed forms in bin/operators.py (lorentz*, induction*) derived once from the definitions with sympy (tests/magnetic/derive.py), turned into formulas in \(l\), \(m\) (tools/derive/fit_rows.py) and into code (tools/derive/gen_table.py) tests/magnetic/derive_check.py, row_check.py, budget_check.py, bin/ru_insane.py, comparison with an independent code differential rotation computed while kore runs, by an exact recurrence algebra (bin/angular.py, bin/diff_rot.py) nothing to fit: the algebra is exact for any degree of \(\Delta\Omega\) tests/diff_rot/angular_check.py, gen_check.py (closed forms of diff_rot_coefficients.py), quad_reference.py, tests/heat_dr/tw_sympy.py

Prerequisites. Python 3 with numpy and scipy (kore's python environment), and sympy for the magnetic derivations (pip install sympy). The differential-rotation tools need no sympy, except tw_sympy.py. Commands are given from the repository root unless a run directory is named.

Notation. At a fixed azimuthal order \(m\) the angular functions are kore's Schmidt harmonics \(Y_l = \sqrt{4\pi/(2l+1)}\,Y_l^m\) (Condon–Shortley phase), with \(\int|Y_l|^2d\Omega = 4\pi/(2l+1)\); \(L = l(l+1)\), and \(L'\) is the \(L\) of the row. The flow and the magnetic field are

\[ \mathbf{u} = ho_0^{-1} abla imes abla imes( ho_0 P Y_l\mathbf{r}) + abla imes(T Y_l\mathbf{r}),\qquad \mathbf{b} = abla imes abla imes(F Y_l\mathbf{r}) + abla imes(G Y_l\mathbf{r}). \]

The rows of the momentum equation are its projections \(\hat{\mathbf{r}}\cdot abla imes abla imes\) (section u, the 2-curl) and \(\hat{\mathbf{r}}\cdot abla imes\) (section v, the 1-curl); those of the induction equation are \(\hat{\mathbf{r}}\cdot\) (section f) and \(\hat{\mathbf{r}}\cdot abla imes\) (section g).

docs.title: A. Operators involving the background magnetic field
A.1 Motivation
docs.text:
The Lorentz force and the induction,

\[ ( abla imes\mathbf{b}) imes\mathbf{B}_0 + ( abla imes\mathbf{B}_0) imes\mathbf{b} \qquad ext{and}\qquad abla imes(\mathbf{u} imes\mathbf{B}_0), \]

are products of a perturbation of degree \(l\) with a background of degree \(n\). Kore needs, for every pair of degrees, every radial term of these products, with its coefficient. With a variable density the factors \( ho_0\) and \( ho_0^{-1}\) add terms in \((\ln ho_0)'\) and \((\ln ho_0)''\). Done by hand, this algebra is long and easy to get wrong.

So the algebra is done by a program, once, from the definitions:

  • sympy derives each block exactly, for a given \((l, l', m)\) (tests/magnetic/derive.py). This needs no trust in a hand calculation or in another code.
  • The results are turned into formulas in \(l\) and \(m\) and written into bin/operators.py. Kore then evaluates formulas while it assembles. Calling sympy at run time instead would take seconds per block (there are thousands of blocks) and would make sympy a requirement of kore.

docs.title: A.2 Method
docs.text:
Step 1: derive one block. For the chosen background, poloidal \(\mathbf{B}_0 = abla imes abla imes(h Y_n^0\mathbf{r})\) or toroidal \(\mathbf{B}_0 = abla imes(k Y_n^0\mathbf{r})\) (\(n\) = 1 or 2), and a column field of degree \(l\), derive.py builds the row expression:

row equation expression u momentum, poloidal \( ho_0\hat{\mathbf{r}}\cdot abla imes abla imes( ho_0^{-1}\mathbf{G})\), \(\mathbf{G} = ( abla imes\mathbf{b}) imes\mathbf{B}_0 + ( abla imes\mathbf{B}_0) imes\mathbf{b}\) v momentum, toroidal \( ho_0\hat{\mathbf{r}}\cdot abla imes( ho_0^{-1}\mathbf{G})\) f induction, poloidal \(\hat{\mathbf{r}}\cdot abla imes(\mathbf{u} imes\mathbf{B}_0)\) g induction, toroidal \(\hat{\mathbf{r}}\cdot abla imes abla imes(\mathbf{u} imes\mathbf{B}_0)\)

The radial functions (\(P, T, F, G, h, k, \ln ho_0\)) stay symbolic; only \( heta\) is explicit. The expression is expanded into monomials, each a coefficient times \(r^p\) times derivatives of the unknown, of the background and of \(\ln ho_0\), for example \(r^{-2}\,h\,F'''\). The coefficient of each monomial still depends on \( heta\). It is projected on \(Y_{l'}\):

\[ c = rac{\int(\ldots)\,Y_{l'}^*\,d\Omega}{\int|Y_{l'}|^2d\Omega}. \]

The integrand is a trigonometric polynomial of low degree, so 80-point Gauss–Legendre quadrature in \( heta\) gives the integral exactly, up to round-off. The result for one block is a list of numbers, one per monomial.

Step 2: which blocks exist (selection rules). A background of degree \(n\) multiplies the perturbation by functions of \( heta\) of degree \(n\). Projected back on the harmonics, degree \(l\) then reaches only \(l' = l + \Delta l\) with \(|\Delta l| \le n\); the curl that turns a poloidal field into a toroidal one shifts the parity of \(\Delta l\) by one. For the dipole (\(n = 1\)), for example, the u row takes \(F\) from \(l \pm 1\) and \(G\) from \(l\); for \(n = 2\), \(F\) from \(l\) and \(l \pm 2\) and \(G\) from \(l \pm 1\). derive.py finds these rules itself: a block that does not exist comes out with no terms.

Step 3: the form of the coefficients in \(l\) and \(m\). Multiplying by a function of \( heta\) of degree \(n\) is multiplying by \(\cos heta\) up to \(n\) times (or differentiating in \( heta\), which the same recurrences express; see part B). Each multiplication by \(\cos heta\) moves \(l\) by one, with the coefficients \(p_l = \sqrt{(l+1)^2-m^2}/(2l+1)\) and \(q_l = \sqrt{l^2-m^2}/(2l+1)\). All the square roots of a coefficient come from these factors, and the \(\phi\) derivatives bring \(im\). A block of a given \(\Delta l\) shares one product of them, the angular factor \(A(l, m, \Delta l)\):

\(\Delta l = 0\) \(\Delta l = \mp1\) \(\Delta l = \mp2\) \(n = 1\) \(im\) \(\sqrt{l^2-m^2}/(2l-1)\), \(\sqrt{(l+1)^2-m^2}/(2l+3)\) — \(n = 2\) \(1/((2l-1)(2l+3))\) \(im\sqrt{l^2-m^2}/(2l-1)\), \(im\sqrt{(l+1)^2-m^2}/(2l+3)\) \( rac{\sqrt{(l^2-m^2)((l-1)^2-m^2)}}{(2l-1)(2l-3)}\), \( rac{\sqrt{((l+1)^2-m^2)((l+2)^2-m^2)}}{(2l+3)(2l+5)}\)

What remains of each coefficient, \(c/A\), is a polynomial in \(l\). It depends on \(m\) only through \(m^2\): the background is axisymmetric, so changing the sign of \(m\) changes only the \(im\) factors, which \(A\) already holds. So every coefficient has the form

\[ c(l, m) = A(l, m, \Delta l)\, ig[a(l) + b(l)\,m^2 ig],\qquad a, b\ ext{polynomials with rational coefficients}. \]

Step 4: find \(a\) and \(b\) by exact interpolation. derive.py gives \(c\) for a range of \((l, m)\), for example \(l\) = 3–9 and \(m\) = 0–3, some 20 to 28 points. For each monomial, polynomials \(a\), \(b\) of increasing degree are tried:

  1. their coefficients are solved by least squares from all the points (each polynomial must have fewer coefficients than there are values of \(l\), so there are more points than unknowns);
  2. each coefficient is rounded to the nearest rational with denominator \(\le 60\);
  3. the rounded polynomial is kept only if it reproduces every point to \(10^{-9}\) of the largest value (in practice \(10^{-13}\)); otherwise the next degree is tried.

This is exact interpolation, not an approximation. The data are exact up to round-off, and the result has rational coefficients and passes through more points than it has unknowns. If the form of step 3 did not hold for some block (a wrong angular factor, a coefficient that is not a polynomial), no polynomial would pass through all the points, and the tool would print None rather than a formula that is slightly off. This is why the tool is called a fit: it finds the closed form from exact samples.

Step 5: kore's scaling and labels. Kore's rows are derive.py's rows times \(-r^5/L'^3\) (u) or \(-r^3/L'^3\) (v, f, g), and times Hendrik for the Lorentz force (the minus sign: kore's matrix A holds minus the right-hand side). Each monomial becomes a label, the name of the radial matrix submatrices.py builds: \(X^{(d)} B^{(j)} \lambda_k\, r^p\) is {row}{-p}{code}{j}[lho{k}]ohr1_D{d} in rows u, v and {row}{-(p+1)}{code}{j}[lho{k}]_D{d} in rows f, g, with code = bpo (\(c_\mathrm{norm} h\)) or bto (\(c_\mathrm{tor} k\)) and \(\lambda_k\) the \(k\)-th derivative of \(\ln ho_0\). An operator then returns \(-A\cdot\sum( ext{polynomial} imes ext{label})/L'^3\) for each block.

docs.title: A.3 Implementation
docs.text:
step file function background profiles \(h\), \(k\) and their derivatives bin/background_field.py h, k, bpoX, btoX step 1, derive one block tests/magnetic/derive.py rows (velocity, bfield, B0, lorentz, project) steps 3–4, closed forms in \(l\), \(m\) tools/derive/fit_rows.py A (angular factors), fit (exact interpolation), main step 5, code tools/derive/gen_table.py main (labels, table entries, label parities) the operators bin/operators.py lorentz, induction (poloidal + toroidal); degree-1 poloidal lorentz_pol, induction_pol (hand-derived forms, plus lorentz_rho and the lho labels for \((\ln\rho_0)'\)); lorentz_tor, induction_tor, *_tor2, *_pol2 (fitted); quad_factors, moff (column offsets) the radial matrices of the labels bin/submatrices.py the magnetic label lists placing the blocks, \(\Delta l = -2..2\) bin/assemble.py the loops over op.lorentz, op.induction

Where each closed form in operators.py comes from:

  • degree-1 poloidal field ('axial', 'dipole', 'FDM' with B0_l = 1, 'G21 dipole', 'Luo_S1'): hand-derived forms, with the \((\ln\rho_0)'\) terms derived separately;
  • degree-2 poloidal field ('Luo_S2', 'FDM' with B0_l = 2): fitted (fit_rows.py pol 2) and generated (gen_table.py);
  • toroidal fields of degree 1 and 2: fitted (fit_rows.py tor 1, tor 2).

docs.title: A.4 Verification
docs.text:
• tests/magnetic/derive_check.py (no run directory, about 40 minutes on one core; --part k/K runs every K-th check, which run_all.sh spreads over its jobs): derive.py against every closed form, term by term: the uniform-density operators, the \((\ln\rho_0)'\) terms, the toroidal forms, and the degree-2 tables (read from the source of operators.py). Degrees \(l\) 3–6, \(m\) 0–3.
  • tests/magnetic/row_check.py (in a run directory): what kore really assembles, i.e. the closed forms times this run's radial matrices, in their Gegenbauer bases, against derive.py evaluated with the run's own profiles. This catches a wrong label, a wrong power of \(r\) or a wrong basis, even when the closed form is right. Degrees up to \(m + 4\) by default.
  • Energy budgets (budget_check.py) and the identity between the work of the Lorentz force, \(\int\rho_0\mathbf{u}^*\cdot\mathbf{F}_L\,dV\), and minus Hendrik times the complex conjugate of the induction work, \(\int\mathbf{b}^*\cdot\nabla\times(\mathbf{u}\times\mathbf{B}_0)\,dV\) (bin/ru_insane.py): spin_doctor computes the powers of the Lorentz force and of the induction from the eigenvectors with its own formulas (on an \((r, \theta)\) grid for toroidal and degree-2 fields), independently of the operators.

Which degrees these checks reach. derive_check (\(l\) 3–6) and row_check with its default limit look at degrees inside the range the closed forms were fitted on. They show that the code equals the fit and the derivation there, not that the formulas hold at large \(l\). The evidence at large \(l\) is:

  • poloidal fields ('axial', 'FDM' of degree 1 and 2, 'G21 dipole', 'Luo_S1', 'Luo_S2'): the eigenvalues agree to round-off with an independent code whose closed forms were derived separately, at lmax up to about 190;
  • toroidal fields (no independent code): the energy budgets, which sum the powers over all degrees of the run (lmax 47–64, residuals \(10^{-11}\) to \(10^{-13}\)), and the Malkus (1967) frequencies (Magnetic field equations). Both test the operators through whole eigenvectors, not coefficient by coefficient;
  • a one-off comparison of every fitted coefficient of the degree-2 fields with derive.py at \(l = 20\), \(m = 3\) and \(l = 31\), \(m = 7\), outside the fitting range: largest relative difference \(4.3\cdot10^{-10}\) (poloidal, 40 blocks) and \(2.0\cdot10^{-10}\) (toroidal, 34 blocks), no term missing (the round-off of derive.py's quadrature at these degrees). The degree-1 fields were not compared there.

docs.title: A.5 How to use it
docs.text:
Derive one block. The Lorentz force of the dipole (--b0 pol1, the default) in the u row of degree 3, column \(F\) of degree 2, \(m = 1\) (derive.py ROW COL LCOL LROW M; about 20 s):

$ cd tests/magnetic && python3 derive.py u F 2 3 1
-271.529003975633 +0.000000000000i   r^-5  F0 h0
-81.458701192690 +0.000000000000i   r^-4  F0 h0 lr1
+54.305800795127 +0.000000000000i   r^-4  F0 h1
+99.560634791066 +0.000000000000i   r^-4  F1 h0
...
-9.050966799188 +0.000000000000i   r^-2  F3 h0
(14 terms)

Read the last line as \(-9.0510\,r^{-2} h F'''\). In operators.lorentz_pol (u row, bpol, \(\Delta l = -1\)) the same term is \(C\cdot 2\,\mathtt{u2bpo0ohr1\_D3}\) with \(C = \sqrt{l^2 - m^2}(l^2-1)/(2l-1) = 4.5255\) (\(l = 3\), \(m = 1\)): the label u2bpo0ohr1_D3 is \(r^{5-2} h F'''\), and \(-r^5\times(-9.0510\,r^{-2}) = +2C\,r^3\). Only the terms with \(\ln\rho_0\) (the anelastic ones, zero for structure 'Boussinesq'):

$ python3 derive.py u F 2 3 1 --rho
-81.458701192690 +0.000000000000i   r^-4  F0 h0 lr1
+27.152900397563 +0.000000000000i   r^-3  F0 h1 lr1
+18.101933598376 +0.000000000000i   r^-3  F1 h0 lr1
+13.576450198782 +0.000000000000i   r^-2  F0 h2 lr1
+9.050966799188 +0.000000000000i   r^-2  F2 h0 lr1
(5 terms)

--b0 chooses another field: pol2 (degree-2 poloidal: 'Luo_S2', FDM with B0_l = 2), tor1, tor2. The induction of the quadrupole in the f row of degree 4 from \(P\) of degree 2 (about 2 s):

$ python3 derive.py f P 2 4 1 --b0 pol2
+28.168588671694 +0.000000000000i   r^-2  P0 h0 lr1
-28.168588671694 +0.000000000000i   r^-2  P0 h1
+28.168588671694 +0.000000000000i   r^-2  P1 h0
(3 terms)

Find the closed forms. tools/derive/fit_rows.py KIND N does steps 1, 3 and 4 for every block. The toroidal \(n = 1\) field, rows f and g only (the derived rows are cached in fit_tor1.pkl, so a second run is instant):

$ python3 tools/derive/fit_rows.py tor 1 --rows f,g --l 2:8 --jobs 8 | tee tor1_fg.log
f P dl+0  P0*k0 r^-2             [a + b m^2] = l*(l + 1)
g P dl-1  P0*k0 r^-3             [a + b m^2] = l*(l - 1)*(l + 1)
g P dl-1  P0*k0*lr1 r^-2         [a + b m^2] = l*(l - 1)*(l + 1)
g P dl-1  P0*k1 r^-2             [a + b m^2] = -l*(l - 1)*(l + 1)
g P dl+1  P0*k0 r^-3             [a + b m^2] = -l*(l + 1)*(l + 2)
g P dl+1  P0*k0*lr1 r^-2         [a + b m^2] = -l*(l + 1)*(l + 2)
g P dl+1  P0*k1 r^-2             [a + b m^2] = l*(l + 1)*(l + 2)
g T dl+0  T0*k0 r^-2             [a + b m^2] = l*(l + 1)

A line ending in None means the polynomial needs more points than the \(l\) range gives: widen the range. For the degree-2 poloidal field, python3 tools/derive/fit_rows.py pol 2 --jobs 8 (\(l\) 3–9) gives all blocks except four of the u row at \(\Delta l = 0\), whose \(a(l)\) has degree 6; --rows u --l 3:14 gives those too. These two runs reproduce every coefficient of operators.induction_pol2 and lorentz_pol2.

Turn them into code. tools/derive/gen_table.py writes the table entries in kore's labels and lists the labels submatrices.py must build, with the vector parity of their column:

$ python3 tools/derive/gen_table.py tor1_fg.log
# induction (rows f, g)
        ('f', 'P', 0): lambda: (l*(l + 1))*f1bto0_D0,
        ('g', 'P', -1): lambda: (l*(l - 1)*(l + 1))*g2bto0_D0 + (l*(l - 1)*(l + 1))*g1bto0lho1_D0 + (-l*(l - 1)*(l + 1))*g1bto1_D0,
        ('g', 'P', 1): lambda: (-l*(l + 1)*(l + 2))*g2bto0_D0 + (-l*(l + 1)*(l + 2))*g1bto0lho1_D0 + (l*(l + 1)*(l + 2))*g1bto1_D0,
        ('g', 'T', 0): lambda: (l*(l + 1))*g1bto0_D0,
# Lorentz force (rows u, v)
# labels (submatrices.py: labl += [...], arg2 += [the parity] for each)
#  vP: ['f1bto0_D0', 'g2bto0_D0', 'g1bto0lho1_D0', 'g1bto1_D0']
#  vT: ['g1bto0_D0']
#  vF: []
#  vG: []

The operator returns -A(l, m, Δl) * entry / L**3 (times par.Hendrik for rows u, v), with the column offset of operators.moff. Compare operators.induction_tor, where the f row is -1j*m*L*f1bto0_D0 (\(A = im\), entry \(L\)) and the g row at \(\Delta l = -1\) is -Cm*l*(l-1)*(l+1)*(g2bto0_D0 + g1bto0lho1_D0 - g1bto1_D0).

Check against kore. derive_check needs no run directory; its last lines are

rows v and T columns: no (ln rho0) terms
derive_check.py: 532 checks, ok

row_check runs in a run directory after submatrices.py; tests/magnetic/mk_run.py NAME 'par.x = ..' builds one:

$ python3 tests/magnetic/mk_run.py rc_s2 "par.structure = 'Boussinesq'; par.B0 = 'Luo_S2'; par.tol_B0 = 1e-15"
rc_s2 ok
$ cd rc_s2 && python3 ../tests/magnetic/row_check.py 7
row f l= 2  column P l= 2: 1.17e-14
row f l= 2  column P l= 4: 4.25e-15
row f l= 2  column T l= 1: 3.34e-15
...
row_check.py (Boussinesq, B0 Luo_S2, B0_tor None, m 1): worst 1.24e-14 -> ok

This takes 12 minutes: each block calls derive.py, and the argument 7 limits the row degrees checked to 7. Use the absolute path of row_check.py if the run directory is elsewhere; with 'Wu 2005', use N 192 in a shell and N 288 in a full sphere to reach round-off. tests/magnetic/run_all.sh runs all the magnetic checks.

Add a new background field.

  1. Its shape. In bin/background_field.py, add the name to B0_TYPES (at the end: its index goes to params.dat), its \(h(r)\) and derivatives to h(r, k) (a polynomial goes in POLY; mind the parity \((-1)^n\) in a full sphere), its degree and equatorial symmetry (B0_l, symmB0), and its normalisation in B0_norm if cnorm is not a number.
  2. Its couplings. If its degree is 1 or 2, the existing operators apply unchanged: they depend on the degree, not on \(h\). For another degree \(n\): derive (rows(..., b0=('pol', n))), add \(n\)'s angular factors to fit_rows.A, find the closed forms, generate the code and add a lorentz_poln/induction_poln pair with the new labels in submatrices.py; assemble.py loops over \(\Delta l = -2..2\), so widen that loop for \(n > 2\).
  3. Check. Extend derive_check.py with the new tables (its section 5 reads them from operators.py), run row_check.py and the budgets on a run with the new field, compare at a few large \(l\) with derive.py, and compare with an independent code or an analytic result where you have one. There is a shorter way for any degree: see A.6.

docs.title: A.6 Any background field: the couplings from the recurrence algebra
docs.text:
Motivation. The closed forms of A.2–A.5 exist for one degree at a time (1 and 2). A field made of many degrees — given degree by degree (B0 = 'general') or built from a differential rotation ('ferraro') — would need a new fit for each degree. bin/mag_algebra.py builds the couplings at run time instead, for any degrees, with the exact recurrence algebra of part B: nothing is fitted, and the result is exact up to round-off at any \(n\) and \(l\).

Method. The background is a sum over degrees of poloidal and toroidal parts. With \(\partial_ heta P_n = -\sin heta\,P_n'(x)\), each part is a few vectors of three kinds, a polynomial \(c(x)\) times \(\hat{\mathbf{r}}\), \(\sin heta\,\hat{ oldsymbol heta}\) or \(\sin heta\,\hat{ oldsymbol\phi}\) (\(c\) is kept as a Legendre series, and \(c(X)\), \(c'(X)\) are sums of the \(P_k(X)\), \(P_k'(X)\) of part B, step 3: in powers of \(x\) the coefficients of \(P_n\) grow as about \((1 + \sqrt2)^n\), and the round-off with them):

part \(\mathbf{B}_0\) \(\mathbf{J}_0 = abla imes\mathbf{B}_0\) poloidal \(h_n\) \( rac{L_0 h}{r}P_n\,\hat{\mathbf{r}} - (h' + rac{h}{r})P_n'\sin heta\,\hat{ oldsymbol heta}\) \(-(h'' + rac{2h'}{r} - rac{L_0 h}{r^2})P_n'\sin heta\,\hat{ oldsymbol\phi}\) toroidal \(k_n\) \(k\,P_n'\sin heta\,\hat{ oldsymbol\phi}\) \( rac{L_0 k}{r}P_n\,\hat{\mathbf{r}} - (k' + rac{k}{r})P_n'\sin heta\,\hat{ oldsymbol heta}\)

The cross products with a perturbation Field \((q, s, t)\) reduce to the operations of angular.py, through

\[ \hat{\mathbf{r}} imes(q, s, t) = (0, t, -s),\qquad \sin heta\,\hat{ oldsymbol heta} = x\hat{\mathbf{r}} - \hat{\mathbf{z}},\qquad \sin heta\,\hat{ oldsymbol\phi} = \hat{\mathbf{z}} imes\hat{\mathbf{r}}, \] \[ (\hat{\mathbf{z}} imes\hat{\mathbf{r}}) imes\mathbf{F} = \hat{\mathbf{r}}(\hat{\mathbf{z}}\cdot\mathbf{F}) - \hat{\mathbf{z}}(\hat{\mathbf{r}}\cdot\mathbf{F}), \]

(the products with \(\hat{\mathbf{z}}\) are zcross), and the multiplication by \(c(x)\) (mult with the matrices \(c(X)\), \(c'(X)\)). The perturbation's components are radial monomials (\(u_r = LP/r\), \(b_ heta\)-part \(F' + F/r\), \(( abla imes\mathbf{b})_t = -(F'' + 2F'/r - LF/r^2)\), …), so the force \(\mathbf{G} = \mathbf{J}_0 imes\mathbf{b} - \mathbf{B}_0 imes\mathbf{J}\) and the induction \(\mathbf{E} = \mathbf{u} imes\mathbf{B}_0\) are sums of (radial monomial) × (sparse matrix on the degrees). The rows follow from

\[ egin{aligned} \hat{\mathbf{r}}\cdot abla imes abla imes\mathbf{V} &= rac{L'\,(q - (rs)')}{r^2},\ \hat{\mathbf{r}}\cdot abla imes\mathbf{V} &= rac{L'\,t}{r},\ ho_0\,\hat{\mathbf{r}}\cdot abla imes abla imes rac{\mathbf{V}}{ ho_0} &= rac{L'\,(q - (rs)' + \lambda_1 rs)}{r^2}, \end{aligned} \]

which need one radial derivative of the monomials (product rule). Each final monomial becomes a label as in step 5 of A.2, with the profile codes hp + degree (\(c_\mathrm{norm}h_n\)) and kt + degree (\(c_\mathrm{tor}k_n\)).

Implementation. mag_algebra.build (the products and the rows), coefficients (cached per \(m\), stored by diagonal), labels (for submatrices.py), dl_range (\(|\Delta l| \le n_\mathrm{max} + 1\), for assemble.py), block (for operators.lorentz, induction when ut.mag_algebra); the profiles degree by degree come from background_field.pol_profiles, tor_profiles.

Verification. For degrees 1 and 2 the eigenvalues equal those of the closed forms to \(\le 6\cdot10^{-13}\) (14 cases, Magnetic field equations); tests/magnetic/algebra_check.py compares every block with derive.py for degrees 1–4; the energy budgets close to round-off for fields of several degrees.

How to use it. par.mag_couplings = 'algebra' for any type, or a type that needs it: 

par.B0 = 'general'; par.B0_profiles = {1: 'r/6 - r**3/10', 3: '0.3*r**3*(1 - r**2)'}
par.B0_tor = 'general'; par.B0_tor_profiles = {2: 'r**2*(1 - r**2)'}
python3 tests/magnetic/algebra_check.py --quick checks degrees 1 and 3 against derive.py.

docs.title: B. Operators involving background differential rotation
B.1 Motivation
docs.text:
A rotation that varies with latitude couples each degree \(l\) of the perturbation to \(l \pm 1\), \(l \pm 2\), …, up to the degree of \(\Delta\Omega\). Kore needs those couplings for every \(l\) up to lmax, which can be a few thousand for the Sun, and for every even degree \(n\) of \(\Delta\Omega\); observed rotation profiles need \(n\) up to 12 or more. Three ways to get them were considered:

  • closed forms (Gaunt-type integrals worked out by hand) exist for \(n\) = 0 and 2 (diff_rot_coefficients.py). Each new \(n\) means a new derivation;
  • quadrature on a \(\theta\) grid (kore's former method, now quad_reference.py) works for any \(n\), but it costs \(O(\mathrm{lmax}^2)\) time and memory (177 s and 2.5 GB per rank at lmax 1025) and fails above \(l \approx 645\), where scipy's harmonics overflow;
  • an exact recurrence algebra (bin/angular.py), the method kore uses. Every function of \(\cos\theta\) that appears is a polynomial, and multiplication by \(\cos\theta\) on the harmonics is exactly a three-term recurrence. So every coupling is a short product of sparse banded matrices: exact up to round-off, for any \(n\), at any degree, in \(O(\mathrm{lmax})\) time and memory (0.014 s and 6.8 MB at lmax 1025). Nothing is fitted, and nothing needs deriving for a new profile.

docs.title: B.2 Method
docs.text:
Step 1: the force. The rotation is \(\Omega = \Omega_\mathrm{ref}[1 + \Delta\Omega(r, heta)]\) with

\[ \Delta\Omega = \mathtt{diff\_rot\_ampl}\sum_n f_n(r)\,P_n(\cos heta),\qquad n\ ext{even}. \]

In the frame of \(\Omega_\mathrm{ref}\) it is the flow \(\mathbf{U}_0 = G\,\Delta\Omega\,r\sin heta\,\hat{ oldsymbol\phi}\) (\(G\) = Gaspard), which acts on the perturbation through

\[ \mathbf{W} = G ig[\Delta\Omega\,(im\,\mathbf{u} + 2\hat{\mathbf{z}} imes\mathbf{u}) + \sin heta\,(r\,\partial_r\Delta\Omega\,u_r + \partial_ heta\Delta\Omega\,u_ heta)\,\hat{ oldsymbol\phi} ig], \]

and on the heat equation through \(imG\Delta\Omega\,s\) and \(\mathbf{u}\cdot abla S_{tw}\), where \(S_{tw}\) is the thermal-wind entropy that balances the rotation.

Step 2: two exact recurrences. With \(x = \cos heta\),

\[ x\,Y_l = p_l\,Y_{l+1} + q_l\,Y_{l-1},\qquad (1 - x^2) rac{dY_l}{dx} = (l+1)\,q_l\,Y_{l-1} - l\,p_l\,Y_{l+1}, \]

\(p_l = \sqrt{(l+1)^2-m^2}/(2l+1)\), \(q_l = \sqrt{l^2-m^2}/(2l+1)\), for kore's Schmidt harmonics. Written on the degree index (row = target \(l'\), column = source \(l\)), they are two tridiagonal matrices: \(X\) (multiplication by \(x\)) and \(D\) (multiplication by \(-\sin heta\,\partial_ heta\)). Their adjoint under \(\int d\Omega\) is \(D^\dagger = 2X - D\).

Step 3: functions of \( heta\) become polynomials in \(X\). Multiplying by \(P_n(x)\) is the matrix \(P_n(X)\), built with the Legendre recurrence \((k+1)P_{k+1} = (2k+1)\,X P_k - k\,P_{k-1}\); \(P_n'(X)\) follows in the same way. \(P_n(X)\) has \(n + 1\) non-zero diagonals, every other one: \(P_n\) couples \(l\) to \(l' = l - n, l - n + 2, \ldots, l + n\). These are the selection rules: P→P and T→T couplings have \(|\Delta l| \le n\), even; P↔T couplings have \(|\Delta l| \le n + 1\), odd (the \(\hat{\mathbf{z}} imes\) and the curl add one degree). The matrices are exact; only their last few rows are wrong, because products of truncated matrices miss the degrees beyond the truncation. They are therefore built a few degrees beyond what is used (lmax + n + 6).

Step 4: vector fields. A vector field is expanded as

\[ \mathbf{F} = \sum_l\,\left[\,q_l Y_l\hat{\mathbf{r}} + s_l\,r abla Y_l + t_l\,r abla Y_l imes\hat{\mathbf{r}}\, ight]. \]

The operations \(\mathbf{W}\) needs are exact sparse products of \(X\), \(D\) and diagonal matrices: multiplication by \(g(x)\), \(\hat{\mathbf{z}} imes\), \(\hat{\mathbf{z}} imes(c\,\hat{\mathbf{r}})\), and the scalar \(\sin heta\,F_ heta\). The formulas are in the docstring of bin/angular.py and in Differential rotation, §3.

Step 5: the 12 primitives. For one degree \(n\), with \(\Delta\Omega = f(r)\,P_n(x)\), \(\mathbf{W}\) is linear in four radial shapes: \(f\,LP/r\) (from \(u_r\)), \(f\,a\) with \(a = (rP)'/r + \lambda_1 P\) (the consoidal part), \(f\,T\) (the toroidal part), and \((rf')\,LP/r\) (the radial shear). Applying the operations of step 4 to each shape and taking the three components \(q\), \(s\), \(t\) of the result gives 4 × 3 = 12 sparse matrices \(C[k][\mathrm{shape}]\) (rows: target degree, columns: source degree).

Step 6: from primitives to radial operators. The u row is the 2-curl \(\hat{\mathbf{r}}\cdot abla imes abla imes\) and the v row is the 1-curl \(\hat{\mathbf{r}}\cdot abla imes\). Applied to a field with components \((q, s, t)\), they combine \(q\) and \(s\) (u) or \(t\) (v) with radial derivatives. Combining the primitives in the same way gives, for each radial operator of the row (for example \(f\,P\), \(f\,P'\), \(f\,(\ln ho_0)'P\), \((rf')P\)), its coefficient for every pair \((l', l)\), multiplied by \(L'\) of the target. For example, f_2C_D0P multiplies \(f\,P\) in the u row.

Step 7: the heat equation and the thermal wind. The heat terms need only \(P_n(X)\), \(P_n'(X)\) and \(P_n'(X)\,D\). The thermal-wind entropy \(S_{tw} = \sum_n \sigma_n(r)P_n(\cos heta)\) follows from thermal-wind balance: in Legendre space, \(D\sigma = (1-x^2)\,\partial_x S_{tw}\) is solved for the \(\sigma_n\) by forward substitution, exactly.

Step 7b: the induction by the rotation. With a magnetic field, \(\mathbf{U}_0\) also shears the field:

\[ abla imes(\mathbf{U}_0 imes\mathbf{b}) = (\mathbf{b}\cdot abla)\mathbf{U}_0 - (\mathbf{U}_0\cdot abla)\mathbf{b} = G\left[-im\Delta\Omega\,\mathbf{b} + \sin heta\left(r\partial_r\Delta\Omega\,b_r + \partial_ heta\Delta\Omega\,b_ heta ight)\hat{ oldsymbol\phi} ight] \]

(the \(\hat{\mathbf{z}} imes\mathbf{b}\) terms of the two cancel). It has the structure of \(\mathbf{W}\) without its \(2\hat{\mathbf{z}} imes\mathbf{u}\), so it has its own primitives (_induction_primitives, the shapes \(f\,LF/r\), \(f(F' + F/r)\), \(fG\), \((rf')LF/r\)). The induction row f (\(\hat{\mathbf{r}}\cdot\)) sees only \(-im\Delta\Omega\,b_r\); the row g (\(\hat{\mathbf{r}}\cdot abla imes = L't/r\)) sees the t components, including the \(\Omega\)-effect from F (induction_coefficients, induction_block, induction_dl_range).

Step 8: into kore. Each radial operator is a label with the profile codes zf, zd, zs + degree for \(f_n\), \(rf_n'\), \(r^2f_n''\) (and tw, tp for \(p_0\sigma_n\), \(p_0\sigma_n'\)). submatrices.py builds its matrix. A block is then \(G\) times the sum, over the degrees \(n\) and the terms, of coefficient × radial operator, divided by \(L'^3\); assemble.py places it at the \(\Delta l\) of the selection rules.

docs.title: B.4 Verification
docs.text:
• tests/diff_rot/angular_check.py (no run directory): each piece of the algebra against something computed another way: the harmonics against exact rational Legendre values (\(l \le 2000\)) and scipy (\(l \le 640\)), their norms up to \(l = 3000\) (also \(m\) = 400 and 1425), \(X\) and \(D\) on a grid and their adjoints, the vector operations against Gauss–Legendre projections at low degree and around \(l = 1200\), and the 12 primitives against the former quadrature builder (quad_reference.py) for \(n \le 16\). Because it checks the algebra itself, it covers every \(n\) and degrees far above what the closed forms reach.
  • tests/diff_rot/gen_check.py (in a run directory): every coupling of \(f_0\) and \(f_2\) against the independent closed forms of diff_rot_coefficients.py, for all \(l \le\) lmax and \(m \le\) mmax (recorded runs: lmax 20 and 1025, agreement to \(10^{-15}\) of the row scale), and, for \(n\) = 4 … nmax, that no coupling falls outside the \(\Delta l\) kore assembles (a coupling there would be dropped silently).
  • The induction by the rotation: tests/magnetic/dr_induction_check.py compares every block of induction_block with derive.rows_dr (sympy, \(\mathbf{U}_0 = w(r)P_n\,r\sin\theta\,\hat{\boldsymbol\phi}\)) for \(n\) up to 6 and \(l\) up to 25; tests/magnetic/rigid_check.py uses that a uniform \(\Delta\Omega = c\) is a rigid rotation, \(\lambda = \lambda(\text{Gaspard } 1 + c) - imc\) exactly, for several background fields and a conducting inner core.
  • tests/heat_dr/tw_sympy.py: the thermal-wind \(\sigma_2\), \(\sigma_4\), \(\sigma_6\) derived symbolically from thermal-wind balance, against the closed forms that gen_check compares the run-time \(\sigma_n\) with.
  • Whole-system checks: bin/ru_insane.py (the assembled rows against a grid evaluation of the force), tests/diff_rot/regress.sh (A and B against an older checkout), tests/heat_dr/run_all.sh (rows, assembly, energy budgets), and the Mukhopadhyay et al. (2025) solar benchmark (run_bekki.py, Benchmarks).

docs.title: B.5 How to use it
docs.text:
The recurrence algebra. Check it against the harmonics on a grid. angular.ylm_grid(m, lmax, x) returns \(Y_l\), \(\partial_\theta Y_l\) and \(imY_l/\sin\theta\):

$ python3
>>> import sys; sys.path.insert(0, 'bin')
>>> import numpy as np, angular
>>> A = angular.Algebra.get(2, 30)                      # m = 2, degrees 0..30
>>> x = np.array([-0.7, 0.1, 0.55])
>>> Y, dY, Z = angular.ylm_grid(2, 30, x)
>>> x*Y[5], A.X.toarray()[:, 5] @ Y                     # x Y_5 = Σ_k X[k, 5] Y_k
(array([ 0.21275696, -0.01739509, -0.03535338]), array([ 0.21275696, -0.01739509, -0.03535338]))
>>> P4, dP4 = A.legendre(4)
>>> np.polynomial.legendre.Legendre.basis(4)(x)*Y[7], P4.toarray()[:, 7] @ Y
(array([-0.09618301,  0.06666419,  0.10236181]), array([-0.09618301,  0.06666419,  0.10236181]))
>>> np.nonzero(P4.toarray()[:, 7])[0]                   # P_4 couples l = 7 to l' = 3..11, every other degree
array([ 3,  5,  7,  9, 11])
>>> -np.sqrt(1 - x**2)*dY[5], A.D.toarray()[:, 5] @ Y   # D = -sinθ ∂θ
(array([ 1.1811106 , -1.58080089,  1.58869119]), array([ 1.1811106 , -1.58080089,  1.58869119]))

The couplings. Compare a few couplings with the closed forms of tests/diff_rot/diff_rot_coefficients.py (names f_* for \(f_2\), f0_* for \(f_0\)), and the primitives with the former quadrature (tests/diff_rot/quad_reference.py). diff_rot reads parameters; in a session outside a run directory, give it a stand-in with lmax. (numpy 2 prints the numbers as np.float64(...).)

$ python3
>>> import sys, types; sys.path[:0] = ['bin', 'tests/diff_rot']
>>> sys.modules['parameters'] = types.SimpleNamespace(par=types.SimpleNamespace(lmax=40))
>>> import numpy as np, diff_rot as dr, diff_rot_coefficients as dc, quad_reference as qr
>>> l, m = 6, 1
>>> [(dl, dr.momentum_coef('f_1C_D0P', 2, l, m, dl).real, dc.f_1C_D0P(l, m, dl)) for dl in (-3, -1, 1, 3)]
[(-3, 20.409040291494..., 20.409040291494...), (-1, -24.739970002053..., -24.739970002053...),
 (1, 50.935260967822..., 50.935260967822...), (3, -201.005201402848..., -201.005201402848...)]
>>> dr.momentum_coef('f_2C_D0P', 2, l, m, 0), dc.f_2C_D0P(l, m, 0)
(397.0909090909...j, 397.0909090909...j)
>>> C, A = dr._primitives(4, 3, 30); Q = qr.primitives(4, 3, 30)
>>> max(np.max(abs(C[k][s].toarray()[:26, :26] - Q[k][s][:26, :26])) for k in C for s in C[k])
6.128431095930864e-14

f_1C_D0P is a P column in the v row, a P↔T coupling, so for \(P_2\) it reaches \(|\Delta l| = n + 1 = 3\).

The checks. python3 tests/diff_rot/angular_check.py --quick takes 10 s and ends with angular_check: ok. python3 tests/heat_dr/tw_sympy.py ends with 0 failures. gen_check runs in a run directory (below).

Add a new rotation profile. Most profiles need no code: use diff_rot_type = 'user' with numpy expressions of \(r\) (and of \(x\), the fractional solar radius, and \(p\) = diff_rot_param) for each even degree:

$ python3 tests/heat_dr/mk_run.py dr_user "par.diff_rot_type = 'user'; par.diff_rot_profiles = {0: '0.1*r**2', 4: '-0.05*(1 - r)'}; par.thermal_wind = 2"
dr_user ok
$ cd dr_user && python3 ../tests/diff_rot/gen_check.py 4 8
closed forms vs diff_rot.py, lmax 20, m = 0..4 (relative to the largest coefficient of the row block)
  n=0 u,P rows: max |diff_rot - closed| / row scale = 3.0e-17  (m, l) = (1, 3)
  ...
Δl selection rules, n = 4..8
  n= 4  largest coefficient outside the assembled Δl range (relative) 0.0e+00
  ...
worst 8.4e-16  ->  ok

Any even degree \(n\) works: the algebra builds \(P_n(X)\) and the couplings for it, so nothing has to be derived. To add a named type instead, add it to TYPES (at the end) and its \(\{n: f_n(r)\}\) to shapes() in bin/diff_rot.py; then run gen_check.py, ru_insane.py and regress.sh (an unchanged profile must give bitwise the same A and B). A new kind of background flow (not of the form \(\Delta\Omega\,r\sin\theta\,\hat{\boldsymbol\phi}\)) needs new primitives: write its \(\mathbf{W}\) with the Field operations as _primitives does, and check it against a quadrature reference written like quad_reference.py.

docs.title: Differential rotation: equations and implementation
docs.text:
This page is the reference for the differential rotation: the physics, the equations, and how the code builds them. The parameters are on the page Background model, and the comparisons with published results on the page Benchmarks. It covers:

  • the physics: what a differentially rotating background does to a linear perturbation (§1);
  • the anelastic (LBR) equations with differential rotation, and the derivation of every term that the differential rotation adds to the momentum and heat equations (§2);
  • the spectral form of these terms: how they couple spherical-harmonic degrees, and how the angular coupling coefficients are obtained (§3);
  • the implementation, term by term: radial profiles, operator labels, the operators, the assembly of the matrices and the diagnostics (§4 to §8);
  • the tests of the implementation, and the known limitations (§9, §10).

Code references give the file and the function.

Contents

  • 0. Notation and code names
  • 1. Physics
  • 2. Equations
  • 3. Spectral form
  • 4. Implementation overview
  • 5. Radial profiles
  • 6. Radial operators and labels
  • 7. The operators and the assembly
  • 8. Diagnostics
  • 9. Tests
  • 10. Limitations

docs.title: 0. Notation and code names
docs.text:
Everything is dimensionless. The length unit is the outer radius \(r_0\) (r = 1 at the outer boundary), and the time unit is \(\tau\), chosen by par.timescale ('rotation' gives \(\tau = 1/\Omega_{\rm ref}\)).

symbol meaning in the code \(r, \theta, \phi\); \(x\) spherical coordinates; \(x = \cos\theta\) \(\varpi\) cylindrical radius \(r\sin\theta\) \(\hat{\mathbf z}\) rotation axis \(\Omega_{\rm ref}\) rotation rate of the frame in which kore solves diff_rot_frame (nHz) for the solar profiles \(G\) \(\Omega_{\rm ref}\tau\), the frame's rotation rate in time units par.Gaspard \(\Delta\Omega(r,\theta)\) relative differential rotation, \(\Omega = \Omega_{\rm ref}(1 + \Delta\Omega)\) par.diff_rot_type \(f_n(r)\) Legendre coefficients of \(\Delta\Omega\): \(\Delta\Omega = \sum_n f_n(r) P_n(x)\), \(n\) even (diff_rot_ampl times \(a_n\) (diff_rot_term_amp) times the shape of the type) zf0, zf2, zf4, …; zd, zs for \(rf_n'\), \(r^2f_n''\) \(\mathbf U_0\) the background flow seen in the rotating frame \(\rho_0, T_0\) background density and temperature prf.density \(h\) \(\ln\rho_0\) profile code lho \(p_0\) \(\rho_0 T_0\) (not the pressure) pss \(g(r)\) gravity gra \(S_0(r)\) spherical background entropy, in units of \(c_p\); \(S_0'\) its gradient dSd (\(S_0'\)), pdS (\(p_0 S_0'\)) \(S_{tw}(r,\theta)\) latitudinal background entropy (thermal wind, or prescribed) \(\sigma_n(r)\) Legendre coefficients of \(S_{tw}\) tw2 = \(p_0\sigma_2\), tp2 = \(p_0\sigma_2'\), … \(\nu, \kappa\) viscosity and thermal diffusivity profiles vsc, kps = \(\kappa p_0\) Beyonce \((N_0\tau)^2\): the buoyancy force is \(\mathrm{Beyonce}\thinspace g s \hat{\mathbf r}\) par.Beyonce ViscosD, ThermaD \(\nu_0\tau/r_0^2\), \(\kappa_0\tau/r_0^2\) par.ViscosD, par.ThermaD \(\mathbf u\), \(s\) velocity and entropy perturbation (\(s = \delta s/c_p\)) \(P, T\) poloidal and toroidal scalars of \(\mathbf u\) sections u and v \(m\) azimuthal order: fields go as \(e^{i m\phi}\) par.m \(l\), \(L\) harmonic degree, \(L = l(l+1)\) l \(l'\), \(l\) target degree (row) and source degree (column) of a coupling l, l + offdiag in operators.py \(Y_l\) Schmidt-normalised spherical harmonic \(Y_l^m\), \(\int\lvert Y_l\rvert^2 d\Omega = n_l = 4\pi/(2l+1)\) utils.Ylm \(\lambda\) eigenvalue, fields \(\propto e^{\lambda t}\), \(\lambda = \sigma - i\omega\): growth rate \(\sigma\), frequency \(\omega\) (\(\omega > 0\) is prograde)

Two code conventions recur everywhere:

  • Sections. The unknowns and the matrix rows are stacked in blocks: section u holds the rows of the radial component of the double curl of the momentum equation (one row block per poloidal degree), section v the rows of the radial component of its curl (one per toroidal degree), and section h the heat equation (one per degree of \(s\), which follows the poloidal degrees).
  • Row weights. Each row is multiplied by a power of \(r\) and of \(\rho_0\), chosen so that every radial coefficient is a polynomial, and divided by \(L'^3\), where \(l'\) is the row degree.

docs.title: 1.1 The background
docs.text:
kore solves in a frame rotating at the constant rate \(\Omega_{\rm ref}\). The background rotates at

\[ \Omega(r,\theta) = \Omega_{\rm ref}\left[1 + \Delta\Omega(r,\theta)\right], \qquad \Delta\Omega = \sum_{n = 0, 2, 4, \dots} f_n(r) P_n(\cos\theta) . \]

Only even \(n\) appear, so the rotation is symmetric about the equator, and the equatorial symmetry of the modes (par.symm) still separates the problem into two classes. In the rotating frame the differential rotation is a steady azimuthal flow

\[ \mathbf U_0 = G\thinspace \Delta\Omega\thinspace r\sin\theta\thinspace \hat{\mathbf e}_ \phi = G\thinspace \Delta\Omega\thinspace \hat{\mathbf z}\times\mathbf r . \qquad (1.1) \]

The factor \(G\) = Gaspard converts the rotation rate \(\Omega_{\rm ref}\Delta\Omega\) to the time unit \(\tau\). It is 1 when \(\tau = 1/\Omega_{\rm ref}\). \(G\) does not choose the frame: \(\Delta\Omega\) is defined relative to the frame, and for the solar profiles the frame rate is set by diff_rot_frame (or fixed at 435 nHz for 'solar').

The spherical background (\(\rho_0\), \(T_0\), \(g\), \(S_0\), \(\nu\), \(\kappa\)) is the same as without differential rotation. The differential rotation adds only two things: the flow \(\mathbf U_0\), and a latitudinal entropy \(S_{tw}(r,\theta)\) (§1.3).

docs.title: 1.2 What the differential rotation does to a perturbation
docs.text:
A perturbation \(\mathbf u\) is carried by the background flow and sheared by it. Linearising the advection \((\mathbf U_0 + \mathbf u)\cdot\nabla(\mathbf U_0 + \mathbf u)\) gives (§2.3) three effects:

  1. Advection at the local rotation rate. A pattern \(e^{i m\phi}\) is carried round at the local rate \(G\Delta\Omega\), which shifts its frequency by \(-m G\Delta\Omega\) locally. With uniform \(\Delta\Omega\) this is just a Doppler shift.
  2. Coriolis force of the local rotation. The Coriolis parameter becomes \(2G(1 + \Delta\Omega)\) instead of \(2G\). Together with (1), a uniform \(\Delta\Omega\) is exactly a change of frame (§2.6).
  3. Transport across the shear. A perturbation that moves across the gradient of \(\Omega\) carries its angular momentum to a place where the background rotates at a different rate. This is the term \(r\sin\theta\thinspace (\mathbf u\cdot\nabla\Delta\Omega)\thinspace \hat{\mathbf e}_ \phi\). It is the only term through which the perturbation can exchange kinetic energy with the background flow (§2.3), so it is what drives shear instabilities.

In the heat equation the entropy perturbation is advected by \(\mathbf U_0\) (the same Doppler shift for \(s\)), and the perturbation velocity advects the latitudinal background entropy \(S_{tw}\).

docs.title: 1.3 Thermal-wind balance
docs.text:
A rotation rate that varies along the rotation axis cannot be balanced by pressure alone. The centrifugal force of the differential rotation then has a curl, and in a stratified fluid only a buoyancy force that varies with latitude, that is a latitudinal entropy gradient, can balance it. This is thermal-wind balance. A differentially rotating star in equilibrium therefore has a background entropy \(S_0(r) + S_{tw}(r,\theta)\). kore computes \(S_{tw}\) from \(\Delta\Omega\) (thermal_wind 1 or 2), prescribes it (thermal_wind = 3), or omits it (thermal_wind = 0).

\(S_{tw}\) is small in amplitude, since it scales as \(G^2/(\mathrm{Beyonce}\thinspace g)\): for the Sun (Beyonce ≈ \(4.9\times10^4\)) its contrast from pole to equator is about \(5\times10^{-6}\) in units of \(c_p\), or \(2\times10^3\) erg g⁻¹ K⁻¹. But the buoyancy it produces through a perturbation scales as \(\mathrm{Beyonce}\thinspace g\thinspace s\). The product does not depend on Beyonce: the feedback of \(S_{tw}\) on the motion is of order \(\Delta\Omega\) relative to the Coriolis force, the same order as the momentum terms of §1.2. In a convection zone, where \(S_0' \approx 0\), \(S_{tw}\) is the only background entropy gradient, and the meridional flow of a perturbation across it (the baroclinic coupling) can destabilise modes.

docs.title: 1.4 What is not modelled
docs.text:
• The background is imposed and fixed: nothing maintains \(\Omega\) or \(S_{tw}\) against viscosity or diffusion, and the perturbation equations have no source terms for them.
  • \(\rho_0\), \(T_0\) and \(g\) stay spherical: no centrifugal distortion, no latitudinal variation of \(\rho_0 T_0\) or \(g\) induced by the thermal wind, and no thermal-wind density in the mass flux. These effects are of relative size \(\Delta\Omega/(\mathrm{Beyonce}\thinspace g)\).
  • The thermal wind is the one consistent with LBR buoyancy. The full anelastic balance would add a term \(p_b S_0'/(\rho_0 g)\) to \(S_{tw}\) (\(p_b\) the background pressure perturbation), the analogue of the \(p_1 S_0'\) term that LBR drops for the perturbations. It matters only where \(S_0' \neq 0\).
  • There is no viscous heating, and the background has no magnetic force: with magnetic = 1 the field acts on the perturbation only (Magnetic field).

docs.title: 2.1 The linear anelastic (LBR) equations
docs.text:
In the frame rotating at \(\Omega_{ m ref}\), with the background of §1.1, a perturbation \((\mathbf u, s)\) obeys, per unit mass (Lantz–Braginsky–Roberts form, with \(\varpi'\) the reduced pressure \(p'/ ho_0\)):

\[ rac{\partial\mathbf u}{\partial t} + 2G hinspace \hat{\mathbf z} imes\mathbf u + \mathbf W(\mathbf u) = - abla\varpi' + \mathrm{Beyonce} hinspace g hinspace s hinspace \hat{\mathbf r} + \mathrm{ViscosD} hinspace \mathbf F_ u(\mathbf u), \qquad (2.1) \] \[ abla\cdot( ho_0\mathbf u) = 0, \qquad (2.2) \] \[ p_0\left[ rac{\partial s}{\partial t} + \mathbf U_0\cdot abla s + u_r S_0' + \mathbf u\cdot abla S_{tw} ight] = \mathrm{ThermaD} hinspace abla\cdot(\kappa hinspace p_0 abla s). \qquad (2.3) \]

Here \(\mathbf F_ u = ho_0^{-1} abla\cdot( ho_0 u hinspace \mathsf S)\) is the viscous force of the anelastic stress tensor \(\mathsf S\), and

\[ \mathbf W(\mathbf u) = (\mathbf U_0\cdot abla)\mathbf u + (\mathbf u\cdot abla)\mathbf U_0 \qquad (2.4) \]

is the linearised advection by the background flow. Without differential rotation, \(\mathbf W = 0\), \(\mathbf U_0\cdot abla s = 0\) and \(S_{tw} = 0\), and (2.1)–(2.3) are kore's standard equations. The differential rotation adds exactly three terms: \(\mathbf W\) in (2.1), and \(p_0\mathbf U_0\cdot abla s\) and \(p_0\mathbf u\cdot abla S_{tw}\) in (2.3).

Remarks:

  • In LBR form the buoyancy depends on \(s\) only. The reduced pressure is a gradient, so it disappears when the curl of (2.1) is taken (§3.2): kore never solves for it.
  • The viscous force, the buoyancy and the diffusion are not changed by the differential rotation.
  • (2.2) is satisfied exactly by the poloidal–toroidal form of \(\mathbf u\) (§3.1).

kore solves the eigenvalue problem for fields \(\propto e^{\lambda t + i m\phi}\), so \(\partial_t o \lambda\) and \(\partial_\phi o i m\).

docs.title: 2.2 The background flow as a local rotation
docs.text:
Write the background rotation in time units as \(\Omega_d(r,\theta) = G\Delta\Omega\), so that \(\mathbf U_0 = \Omega_d\thinspace \hat{\mathbf z}\times\mathbf r\). Two identities are used below:

\[ \mathbf U_0\cdot\nabla = \Omega_d\thinspace \partial_\phi, \qquad (\mathbf v\cdot\nabla)(\hat{\mathbf z}\times\mathbf r) = \hat{\mathbf z}\times\mathbf v , \]

for any vector \(\mathbf v\). In components, with \(\hat{\mathbf z} = \cos\theta\thinspace \hat{\mathbf r} - \sin\theta\thinspace \hat{\mathbf e}_\theta\),

\[ \hat{\mathbf z}\times\mathbf u = \left(-\sin\theta\thinspace u_\phi,\ -\cos\theta\thinspace u_\phi,\ \sin\theta\thinspace u_r + \cos\theta\thinspace u_\theta\right) \qquad (2.5) \]

in the \((\hat{\mathbf r}, \hat{\mathbf e}_\theta, \hat{\mathbf e}_ \phi)\) basis.

docs.title: 2.3 Derivation of the momentum term
docs.text:
Advection of the perturbation by \(\mathbf U_0\). \((\mathbf U_0\cdot abla)\mathbf u = \Omega_d hinspace \partial_\phi\mathbf u\), where \(\partial_\phi\) also acts on the unit vectors: \(\partial_\phi\hat{\mathbf r} = \sin heta hinspace \hat{\mathbf e}_ \phi\), \(\partial_\phi\hat{\mathbf e}_ heta = \cos heta hinspace \hat{\mathbf e}_ \phi\), \(\partial_\phi\hat{\mathbf e}_ \phi = -\sin heta hinspace \hat{\mathbf r} - \cos heta hinspace \hat{\mathbf e}_ heta\). With (2.5) this is

\[ (\mathbf U_0\cdot abla)\mathbf u = \Omega_d\left[i m hinspace \mathbf u + \hat{\mathbf z} imes\mathbf u ight], \]

where \(i m hinspace \mathbf u\) means \(i m\) times each component.

Advection of \(\mathbf U_0\) by the perturbation.

\[ (\mathbf u\cdot abla)\mathbf U_0 = (\mathbf u\cdot abla\Omega_d) hinspace \hat{\mathbf z} imes\mathbf r + \Omega_d hinspace (\mathbf u\cdot abla)(\hat{\mathbf z} imes\mathbf r) = r\sin heta hinspace (\mathbf u\cdot abla\Omega_d) hinspace \hat{\mathbf e}_ \phi + \Omega_d hinspace \hat{\mathbf z} imes\mathbf u . \]

Sum. With \(\mathbf u\cdot abla\Delta\Omega = u_r\partial_r\Delta\Omega + (u_ heta/r)\partial_ heta\Delta\Omega\),

\[ \mathbf W = G\left[\Delta\Omega\left(i m hinspace \mathbf u + 2\hat{\mathbf z} imes\mathbf u ight) + \sin heta\left(r hinspace \partial_r\Delta\Omega hinspace u_r + \partial_ heta\Delta\Omega hinspace u_ heta ight)\hat{\mathbf e}_ \phi ight]. \qquad (2.6) \]

This is the force that operators.differential_rotation discretises. The three parts are those of §1.2: the Doppler term \(i m\Delta\Omega hinspace \mathbf u\); the Coriolis force of the local rotation \(2\Delta\Omega hinspace \hat{\mathbf z} imes\mathbf u\), which adds to the frame's \(2\hat{\mathbf z} imes\mathbf u\); and the shear term.

For \(\Delta\Omega = f(r)P_n(x)\), using \(\partial_ heta P_n(\cos heta) = -\sin heta hinspace P_n'(x)\), the components are

\[ egin{aligned} W_r/G &= f P_n\left[i m hinspace u_r - 2\sin heta hinspace u_\phi ight],\cr W_ heta/G &= f P_n\left[i m hinspace u_ heta - 2x hinspace u_\phi ight],\cr W_\phi/G &= f P_n\left[i m hinspace u_\phi + 2\sin heta hinspace u_r + 2x hinspace u_ heta ight]\cr &\quad + \sin heta\left[(r f') hinspace P_n hinspace u_r - f\sin heta hinspace P_n' hinspace u_ heta ight]. \end{aligned} \qquad (2.7) \]

The profile enters only as \(f\) and \(r f'\); the second derivative \(r^2 f''\) appears later, when the double curl differentiates \(W\) in \(r\) (§3.4).

Energy. For a mode, \(2 hinspace\mathrm{Re}\int ho_0 hinspace \mathbf u^\ast\cdot\mathbf W hinspace dV\) is the rate at which \(\mathbf W\) removes kinetic energy. The Doppler part gives \(i m\int ho_0\Delta\Omega\lvert\mathbf u vert^2 dV\), which is imaginary. The Coriolis part gives \(\mathbf u^\ast\cdot(\hat{\mathbf z} imes\mathbf u) = \hat{\mathbf z}\cdot(\mathbf u imes\mathbf u^\ast)\), which is also imaginary. Only the shear term, \(2G hinspace\mathrm{Re}\int ho_0 hinspace r\sin heta hinspace u_\phi^\ast hinspace (\mathbf u\cdot abla\Delta\Omega) hinspace dV\), exchanges energy with the background. These parts shift the frequency (residω) or change the growth rate (residσ) in spin_doctor (§8).

docs.title: 2.4 Thermal-wind entropy
docs.text:
The balance. The steady background satisfies, in the rotating frame and per unit mass,

\[ (\mathbf U_0\cdot abla)\mathbf U_0 + 2G hinspace \hat{\mathbf z} imes\mathbf U_0 = - abla\varpi_b + \mathrm{Beyonce} hinspace g hinspace S_{tw} hinspace \hat{\mathbf r}, \]

where \(\varpi_b\) collects the pressure and gravity potential terms. With \(\mathbf U_0 = \Omega_d hinspace \hat{\mathbf z} imes\mathbf r\), the left side is \(-(\Omega_d^2 + 2G\Omega_d) hinspace \varpi hinspace \hat{\mathbf e}_ \varpi = -G^2\left[(1 + \Delta\Omega)^2 - 1 ight]\varpi hinspace \hat{\mathbf e}_ \varpi\), the centrifugal and Coriolis forces of the differential rotation (\(\hat{\mathbf e}_ \varpi\) the cylindrical radial unit vector). The \(\phi\)-component of the curl removes \(\varpi_b\). Using \(( abla imes F\hat{\mathbf e}_ \varpi)_ \phi = \partial_z F\) and \(( abla imes F\hat{\mathbf r})_ \phi = -r^{-1}\partial_ heta F\),

\[ rac{1}{r} rac{\partial S_{tw}}{\partial heta} = rac{G^2 hinspace r\sin heta}{\mathrm{Beyonce} hinspace g} hinspace rac{\partial (1 + \Delta\Omega)^2}{\partial z}, \qquad rac{\partial}{\partial z} = \cos heta hinspace rac{\partial}{\partial r} - rac{\sin heta}{r} rac{\partial}{\partial heta}. \qquad (2.8) \]

In the variable \(x\). With \(\partial_ heta = -\sin heta hinspace \partial_x\) and \(\partial_z = x\partial_r + r^{-1}(1 - x^2)\partial_x\), (2.8) becomes

\[ egin{gathered} rac{\partial S_{tw}}{\partial x} = - rac{r^2 G^2}{\mathrm{Beyonce} hinspace g}\left[x hinspace rac{\partial F}{\partial r} + rac{1 - x^2}{r} rac{\partial F}{\partial x} ight], \qquad (2.9)\cr F = egin{cases} 2\Delta\Omega & ext{(linear)} \cr (1 + \Delta\Omega)^2 - 1 & ext{(exact)} \end{cases} \end{gathered} \]

thermal_wind = 1 uses the linear form, thermal_wind = 2 the exact one. Only the exact form is independent of the frame: \(G^2(1 + \Delta\Omega)^2\) is the square of the physical rotation rate, the same whatever \(\Omega_{ m ref}\) the profile is written against, whereas \(G^2\cdot 2\Delta\Omega\) is \(2\Omega_{ m ref}(\Omega - \Omega_{ m ref}) au^2\) and changes with the frame. With thermal_wind = 1 the modes therefore move with the choice of frame, at second order in \(\Delta\Omega\).

The right side of (2.9) is a polynomial in \(x\) of degree \(n_{\max} + 1\) (linear) or \(2n_{\max} + 1\) (exact), so \(S_{tw} = \sum_n \sigma_n(r) P_n(x)\) has even degrees up to \(n_{\max} + 2\) or \(2n_{\max} + 2\). The \(l = 0\) part \(\sigma_0\) is a spherical entropy, absorbed in \(S_0\), and set to zero.

Closed forms for \(\Delta\Omega = f_0 + f_2 P_2\). Writing the bracket of (2.9) on \(P_1\) and \(P_3\) (with \(x P_2 = frac{3}{5}P_3 + frac{2}{5}P_1\), \(3x(1 - x^2) = frac{6}{5}(P_1 - P_3)\), \(P_2' = 3P_1\), \(P_4' = 7P_3 + 3P_1\)) and matching coefficients gives, with \(e = 0\) for thermal_wind = 1 and \(e = 1\) for thermal_wind = 2,

\[ egin{aligned} \sigma_2 &= - rac{2r^2G^2}{\mathrm{Beyonce} hinspace g}\Bigg[(1 + e f_0)\left( rac{f_0'}{3} + rac{f_2'}{21} + rac{4}{7} rac{f_2}{r} ight)\cr &\qquad + rac{e hinspace f_2 (f_0' + f_2')}{21}\Bigg],\cr \sigma_4 &= - rac{6r^2G^2}{35 hinspace \mathrm{Beyonce} hinspace g}\Bigg[(1 + e f_0)\left(f_2' - rac{2f_2}{r} ight)\cr &\qquad + e\left(f_2 f_0' + rac{4}{11}f_2 f_2' + rac{14}{11} rac{f_2^2}{r} ight)\Bigg],\cr \sigma_6 &= -e hinspace rac{4r^2G^2}{77 hinspace \mathrm{Beyonce} hinspace g} hinspace f_2\left(f_2' - rac{2f_2}{r} ight). \end{aligned} \qquad (2.10) \]

kore computes the \(\sigma_n\) from (2.9) by the Legendre-series algebra of §5.4, for any degrees of \(\Delta\Omega\); (2.10) is kept as a validation (tests/diff_rot/gen_check.py, §9). Two analytic checks:

  • Cylindrical rotation, \(\Delta\Omega = \varepsilon\varpi^2\), i.e. \(f_0 = frac{2}{3}\varepsilon r^2\), \(f_2 = - frac{2}{3}\varepsilon r^2\): \(\sigma_2 = \sigma_4 = \sigma_6 = 0\). A rotation constant on cylinders is barotropic and needs no thermal wind.
  • Conical rotation, \(\Delta\Omega = \varepsilon\sin^2 heta\), i.e. \(f_0 = frac{2}{3}\varepsilon\), \(f_2 = - frac{2}{3}\varepsilon\) (linear form): \(\sigma_2 = 16\varepsilon r/(21 hinspace\mathrm{Beyonce} hinspace g)\), \(\sigma_4 = -8\varepsilon r/(35 hinspace\mathrm{Beyonce} hinspace g)\), and \(S_{tw}( ext{pole}) - S_{tw}( ext{equator}) = \varepsilon r/(\mathrm{Beyonce} hinspace g)\): an equator rotating faster (\(\varepsilon > 0\)) needs warmer poles.

Prescribed latitudinal entropy (thermal_wind = 3). \(\partial_ heta S_{tw}\) = dSdtheta \(\sin 2 heta\), independent of \(\Omega\) and of \(r\). Since \(\sin 2 heta = - frac{2}{3} hinspace dP_2/d heta\),

\[ \sigma_2 = - frac{2}{3} hinspace exttt{dSdtheta}, \qquad \sigma_n = 0 \quad (n \ge 4). \]

dSdtheta is in the units of \(s\) (\(\delta s/c_p\)); negative values give warm poles. \(\Omega\) still enters through \(\mathbf W\) and the advection of \(s\). For a uniformly rotating background with a prescribed \(S_{tw}\), use diff_rot_type = 'rigid' with diff_rot_ampl = 0.

docs.title: 2.5 The heat-equation terms
docs.text:
\(S_{tw}\) does not depend on \(\phi\), so \(\mathbf U_0\cdot\nabla S_{tw} = 0\), and \(\mathbf U_0\cdot\nabla s = G\Delta\Omega\thinspace \partial_\phi s\). The left side of (2.3) gains

\[ p_0\left[\thinspace \underbrace{i m G\Delta\Omega\thinspace s}_ {\text{(a) advection}} + \underbrace{u_r\frac{\partial S_{tw}}{\partial r}}_ {\text{(b) radial}} + \underbrace{\frac{u_\theta}{r}\frac{\partial S_{tw}}{\partial\theta}}_ {\text{(c) latitudinal}}\thinspace \right]. \qquad (2.11) \]

(a) is always included. (b) and (c) are included for thermal_wind 1, 2, 3; thermal_wind_radial = 0 drops (b). (a) is anti-Hermitian under the entropy pairing \(\int s^\ast(\cdot)\thinspace dV\), so it only shifts the frequency; (b) and (c) exchange entropy variance with the flow.

docs.title: 2.6 An exact result: the rigid offset
docs.text:
For a uniform \(\Delta\Omega = a\) (diff_rot_type = 'rigid'), \(\partial\Delta\Omega = 0\), \(S_{tw} = 0\), and (2.6) and (2.11) reduce to \(G a(i m\mathbf u + 2\hat{\mathbf z}\times\mathbf u)\) and \(i m G a\thinspace p_0 s\). Equations (2.1) and (2.3) become those of uniform rotation at rate \(G(1 + a)\), with \(\lambda\) replaced by \(\lambda + i m G a\). So

\[ \lambda(a, G) = \lambda_0\big(G(1 + a)\big) - i m G a , \qquad (2.12) \]

where \(\lambda_0(G)\) is the eigenvalue without differential rotation. This identity tests the Doppler and Coriolis parts of the operators and their signs (§9).

docs.title: 3.1 Fields
docs.text:
At fixed \(m\) and equatorial symmetry, each field is a sum over degrees,

\[ \mathbf u = \sum_l\left[ ho_0^{-1} abla imes abla imes( ho_0 P_l Y_l hinspace \mathbf r) + abla imes(T_l Y_l hinspace \mathbf r) ight], \qquad s = \sum_l s_l Y_l , \]

where \(P\) and \(s\) use the poloidal degrees and \(T\) the toroidal ones (utils.ell(m, lmax, symm) returns both lists). This form satisfies (2.2) exactly. For one degree, with \(Z_l = i m Y_l/\sin heta\) and

\[ a_l = rac{(r P_l)'}{r} + h' P_l = rac{P_l}{r} + P_l' + h' P_l , \qquad (3.1) \]

the components are

\[ u_r = rac{L P_l}{r} Y_l, \qquad u_ heta = a_l hinspace \partial_ heta Y_l + T_l Z_l, \qquad u_\phi = a_l Z_l - T_l hinspace \partial_ heta Y_l . \qquad (3.2) \]

These expressions underlie diff_rot._primitives (through the basis fields of §3.3), utils4pp.diff_rot_setup and ru_insane.py.

docs.title: 3.2 Projection of a vector field, and kore's rows
docs.text:
Any vector field \(\mathbf F\) is projected on vector spherical harmonics as

\[ egin{gathered} \mathbf F = \sum_l\left[F^q_l hinspace Y_l hinspace \hat{\mathbf r} + F^s_l hinspace r abla Y_l + F^t_l hinspace r abla Y_l imes\hat{\mathbf r} ight], \qquad (3.3)\cr r abla Y = \partial_ heta Y hinspace \hat{\mathbf e}_ heta + Z hinspace \hat{\mathbf e}_ \phi, \qquad r abla Y imes\hat{\mathbf r} = Z hinspace \hat{\mathbf e}_ heta - \partial_ heta Y hinspace \hat{\mathbf e}_ \phi , \end{gathered} \]

with, since \(\int(\lvert\partial_ heta Y_l vert^2 + \lvert Z_l vert^2) hinspace d\Omega = L n_l\),

\[ egin{aligned} F^q_l &= rac{1}{n_l}\int F_r Y_l^\ast hinspace d\Omega,\cr F^s_l &= rac{1}{L n_l}\int\left(F_ heta hinspace \partial_ heta Y_l^\ast + F_\phi Z_l^\ast ight)d\Omega,\cr F^t_l &= rac{1}{L n_l}\int\left(F_ heta Z_l^\ast - F_\phi hinspace \partial_ heta Y_l^\ast ight)d\Omega . \end{aligned} \qquad (3.4) \]

By (3.2) the velocity has \(u^q = L P/r\), \(u^s = a\), \(u^t = T\).

Taking curls removes the pressure:

\[ \hat{\mathbf r}\cdot abla imes\mathbf F = \sum_l rac{L}{r}F^t_l Y_l, \qquad \hat{\mathbf r}\cdot abla imes abla imes\mathbf F = \sum_l rac{L}{r^2}\left[F^q_l - \partial_r(r F^s_l) ight]Y_l . \qquad (3.5) \]

(The toroidal part \(F^t r abla Y imes\hat{\mathbf r} = abla imes(F^t Y\mathbf r)\) has no radial curl-curl, and the spheroidal part \(F^q Y\hat{\mathbf r} + F^s r abla Y\) has the curl \(r^{-1}\left[F^q - \partial_r(r F^s) ight] r abla Y imes\hat{\mathbf r}\).)

kore's rows of degree \(l'\) are (3.5) multiplied by \(r^{ m rpower} ho_0^{ m rhopower}\) and divided by \(L'^3\). With the defaults rpower_u = 5, rpower_v = 3, rhopower_u = rhopower_v = 1:

\[ \mathrm{row}_ u(\mathbf F) = rac{r^3 ho_0}{L'^2}\left[F^q_{l'} - \partial_r(r F^s_{l'}) ight], \qquad \mathrm{row}_ v(\mathbf F) = rac{r^2 ho_0}{L'^2}F^t_{l'} . \qquad (3.6) \]

For example, \(\mathbf F = \mathbf u\) gives \(\mathrm{row}_ u = \left[L r^2 ho_0 P - r^3 ho_0(2P' + rP'' + h'P + r h'' P + r h' P') ight]/L^2\) and \(\mathrm{row}_ v = r^2 ho_0 T/L^2\), which is operators.inertia. The diff-rot operator is (3.6) applied to \(\mathbf W\).

docs.title: 3.3 Angular primitives
docs.text:
Insert one source degree \(l\) of (3.2) into (2.7), with \(\Delta\Omega = f(r)P_n(x)\). Each component of \(\mathbf W\) is a sum of four radial "shapes" times angular functions:

shape radial factor from q \(f hinspace L P_l/r\) \(u_r\) with \(f\) a \(f hinspace a_l\) the consoidal part of \(u_ heta\), \(u_\phi\) T \(f hinspace T_l\) the toroidal part dq \((r f') hinspace L P_l/r\) \(u_r\) in the shear term

From (2.7) and (3.2), the angular functions, per unit \(G\) and per unit shape, are (\(Y = Y_l\), \(Z = Z_l\)):

shape \(W_r\) \(W_ heta\) \(W_\phi\) q \(i m P_n Y\) 0 \(2\sin heta hinspace P_n Y\) a \(-2 i m P_n Y\) \(P_n(i m hinspace \partial_ heta Y - 2xZ)\) \(P_n(i m Z + 2x hinspace \partial_ heta Y) - \sin^2 heta hinspace P_n' hinspace \partial_ heta Y\) T \(2\sin heta hinspace P_n hinspace \partial_ heta Y\) \(P_n(i m Z + 2x hinspace \partial_ heta Y)\) \(P_n(-i m hinspace \partial_ heta Y + 2xZ) - \sin^2 heta hinspace P_n' Z\) dq 0 0 \(\sin heta hinspace P_n Y\)

Projecting each entry on the target degree \(l'\) with (3.4) defines twelve matrices \(C^k_{ m sh}[l', l]\), with \(k \in \lbrace q, s, t brace\) the projection and sh the shape. Then, for the target degree \(l'\),

\[ W^k_{l'} = G\sum_l\left[C^k_q hinspace f rac{L_l P_l}{r} + C^k_a hinspace f a_l + C^k_T hinspace f T_l + C^k_{dq} hinspace (r f') rac{L_l P_l}{r} ight]. \qquad (3.7) \]

The angular algebra. The \(C^k_{ m sh}\) are not computed by integration but built exactly, as sparse products of a few matrices on the degree index (bin/angular.py). Multiplying a field by a function of \(x\) maps degree \(l\) to a few neighbouring degrees, by two exact recurrences of the Schmidt harmonics (\(p_l\), \(q_l\) as in (3.8) below):

\[ egin{aligned} x hinspace Y_l &= p_l Y_{l+1} + q_l Y_{l-1} && o X,\cr (1 - x^2) rac{dY_l}{dx} = -\sin heta hinspace \partial_ heta Y_l &= (l+1)q_l Y_{l-1} - l p_l Y_{l+1} && o D , \end{aligned} \]

with rows the target degree and columns the source degree. Their adjoints under \(\int d\Omega\) (with \(N = \mathrm{diag}(n_l)\)) are \(X^\dagger = N^{-1}X^{ m T}N = X\) and \(D^\dagger = N^{-1}D^{ m T}N = 2X - D\) (integration by parts). \(P_n(X)\) and \(P_n'(X)\) follow from the three-term recurrences \((k+1)P_{k+1} = (2k+1)XP_k - kP_{k-1}\), \(P_{k+1}' = (k+1)P_k + XP_k'\). Write \(R_l = Y_l\hat{\mathbf r}\), \(S_l = r abla Y_l\), \(T_l = r abla Y_l imes\hat{\mathbf r}\) for the basis fields of (3.3), \(L\) for \(\mathrm{diag}(l(l+1))\) acting on the source and \(1/L'\) for the division of each row by its \(L'\) (0 for \(l' = 0\)). The operations needed by (2.7) are then:

operation result on \((q, s, t)\) from \(g(x) hinspace R_l\) \(q\): \(g(X)\) \(g(x) hinspace S_l\) \(s\): \((g(X)L - g'(X)D)/L'\), \(t\): \(-i m hinspace g'(X)/L'\) \(\int g abla Y_l\cdot abla Y_{l'}^\ast = \int Y_{l'}^\ast(L_l g Y_l - g' DY_l)\) \(g(x) hinspace T_l\) \(s\): \(i m hinspace g'(X)/L'\), \(t\): \((g(X)L - g'(X)D)/L'\) the same, rotated by \(\hat{\mathbf r} imes\) \(\hat{\mathbf z} imes(c hinspace Y\hat{\mathbf r})\) \(s\): \(-i m hinspace c/L'\), \(t\): \(D^\dagger c/L'\) \(\hat{\mathbf z} imes\hat{\mathbf r} = \sin heta hinspace \hat{\mathbf e}_ \phi\) \(\hat{\mathbf z} imes S_l\) \(-i m R_l - x T_l\) (2.5) \(\hat{\mathbf z} imes T_l\) \(-(DY_l)\hat{\mathbf r} + x S_l\) (2.5) \(\sin heta hinspace F_ heta\) (a scalar) \(-D s + i m hinspace t\) \(\sin heta hinspace \partial_ heta Y = -DY\)

diff_rot._primitives composes them, per unit \(G\) and per unit shape:

\[ egin{aligned} \mathbf W_{ m sh} &= P_n(x)\left[i m hinspace \mathbf u_{ m sh} + 2\hat{\mathbf z} imes\mathbf u_{ m sh} ight] + \hat{\mathbf z} imes\left[-P_n'(x)\sin heta hinspace u_{ heta,{ m sh}} hinspace \hat{\mathbf r} ight],\cr \mathbf W_{dq} &= \hat{\mathbf z} imes\left[P_n(x) hinspace Y\hat{\mathbf r} ight], \end{aligned} \]

with \(\mathbf u_q = R_l\), \(\mathbf u_a = S_l\), \(\mathbf u_T = T_l\) (the second term, the \(u_ heta\) part of the shear term, vanishes for the shape q). Every product is a sparse product of banded matrices, so the cost is \(O(l_{\max})\) and the result is exact to round-off at any degree. The matrices are built up to \(l_w\) = lmax + n + 6, because a product of matrices truncated at \(l_w\) is wrong only in its last few degrees.

tests/diff_rot/quad_reference.py computes the same primitives by Gauss–Legendre quadrature of the table above, as an independent check (§9). That costs \(O(l_{\max}^3)\), and it fails from \(l = 646\) on, where scipy.special.sph_harm_y returns NaN.

docs.title: 3.4 From the primitives to the radial operators
docs.text:
Put (3.7) into (3.6) and expand \(a_l\) with (3.1). For the \(v\) rows this is direct:

\[ \mathrm{row}_ v(\mathbf W) = \frac{G r^2\rho_0}{L'^2}\left[(L_l C^t_q + C^t_a)\frac{fP}{r} + C^t_a\thinspace f(P' + h'P) + C^t_T\thinspace f T + L_l C^t_{dq}\frac{(rf')P}{r}\right]. \]

For the \(u\) rows, \(\partial_r(r W^s)\) differentiates the profile and the unknowns: with \(r a = P + rP' + r h' P\),

\[ \begin{aligned} \partial_r(r f a) &= f'(P + rP' + rh'P) + f(2P' + rP'' + h'P + rh''P + rh'P'),\cr \partial_r\left(r\thinspace C_{dq}^s (rf')\frac{L_lP}{r}\right) &= L_l C^s_{dq}\left[(f' + r f'')P + (rf')P'\right], \end{aligned} \]

which is where \(r^2 f''\) enters. Collecting the coefficient of each radial operator gives the table below. Each coefficient is a matrix in \((l', l)\), and in the code it is stored multiplied by \(L'\); the operator then divides by \(L'^3\) (§7.1), so the net factor is \(1/L'^2\) as in (3.6). The radial operators include the row weights, and their labels (§6) use the profile codes {a}, {s}, {p} of \(f_n\), \(r f_n'\), \(r^2 f_n''\), that is zf, zd, zs followed by the degree character (zf0, zd0, zs0 for \(n = 0\), zf2, … ; §5.3).

(\(C^q_{dq} = 0\), since the shear term has no radial component, so df_2C_D0P keeps \(L_l C^q_{dq}\) only formally.)

docs.title: 3.5 Selection rules
docs.text:
• The angular factors of (2.7) are \(P_n\), \(xP_n\), \(\sin\theta P_n\) and \(\sin^2\theta\thinspace P_n'\), polynomials in \(x\) (up to the \(\sin\theta\) factors absorbed by \(\partial_\theta Y\) and \(Z\)) of degree at most \(n + 1\). So \(W\) from degree \(l\) reaches the target degrees \(\lvert l' - l\rvert \le n + 1\).
  • \(\Delta\Omega\) is even in \(x\), so \(\mathbf W\) keeps the equatorial symmetry of \(\mathbf u\). In kore's ordering the poloidal and toroidal degrees of one symmetry class alternate, so same-type couplings (\(P \to P\), \(T \to T\)) have even \(\Delta l\) and mixed ones (\(P \leftrightarrow T\)) odd \(\Delta l\).
  • Together: \(\lvert\Delta l\rvert \le n\) for \(P \to P\) and \(T \to T\), and \(\le n + 1\) for \(P \leftrightarrow T\) (diff_rot.max_dl). For \(\Delta\Omega = f_0 + f_2P_2\): \(\Delta l \in \lbrace 0, \pm 2\rbrace\) and \(\lbrace\pm 1, \pm 3\rbrace\); the \(f_0\) terms alone have \(\Delta l = 0\) and \(\pm 1\), like the Coriolis force.
  • For \(m = 0\) the Doppler term vanishes, but the Coriolis and shear terms do not.

The coupled problem is therefore wider than with uniform rotation: the row block of degree \(l'\) has entries in the column blocks of up to \(n_{\max} + 1\) neighbouring degrees of each type.

docs.title: 3.6 Closed forms for \(P_0\) and \(P_2\)
docs.text:
For \(n = 0\) and \(n = 2\) the coefficients of the table of §3.4 also have closed forms. kore builds every degree with the algebra of §3.3, and the closed forms check it, in tests/diff_rot/diff_rot_coefficients.py (44 functions, \(\lvert\Delta l\rvert \le 3\), and the \(\sigma_n\) of (2.10)): f_* and df_*, d2f_* for \(f_2\) (\(P_2\), unnormalised, despite "Y20" in the comments), f0_*, df0_*, d2f0_* for \(f_0\). Each function takes the target degree l, m and offdiag = \(l - l'\) (source minus target) and returns the coefficient, already multiplied by \(L'\), with explicit conditions where a degree would fall below \(m\) or below 1.

Two worked examples show the structure.

  • \(T \to T\), \(P_0\), \(\Delta l = 0\). With \(P_n = 1\), the T entries of the table of §3.3 give \(C^t_T = \left[i m L n_l + 2\int x(\partial_\theta Y Z^\ast - Z\partial_\theta Y^\ast)d\Omega\right]/(L n_l)\). For real \(Y\) and \(\partial_\theta Y\) the integral is \(-2im\int x Y\partial_\theta Y\thinspace d\theta\thinspace d\phi = -i m n_l\), so \(L C^t_T = i m (L - 2)\), which is f0_1C_D0T = 1j*(-2 + l + l**2)*m. The \(i m L\) is the Doppler term, and \(-2im\) is the local Coriolis force: compare operators.coriolis, whose \(T \to T\) row is \(-2 i m G\thinspace v_1/L^3\).
  • \(P \to T\), \(P_0\), \(\Delta l = -1\). For constant \(f_0 = a\), f0_1C_D0P = \(2(l-1)^2(l+1)\sqrt{l^2 - m^2}/(2l - 1)\) and f0_1C_lho1_D0P = f0_1C_D1P = \(-2(l^2 - 1)\sqrt{l^2 - m^2}/(2l - 1)\) are \(2L\) times the coefficients \(C(l - 1)\) and \(-C\) of the \(\Delta l = -1\) Coriolis row, \(C = (l-1)\sqrt{l^2 - m^2}/(l(2l - 1))\) (operators.coriolis). So a uniform \(f_0 = a\) gives exactly \(a\) times the Coriolis operator plus \(i m G a\) times the inertia operator, which is (2.12) at the matrix level.

The algebra (§3.3) and the closed forms agree to round-off, \(\le 1.3\times 10^{-15}\) of the largest coefficient of the same row block, up to lmax 1025 (tests/diff_rot/gen_check.py, §9). Entry by entry, the closed forms are the more accurate: a few coefficients are small differences of terms of size \(O(L)\) in the algebra of §3.4 (for example df0_2C_D1P = \(2im\) exactly, \(-L(C^s_a + L_l C^s_{dq})\) in the algebra), so their own relative error grows like \(L\epsilon\), about \(10^{-10}\) at \(l \approx 1000\), while staying at round-off on the scale of the row, which is the scale at which they enter \(A\).

docs.title: 3.7 The heat-equation terms in harmonic form
docs.text:
Multiplication by a function of \(x\) is a matrix on the degree index. With Schmidt harmonics and \(p_l = \sqrt{(l+1)^2 - m^2}/(2l+1)\), \(q_l = \sqrt{l^2 - m^2}/(2l+1)\):

\[ \begin{aligned} x\thinspace Y_l &= p_l Y_{l+1} + q_l Y_{l-1} &&\to X,\cr (1 - x^2)\frac{dY_l}{dx} &= (l+1)q_l Y_{l-1} - l p_l Y_{l+1} &&\to D , \end{aligned} \qquad (3.8) \]

with rows the target degree and columns the source degree. Multiplying by \(P_n(x)\) is then the matrix \(P_n(X)\), and by \(P_n'(x)\) the matrix \(P_n'(X)\). These are the matrices of the angular algebra of §3.3 (angular.Algebra), shared by the momentum and heat terms.

For one source degree, \(\partial_\theta S_{tw} = -\sin\theta\sum_n\sigma_n P_n'(x)\), and \(\sin\theta\thinspace \partial_\theta Y = -(1 - x^2)\thinspace dY/dx = -DY\). With (3.2), the three terms of (2.11) projected on degree \(l'\) are, before the row weight and the \(p_0\) factor,

\[ \begin{aligned} \text{(a)}\quad & i m G\sum_n f_n\thinspace \left[P_n(X)\right]_ {l'l}\thinspace s_l ,\cr \text{(b)}\quad & \frac{L_l P_l}{r}\sum_n\sigma_n'\thinspace \left[P_n(X)\right]_ {l'l} ,\cr \text{(c)}\quad & \frac{a_l}{r}\sum_n\sigma_n\thinspace \left[P_n'(X)\thinspace D\right]_ {l'l} ,\cr \text{(c}')\quad & -\frac{i m T_l}{r}\sum_n\sigma_n\thinspace \left[P_n'(X)\right]_ {l'l} . \end{aligned} \qquad (3.9) \]

(c) and (c′) are the poloidal and toroidal parts of the latitudinal term. The couplings are \(\Delta l \in \lbrace 0, \pm 2, \dots, \pm n_{\max}\rbrace\) for (a) (\(s \to s\)), \(\lbrace 0, \pm 2, \dots, \pm n_{tw}\rbrace\) for (b), (c) (\(P \to s\)) and \(\lbrace\pm 1, \dots, \pm(n_{tw} - 1)\rbrace\) for (c′) (\(T \to s\)), with \(n_{tw}\) the highest degree of \(S_{tw}\) (diff_rot.tw_nmax).

docs.title: 4. Implementation overview
docs.text:
Everything specific to the differential rotation is in one module, bin/diff_rot.py, built on the angular algebra of bin/angular.py. The rest of kore calls it:

stage what it does for the differential rotation where parameters switches, profile choice, amplitude, 'user' profiles bin/params_default.py angular algebra \(X\), \(D\), \(P_n(X)\), the vector operations, harmonics on a grid bin/angular.py everything else profiles, thermal wind, angular couplings, labels, blocks, Δl ranges bin/diff_rot.py radial matrices builds the matrices of the labels it is given (into submatrices.npz) submatrices.py (dr.labels()), radial_profiles.burrito (dr.profile_functions()) operators thin wrappers operators.differential_rotation, operators.thermal_diffrot assembly places the blocks, over the Δl of dr.dl_range assemble.py diagnostics powers and budgets on an \((r, \theta)\) grid, independently of the algebra utils4pp.diff_rot_setup, spin_doctor.py

diff_rot.py imports only parameters and angular at the top; utils and radial_profiles are imported inside the functions that need them. radial_profiles.burrito imports diff_rot when it meets a differential-rotation profile code, so there is no import cycle, and the angular part (_primitives, momentum_coefficients) can be imported and tested without a run directory.

docs.title: 4.1 Parameters
docs.text: The parameters are listed in Background model. Gaspard, Beyonce, ViscosD and ThermaD must be computed for \(\Omega_{\rm ref}\), and set after par.set_scales(), which resets them. With timescale = 'rotation' it sets Beyonce = 0, and thermal_wind 1 and 2 then stop submatrices.py with an error through diff_rot.check, since \(S_{tw} \propto 1/\mathrm{Beyonce}\).

docs.title: 5.1 The profiles \(f_n\) of each type
docs.text:
diff_rot.shapes defines the shape of each degree; \(f_n\) = diff_rot_ampl × \(a_n\) × shape, with \(a_n\) = diff_rot_term_amp[n/2] (1 in the table below). With \(a\) = diff_rot_ampl, \(p\) = diff_rot_param, and \(x\) the fractional solar radius (diff_rot.solar_x: \(x = r\cdot\)r_out with a solar structure (background.md), \(x = r\) otherwise):
