  • 'rigid'. The flow passes through the wall into the solid at rest, whose rows take its \(\mathbf u imes\mathbf B_0\): its flux leaves the fluid for the solid's field, as at a slipping wall, and stays out of the induction work (INDU_WALLS).

With a thin layer whose \(c\) is not zero this holds to the order of the approximation, as without the forcing.

Rotating solids (rotdyn = 1). The solids store their rotational and gravitational energy, and exchange energy with the fluid through the torques: the full budget gains that energy on the left, and the power of the viscous torques and the inner core's relaxation loss on the right, while the \(\mathbf u imes\mathbf B_0\) flux through the moving no-slip walls is minus the power of the magnetic torques and leaves the induction work (INDU_WALLS). Only with both torques on the solids (vtrq and mtrq 1); Rotating solids equations.

How the terms are computed. spin_doctor's Lorentz force (utils4pp.lorentz4pp) acts per volume, and its power \(\int\mathbf u^*\cdot\mathbf G\,dV\) has no \( ho_0\). Its induction term (induction4pp) takes the components of \(\mathbf u\) with their \(\lambda_1\) part, and holds for the non-solenoidal \(\mathbf u\) of a variable density (resid𝐛 closes to \(10^{-10}\) with 'Wu 2005', Checks). These spectral formulas are used for a poloidal field of degree 1 alone, with the closed-form couplings and no differential rotation. Otherwise (utils4pp.use_grid: a toroidal part, a poloidal field of degree other than 1, a differential rotation, the recurrence-algebra couplings, or KORE_MAG_GRID=1 in the environment) both come instead from utils4pp.magnetic_powers_grid, computed on an \((r, heta)\) grid from the vector fields \(\mathbf u\), \(\mathbf b\), \( abla imes\mathbf b\), \(\mathbf B_0\), \( abla imes\mathbf B_0\) (with the wall terms of the induction work); for a poloidal field it agrees with the spectral formulas to the 10 printed digits.

With a differential rotation. spin_doctor's induction work includes \(\mathbf U_0 imes\mathbf b\) (on the \((r, heta)\) grid). Because \(\mathbf U_0 imes\mathbf b\) does not vanish at a wall where \(\Delta\Omega e 0\), it carries magnetic energy through the wall into the field outside: resid𝐛 (the fluid) uses the induction work with its wall terms, resid𝐄 (the full budget, which counts the energy outside) the volume work alone (utils4pp.INDU_WALLS), plus the power of the rotation's force on the flow. Where a conducting solid turns with the fluid (a conducting inner core, a thin layer, a resolved mantle), the flux of \(\mathbf U_0 imes\mathbf b\) through its surface is the induction work of the solid's own rotation, \(\mathrm{Re}\int(\mathbf V imes\mathbf b)\cdot( abla imes\mathbf b)^*dV\) over it (\(\mathbf V\) rigid, the potential field beyond carries none), and resid𝐄 keeps it (utils4pp.INDU_ROT_SOLID). Without it resid𝐄 was about \(10^{-4}\) for a conducting inner core turning with \(\Delta\Omega(r_i) eq 0\); with it the budget is the same in every frame.

docs.title: Checks
docs.text:
The magnetic terms are checked in several independent ways, by the suites in tests/ (each has a README that lists its scripts):

  • Symbolic derivation. Every coupling of the Lorentz force and the induction is compared, term by term, with a projection computed from the definitions with sympy (tests/magnetic, Derivation tools).
  • Exact solutions. Free-decay rates of the field with insulating walls, a conducting inner core, a thin conducting layer and a resolved mantle (tests/decay, tests/twa, tests/mantle); a uniform offset of the rotation rate.
  • Published results. The inertial modes of Wu (2005), the modes of the Malkus (1967) field, and the torsional modes of Luo & Jackson (2022).
  • Limits. A thin resolved mantle against the thin-wall approximation; smoothed current sheets against the sheet conditions (tests/sheet); the Bessel inner core against the Chebyshev one (tests/forced_field); a weakly stratified 'Wu 2005' against 'Boussinesq'.
  • Budgets. resid𝐛 and resid𝐄 close to round-off for resolved modes, with every combination of walls, inner core, density profile, differential rotation and forcing (tests/magnetic, tests/forced_field, tests/inner_core).

docs.title: Magnetic field
docs.text:
With magnetic = 1, kore adds a background magnetic field of your choice and solves for small perturbations of the flow and of the field together: the Lorentz force acts on the flow, and the flow induces a perturbation of the field. The background field is fixed, steady and axisymmetric. It is imposed, not computed: there is no dynamo, and the background flow does not react to it.

The field does not enter the thermal-wind balance. The thermal-wind entropy is computed from the rotation alone, as without a field, and the Lorentz force acts only on the perturbations. This is exact for a current-free field, such as B0 = 'axial' or 'dipole', and a good approximation when the magnetic force is weak compared with the Coriolis force of the differential rotation (Validity and caveats).

This page shows how to set up a run and choose the background field. The equations and the formula of every field are on Magnetic field equations.

docs.title: Parameters and a first run
docs.text:
Two dimensionless numbers set how strong the field is and how fast it diffuses, both measured against the rotation:

parameter meaning Le Lehnert number: the Alfvén speed of the field over the rotation speed of the outer wall Em magnetic Ekman number: the magnetic diffusivity over the rotation rate times the radius squared

Two combinations are common: the magnetic Prandtl number Ek/Em and the Elsasser number Le**2/Em. The exact definitions are on Magnetic field equations.

A first run. A uniform field along the rotation axis, in a shell with insulating walls, with Elsasser and magnetic Prandtl numbers both equal to one. Add these lines at the end of a bin/parameters.py like the default one (which already imports numpy and sets m, symm, N, lmax and the target):

par.Ek = 1e-3                # Ekman number
par.Em = 1e-3                # magnetic Ekman number: Pm = Ek/Em = 1
par.Le = np.sqrt(1e-3)       # Lehnert number: Elsasser number Le**2/Em = 1
par.set_scales()             # call it again: it sets Hendrik and MagnetD from Le and Em

par.structure = 'Boussinesq' # any structure works (Background model)
par.magnetic = 1
par.thermal = 0              # no entropy equation
par.B0 = 'axial'             # the poloidal background field (tables below)
par.cnorm = 'mag_energy'     # its amplitude: the integral of B0**2 over the fluid is 1
par.B0_tor = None            # no toroidal background field
par.innercore = 'insulator'
par.mantle = 'insulator'
par.ricb = 0.35; par.bci = 1; par.bco = 1   # no-slip walls

set_scales() converts Le and Em into the factors that multiply the Lorentz force (Hendrik) and the magnetic diffusion (MagnetD), so call it after setting them. Two values of timescale are magnetic: 'Alfven' (the Alfvén time) and 'magnetic' (the magnetic diffusion time).

docs.title: Choosing the background field
docs.text: The background field is the sum of two parts: a poloidal part, whose field lines lie in meridional planes like those of a dipole, and a toroidal part, whose field lines are circles around the rotation axis. Choose a shape for each with B0 and B0_tor, then set their amplitude. B0 defaults to 'axial' and B0_tor to None; for a toroidal field alone, set B0 = None.

docs.title: Equatorial symmetry
docs.text:
• A poloidal field of odd degree is dipolar (antisymmetric about the equator), one of even degree quadrupolar (symmetric). For a toroidal field it is the other way round: degree 1 is symmetric, degree 2 antisymmetric.
  • The two parts must have the same symmetry. A dipole therefore combines with a toroidal field of degree 2, not 1.
  • symm still selects the symmetry of the flow.

docs.title: Poloidal field: B0
docs.text:
The formulas are on Magnetic field equations.

B0 the field extra parameters (default) geometry 'axial' (default) uniform, along the rotation axis – shell or full sphere 'dipole' the field of a dipole at the centre – shell only 'FDM' the slowest free-decay mode of degree B0_l (1 or 2) B0_l (1) shell or full sphere 'G21 dipole' a full-sphere dipole (Gerick et al. 2021) B0_ic shell or full sphere 'Luo_S1' the same shape (Luo & Jackson 2022) B0_ic shell or full sphere 'Luo_S2' a full-sphere quadrupole (Luo & Jackson 2022) B0_ic shell or full sphere 'confined' a field that is zero outside a spherical layer B0_l (1), B0_conf_r1 (0.0), B0_conf_r2 (0.6), B0_conf_p (12) the layer must lie in the fluid 'general' your own radial profile for each degree B0_profiles, B0_param shell or full sphere 'ferraro' field lines along the surfaces of constant rotation (below) B0_ferraro_G ('w'), B0_ferraro_nmax (15) needs diff_rot = 1 None no poloidal field
  • Full-sphere shapes with an inner core. 'G21 dipole', 'Luo_S1' and 'Luo_S2' are defined for a full sphere. With an inner core, B0_ic = 'potential' (default) continues the field into the core as a current-free field; B0_ic = 'frozen currents' keeps the full-sphere formula.
  • 'confined' fills the layer from B0_conf_r1 to B0_conf_r2. The defaults reach the centre, which suits a full sphere; with an inner core, set B0_conf_r1 at or above ricb. B0_conf_p (at least 3) sets how smoothly the field vanishes at the edges.

  • 'general' takes a numpy expression of r and p for each degree. In a full sphere the profile of degree n should behave as r**n near the centre. Example:

    par.B0_profiles = {1: 'r/6 - r**3/10', 3: '0.3*r**3*(1 - r**2)'}

  • At the walls. 'general' and 'ferraro' are treated as fields produced by currents inside the fluid. If they do not match a current-free field at an insulating wall, a current sheet forms there (Current sheets at slipping walls). Use 'axial' for a uniform field and 'dipole' for a dipole at the centre, rather than writing them as 'general'.

docs.title: Toroidal field: B0_tor
docs.text:
A toroidal field is purely azimuthal, so differential rotation does not wind it up; it suits any rotation. The formulas are on Magnetic field equations.

B0_tor the field extra parameters (default) None (default) no toroidal field 'Malkus' grows linearly with distance from the axis (Malkus 1967) B0_tor_l (1) 'wall' zero at both walls B0_tor_l (1) 'user' a radial shape given as an expression of r and p B0_tor_profile, B0_tor_param, B0_tor_l (1) 'general' your own radial profile for each degree B0_tor_profiles, B0_tor_param

B0_tor_l is 1 or 2. A 'user' profile must be smooth, since its second derivative enters the equations. Expressions must not contain #.

A toroidal field that is not zero at a wall ends there in a current sheet, unless a conductor beyond the wall carries it on (Current sheets at slipping walls). With the rotating solids it must vanish at both walls.

docs.title: Amplitude
docs.text:
The shapes above have arbitrary scales, so the size of the field is set separately: the field is Le times a dimensionless field whose size is set by cnorm (poloidal part) and cnorm_tor (toroidal part).

value meaning a number (default 1) multiplies the formula as it is 'mag_energy' the integral of the squared field over the fluid is 1 (Luo & Jackson 2022). Recommended 'Schmitt2012' the integral of the squared field over the fluid is 4 'rms_cmb' the rms radial field at the outer wall is 1 (cnorm only, not for 'confined', 'general', 'ferraro') 'rms_Bs' the volume rms of the cylindrical radial field \(B_s\) over the fluid is 1 (cnorm only, not for 'axial', whose \(B_s\) is zero). The field of torsional oscillations

With 'mag_energy', Le and the Elsasser number refer to a field of fixed energy, whatever its shape. With a number, the strength of the field depends on the arbitrary scale of the formula.

docs.title: With a differential rotation
docs.text:
With diff_rot = 1 (Background model), the shear acts on the field in two ways:

  • It shears the perturbation field. kore includes this for any rotation profile.
  • It winds up the background poloidal field into an azimuthal field, which grows until magnetic diffusion balances it. kore keeps the background fixed and does not follow this growth. The background is therefore steady only if nothing is wound up, or if it already contains the balanced azimuthal field.

docs.title: The Ferraro condition
docs.text:
Differential rotation does not wind up a poloidal field line if the rotation rate is the same all along it (Ferraro's law of isorotation). A toroidal field always satisfies it; a poloidal field usually does not.

At the start of a run with a poloidal field and diff_rot = 1, kore prints how far the field and the rotation are from this condition (definition) and warns if the mismatch is significant. Set ferraro_policy = 'refuse' to make it stop instead.

docs.title: Four ways to a steady background
docs.text:
set-up what kore does other parameters (default) use it when B0 = 'ferraro' keeps the rotation, and uses a poloidal field whose lines lie along the surfaces of constant rotation B0_ferraro_G ('w'), B0_ferraro_nmax (15, odd) the rotation is given, and any field that it does not wind up will do diff_rot_type = 'ferraro' keeps the field, and uses a rotation that is constant along each field line diff_rot_F ('psi'), diff_rot_nmax (8) the field is given, and the rotation only has to fit it B0 = 'confined' nothing: you put the field in a layer where the rotation is uniform B0_conf_r1, B0_conf_r2 the field lives away from the shear (e.g. below the tachocline) B0_wound = 1 keeps both, and adds the azimuthal field that the shear winds up, balanced by diffusion B0_wound_eta (1.0) both are given and do not match

B0 = 'ferraro'. The field lines follow the surfaces of constant rotation, so nothing is wound up. B0_ferraro_G, a function of the rotation rate w, sets how much magnetic flux passes between the axis and each surface. Where the rotation is uniform the field vanishes. kore prints how well the field stays inside the fluid. cnorm must be a number, 'mag_energy' or 'Schmitt2012'.

diff_rot_type = 'ferraro'. kore keeps the poloidal field and replaces the rotation by one that is constant along each field line. diff_rot_F gives the rotation rate of each field line as a function of the flux function psi. With a quadrupolar field, diff_rot_F must be even in psi.

B0 = 'confined'. If the rotation is uniform in the layer of the field, as below the solar tachocline, nothing is wound up.

B0_wound = 1. kore keeps the poloidal field and the rotation as given, and adds the azimuthal field that the shear winds up, at the strength where diffusion balances the winding. Its strength follows from the physics, not from cnorm: it grows with the shear and with the inverse of the diffusivity, and can be many times stronger than the poloidal field. B0_wound_eta is the diffusivity used for this balance, in units of MagnetD. This background holds only while something maintains the rotation against the magnetic braking. Read Validity and caveats before using it.

B0 = 'ferraro' and diff_rot_type = 'ferraro' describe a field and a rotation that have reached isorotation. B0_wound = 1 describes a shear that something maintains across the field lines.

A conducting inner core must rotate rigidly with the fluid at its surface, so the rotation at ricb must not depend on latitude.

docs.title: Inner core and walls
docs.text:
The perturbation field is matched at each wall to the field beyond it. The mantle is an insulator, possibly with a conducting layer at its base: either a thin one, described by boundary conditions alone, or one of any thickness whose field kore solves for. The inner core is an insulator (again possibly with a thin conducting layer), or a conductor whose field kore solves for.

setting values (default) notes mantle 'insulator' (default), 'TWA' or 'resolved' 'TWA': a thin conducting layer; 'resolved': a conducting layer of any thickness (both below) innercore 'insulator' (default), 'conducting, Chebys', 'conducting, Bessel' or 'TWA' need ricb > 0; 'conducting, Bessel' in forced runs only (Forced runs) N_cic 64 number of Chebyshev polynomials for the inner-core field with 'conducting, Chebys' (even, at least 4) mu_i2o 1.0 magnetic permeability, inner core over fluid sigma_i2o 1.0 electrical conductivity, inner core over fluid B0_ic 'potential' for 'G21 dipole', 'Luo_S1', 'Luo_S2' with an inner core (above)

Matching conditions: Magnetic field equations.

docs.title: Thin conducting layer
docs.text:
A thin conducting layer, such as the base of the Earth's mantle, carries currents that couple the field across it. 'TWA' (the thin-wall approximation of Roberts, Glatzmaier & Clune 2010) models such a layer, at the base of the mantle or on an insulating inner core, through boundary conditions alone, without extra unknowns.

setting default meaning c_cmb, c_icb 1e-5, 0 thickness times permeability of the layer, relative to the wall radius and to the fluid's permeability c1_cmb, c1_icb 1e-5, 0 conductance of the layer: thickness times conductivity, relative to the wall radius and to the fluid's conductivity muw_cmb, muw_icb 1.0 permeability of the layer relative to vacuum mu 1.0 permeability of the fluid relative to vacuum (used only by the thin-wall conditions) B0_cmb 'wall' how the background field meets a thin layer at the outer wall: 'wall' adjusts it to the layer, 'plain' keeps it as given
  • With the default permeabilities the conductance c1 sets nearly all of the effect of the layer.
  • Validity. The layer must be thin compared with its magnetic skin depth at the frequency of the mode. spin_doctor prints the estimated relative error, εTWA; keep it below about 1 %.
  • With differential rotation, a conducting layer turns with the fluid next to it, so the rotation must be uniform in latitude at that wall.
  • On the exact spheroid (centrifugal_shape = 'spheroid') the layer at the outer wall works in its thin limit, c_cmb = 0 and mu = 1, with a no-slip or a slipping fluid at the wall. The layer lies between two level surfaces, so in an oblate body it is a little thicker at the equator than at the poles (The exact spheroid).

The conditions: Magnetic field equations.

docs.title: Resolved conducting mantle
docs.text:
When the conducting layer is too thick, too conducting, or the mode too slow for the thin-wall approximation, use mantle = 'resolved'. kore then puts a conducting layer between the outer wall and r_surface, with an insulator beyond, and solves for the field inside it. The layer is solid and at rest, and its conductivity may vary with radius.

setting default meaning r_surface 1.83 outer radius of the layer, the outer wall being at 1 (1.83 is the whole mantle of the Earth) N_mantle 64 number of Chebyshev polynomials for the field in the layer (at least 4) sigma_mantle 1.0 conductivity of the layer relative to the fluid's: a number, or an expression of r and p such as '1e-2*exp(-p*(r - 1))' sigma_mantle_param 0.0 the p of that expression
  • Resolution. The conductivity profile must be smooth; kore stops if N_mantle does not resolve it. Check the field in the layer with a second run at a larger N_mantle.
  • With differential rotation the rotation must be uniform in latitude at the outer wall.
  • The layer and the fluid have the permeability of vacuum (mu = 1).
  • On the exact spheroid (centrifugal_shape = 'spheroid') the layer ends at the level surface r_surface, a spheroid of the same flattening, and with the flow the outer wall must be no-slip (bco = 1) (The exact spheroid).

The equations: Magnetic field equations.

docs.title: Current sheets at slipping walls
docs.text:
A background field that does not match the field beyond an insulating wall ends there in a sheet of electric current. This happens for a toroidal field that is not zero at the wall, or a poloidal field that does not match the current-free field outside. A conductor beyond the wall (a conducting inner core, a resolved mantle or a conducting thin layer) carries the field on, with no sheet. The sheet pushes the fluid along the wall. A no-slip wall takes that push; along a stress-free wall, kore includes it in the boundary conditions (Magnetic field equations).

An inviscid fluid cannot take this push, so a current sheet stops an inviscid run. Use a field that matches at the wall (such as B0_tor = 'wall'), a viscous fluid, or a conductor beyond the wall.

docs.title: The field without the flow
docs.text:
Free decay: hydro = 0. Without the momentum equation the field only diffuses (and is carried by the differential rotation, if any). Each mode decays at a rate set by the conductivity, the walls and the inner core, which for uniform conductivity is known exactly: a useful check of the boundary conditions. B0 still sets the equatorial symmetry of the perturbation. With thermal = 1 the same switch gives the free decay of the entropy. This works for eigenvalue problems only.

Kinematic induction. bin/just_induction.py and bin/solve_ind.py give the field that a given flow induces, without the force of that field on the flow. Build a magnetic eigenvalue problem (submatrices.py, assemble.py), put the flow in flow.npy (Output files) from a run with the same N, lmax, m, symm and ricb, then run

./bin/just_induction.py [lambda]
mpiexec -n 4 ./bin/solve_ind.py

The optional lambda is the time dependence of the flow, a complex number such as the eigenvalue of a mode; by default it is \(i\) times forcing_frequency. The field is written to magnetic.npy.

docs.title: Forced runs
docs.text:
With a field, every forcing except the wave-like tide (forcing 1) works as without one: the field is solved together with the flow at the forcing frequency, and spin_doctor checks the budgets (Tidal forcing, Libration, Thermal forcing, Spherical Couette flow, Convective forcing).

  • A conducting inner core at one frequency. innercore = 'conducting, Bessel' uses the exact solution inside a uniform conducting core at the forcing frequency, so it adds no unknowns. It gives the same result as 'conducting, Chebys', but only for forced runs at forcing_frequency (not for frequency scans).
  • Walls that turn. In the libration (forcing 7 with m = 0) and the rotating walls (forcing 12), a conducting solid behind a turning wall turns with it.

docs.title: A boundary that moves
docs.text:
Forcings 6, 9, 10 and 14, and forcing 7 with m = 2, represent a boundary that moves or is not spherical. The walls stay spherical and the forcing prescribes the radial flow at the wall. A conducting solid behind the wall moves too, and forced_walls sets how:

forced_walls the solid behind the wall suits 'rigid' stays at rest; only its shape moves past the sphere a triaxial mantle that librates (7 with m = 2), the flattened inner core of forcing 6 'deforming' deforms with the boundary a boundary that moves (9, 10), a tide (14) None (default) 'rigid' for forcings 6 and 7, 'deforming' for 9, 10 and 14

With insulating solids forced_walls changes nothing. A moving wall that the background field reaches needs the same magnetic permeability on both sides (mu, mu_i2o and the thin layer's muw equal to 1); kore stops otherwise. The eccentricity tide (forcing 2) needs insulating walls.

The equations: Magnetic field equations.

docs.title: What is supported
docs.text:
kore checks the combination of options at startup and stops, with a message, on any it cannot handle.

Supported: a shell or a full sphere; any structure; eigenvalue problems and forced runs; with or without differential rotation; a viscous fluid, or an inviscid one in a full sphere; with or without the flow (hydro = 0); insulating walls, a thin conducting layer, a resolved conducting mantle or a conducting inner core; rotating solids (Rotating solids). The magnetic diffusivity of the fluid is uniform.

The main restrictions:

  • a background field is required, and Le and Em must not be zero;
  • a conducting inner core, or a conducting layer at a wall, needs the rotation to be uniform in latitude at that wall;
  • walls with zero radial stress (bci or bco = 2) do not work with a conducting solid behind them;
  • the poloidal and toroidal parts must have the same equatorial symmetry;
  • 'conducting, Bessel' works only in forced runs at a single frequency;
  • a current sheet at the wall of an inviscid fluid stops the run;
  • the wave-like tide (forcing 1) does not work with a field.

Combining features shows how the field combines with the other features.

docs.title: Output
docs.text:
solve.py writes the perturbation field to magnetic.npy, plus magnetic_ic.npy for a conducting inner core and magnetic_mantle.npy for a resolved mantle (Output files). Each eigenvector is normalised so that its total (kinetic plus magnetic) energy is 1.

spin_doctor includes the Lorentz force in its budgets and prints two more residuals: resid𝐛, the energy budget of the induction equation, and resid𝐄, the full energy budget including the field outside the fluid. Like residσ (Solver), they should be small for a resolved mode; with a thin conducting layer of non-zero thickness, resid𝐄 is only as small as the approximation error εTWA. It also prints Mag/Kin, the ratio of magnetic to kinetic energy, and writes magnetic.dat (Output files).

docs.title: Practical tips
docs.text:
The field, more than the flow, usually sets the resolution and memory a run needs.

  • Resolution. Where a poloidal field crosses a no-slip wall, a thin magnetic boundary layer (a Hartmann layer) forms. It usually sets N, and it gets thinner at lower Ekman numbers. A toroidal field alone has no Hartmann layer and converges faster. A full sphere needs about twice the N of a shell. Always compare the residuals at two values of N.
  • 'confined' converges more slowly than the other fields.
  • tol_B0 (default 1e-8) is the relative truncation of the background field's radial series. Lower it for more accurate operators, at some cost in memory.
  • mag_couplings. 'closed' (default) uses closed formulas, which exist for fields of degree 1 and 2. 'algebra' works for any degree and is used automatically for 'general', 'ferraro' and B0_wound = 1. Both give the same eigenvalues.
  • Memory. Fields of high degree couple more harmonics and need more memory. If MUMPS stops with INFOG(1) = −9, raise st_mat_mumps_icntl_14 in petsc_opts (Solver).

docs.title: Validity and caveats
docs.text:
kore holds the background field and the background flow fixed. This leaves out two effects:

  • Ohmic decay. A field that carries electric current would slowly decay. Only the wound field is steady by itself.
  • The Lorentz force of the background field on the background flow. The rotation is imposed, and the thermal wind is computed from the rotation alone.

docs.title: When the field leaves the thermal wind unchanged
docs.text:
Exactly, for a current-free field. A poloidal field that carries no current in the fluid exerts no force, so the thermal wind is exact. B0 = 'axial' and 'dipole' are such fields.

Approximately, for any other field, under three conditions (the derivations are in Magnetic field equations):

  1. The magnetic force in the meridional plane is weak compared with the Coriolis force of the differential rotation:

    \[ \frac{\mathrm{Le}^2\,\lvert\mathbf B_0\rvert^2}{\rho_0} \ll 2\,\lvert\Delta\Omega\rvert , \]

    with \(\rho_0\) the background density, \(\mathbf B_0\) the whole dimensionless field (wound part included) and \(\Delta\Omega\) the relative differential rotation.

  2. The magnetic braking is slow. A poloidal field crossed by the shear brakes it. The braking must be slow compared with the mode frequencies and damping rates, and with whatever maintains the rotation.

  3. The field is steady: the Ferraro condition holds, or B0_wound = 1 balances the winding.

The direct effect of the field on a mode, which kore includes in full, can be much larger than its effect on the thermal wind. So a field can change the modes noticeably while leaving the thermal wind unchanged.

docs.title: Wound fields and the tachocline
docs.text: A B0_wound background is a snapshot: it holds only for modes faster than the magnetic braking and the Ohmic decay. With molecular diffusivities, even a weak poloidal field in the solar radiative interior would quickly enforce isorotation along its field lines (the tachocline confinement problem: Gough & McIntyre 1998). A field below the tachocline is better represented by a 'confined' field whose layer lies there, where the rotation is uniform. A toroidal B0_tor can be added in the tachocline and the convection zone, since a toroidal field is never wound up.

docs.title: The Sun, Jupiter and Saturn
docs.text:
Estimates with published values (details):

  • Sun, convection zone and tachocline. The approximation holds for fields up to about \(2\times10^4\) G. At the base of the convection zone a \(10^4\) G field can noticeably affect modes with several wavelengths along the field.
  • Sun, radiative interior. The rotation is uniform; use a 'confined' field there.
  • Jupiter and Saturn. The approximation holds easily, and the fields have a negligible effect on the large-scale inertial modes.

docs.title: Checklist for solar inertial modes
docs.text:
Solar inertial modes have periods longer than a rotation, so the field's effect on them is relatively large and the background must stay steady over their lifetime.

  • Time scales. The magnetic braking and decay must be slow compared with the damping of the modes.
  • Sensitivity. Low-frequency modes feel the field most. Scan Le and B0_wound_eta rather than trusting one value.
  • Critical layers and continua. Check convergence in N and lmax, and distinguish discrete modes from continuous parts of the spectrum.
  • Thermal wind. Keep it on (thermal_wind 1 or 2) and check condition 1 above.
  • Consistent diffusivities. Take a turbulent magnetic Prandtl number near one (Em close to Ek), and build the wound field with the same diffusivity (B0_wound_eta = 1).
  • Radiative interior. Keep the field where the rotation is uniform: use 'confined', not B0_wound.
  • Measurability. A frequency shift matters only above about 1 nHz.
  • Field geometry. The field inside the Sun is not known. Compute the same modes with more than one geometry at a similar strength; the spread shows how much the results depend on the assumed field.

docs.title: Further reading
docs.text:
• Magnetic field equations: the equations, every field profile, the boundary conditions and the energy budgets.
  • Derivation tools: how the magnetic terms are derived and checked.
  • Output files: the columns of magnetic.dat.

docs.title: Numerical method
docs.text: This page shows how kore turns the anelastic equations into the sparse matrices of an eigenvalue problem: the unknowns, the radial basis, the rows, the boundary conditions and the checks of a solution. The terms of a differential rotation are built in the same way (Differential rotation, §3 to §7).

docs.title: Unknowns
docs.text:
At fixed \(m\) and equatorial symmetry, the velocity is written with a poloidal scalar \(P\) and a toroidal scalar \(T\),

\[ \mathbf u = rac{1}{ ho_0} abla imes abla imes\left( ho_0 P hinspace\mathbf r ight) + abla imes\left(T hinspace\mathbf r ight), \]

so that \( abla\cdot( ho_0\mathbf u) = 0\) holds exactly and the mass equation is never solved. For one harmonic \(Y = Y_l^m( heta,\phi)\), with \(P = P_l(r) hinspace Y\), \(T = T_l(r) hinspace Y\) and \(\mathcal L = l(l+1)\),

\[ u_r = rac{\mathcal L hinspace P_l}{r} hinspace Y, \qquad \mathbf u_h = \left(P_l' + rac{P_l}{r} + rac{d\ln ho_0}{dr}P_l ight) r abla Y + T_l hinspace abla Y imes\mathbf r , \]

with a prime for \(d/dr\) (utils4pp.cheb2space_pol, cheb2space_tor). With thermal = 1 the third unknown is \(s = s_l(r) hinspace Y\). With compositional = 1 the composition \(c = c_l(r) hinspace Y\), of the degrees and parity of \(s\), comes after the unknowns of the field and before those of the rotating solids, so that a run without it keeps the layout of its matrices.

docs.title: Radial basis
docs.text:
Each radial function \(P_l\), \(T_l\), \(s_l\), \(c_l\) is expanded in Chebyshev polynomials: N of them on the shell \([\)ricb\(, 1]\), or, in a full sphere (ricb = 0), the N/2 polynomials on \([-1, 1]\) that have the parity of the field. A radial derivative of order \(k\) maps Chebyshev coefficients to coefficients in the Gegenbauer (ultraspherical) basis \(C^{(k)}\), where it is a sparse matrix, and so is the product with a profile expanded in Chebyshev polynomials. The rows of each section are written in the Gegenbauer basis of its highest derivative: \(C^{(4)}\) for u, \(C^{(2)}\) for v, h and c (\(C^{(0)}\) for h with ThermaD = 0, \(C^{(1)}\) if a thermal wind is included; \(C^{(0)}\) for c with CompoD = 0). This makes \(A\) and \(B\) sparse.

An inviscid fluid (ViscosD = 0, in a full sphere) has its u rows in \(C^{(2)}\) and its v rows in \(C^{(1)}\). With a magnetic field, or a background flow, those rows also hold third and second derivatives, and inviscid_basis sets how they are written. With 'low' (the default) the rows stay in \(C^{(2)}\) and \(C^{(1)}\), and those terms are converted back exactly, which makes their blocks of \(A\) dense. With 'high' the rows are in \(C^{(3)}\) and \(C^{(2)}\), and \(A\) stays sparse, but the eigenvalues converge much more slowly with N: at N = 128 the torsional modes of Luo & Jackson (2022) are \(10^{-4}\) off with 'high' against \(5\cdot10^{-6}\) with 'low'. Use 'high' only when the dense blocks cost too much memory, at N of about 1000 or more.

docs.title: Rows
docs.text:
The pressure is removed by taking the radial components of the curl and of the double curl of the momentum equation; \( abla\Pi\) drops out of both because it is a gradient. Each term becomes a radial operator acting on \(P_l\), \(T_l\) or \(s_l\):

section rows equation used u of \(P_l\) \(r^5 ho_0 hinspace\hat{\mathbf r}\cdot abla imes abla imes( ext{momentum})/\mathcal L^3\) v of \(T_l\) \(r^3 ho_0 hinspace\hat{\mathbf r}\cdot abla imes( ext{momentum})/\mathcal L^3\) h of \(s_l\) \(r^2 hinspace( ext{heat equation})/\mathcal L^3\) c of \(c_l\) \(r^2 hinspace( ext{equation of the composition})/\mathcal L^3\)

All rows are projected on \(Y_l^m\) and divided by \(\mathcal L^3\), with \(l\) the degree of the row. The powers of \(r\) are rpower_u (5) and rpower_v (3), the smallest that keep every operator a polynomial in \(r\). The factor \( ho_0\) (rhopower_u = rhopower_v = 1) improves the accuracy of the viscous rows near a surface where \( ho_0\) is small. Without viscosity (ViscosD = 0), which kore takes in a full sphere only (it stops an inviscid fluid in a shell), the momentum rows are \(r^3 ho_0^2\) and \(r^2 ho_0\) times the equations. With ThermaD = 0 the heat rows are divided by \(p_0\), \(r hinspace(\partial_t s + u_r hinspace dS/dr)/\mathcal L^3\), which is better conditioned where \(p_0\) is small (and \(r^2/p_0\) times the equation with the thermal wind or a background flow); with CompoD = 0 those of the composition are divided by \( ho_0\) in the same way. The Coriolis force couples \(l\) to \(l\pm1\); the other terms keep \(l\).

term function in bin/operators.py profiles \(\partial_t\mathbf u\) inertia \(\ln ho_0\) \(2 hinspace\mathrm{Gaspard} hinspace\hat{\mathbf z} imes\mathbf u\) coriolis \(\ln ho_0\) \(\mathrm{ViscosD} hinspace ho_0^{-1} abla\cdot( ho_0 u\mathsf S)\) viscous_diffusion \(\ln ho_0\) (up to its 4th derivative), \( u\) (up to its 2nd) \(\mathrm{Beyonce} hinspace g hinspace s hinspace\hat{\mathbf r}\) buoyancy \(g\) \(p_0 hinspace\partial_t s\) entropy \(p_0\) \(p_0 hinspace u_r hinspace dS/dr\) thermal_advection \(p_0 hinspace dS/dr\) (\(dS/dr\) if ThermaD = 0) \(\mathrm{ThermaD} hinspace abla\cdot(\kappa p_0 abla s)\) thermal_diffusion \(\kappa p_0\) \(\mathrm{BeyonceC} hinspace g hinspace c hinspace\hat{\mathbf r}\) comp_buoyancy \(g\) \( ho_0 hinspace\partial_t c\) composition \( ho_0\) \( ho_0 hinspace u_r hinspace dC/dr\) comp_advection \( ho_0 hinspace dC/dr\) (\(dC/dr\) if CompoD = 0) \(\mathrm{CompoD} hinspace abla\cdot(D ho_0 abla c)\) comp_diffusion \(D ho_0\)

submatrices.py writes one sparse matrix per radial operator, for example u1lho2_D0 for \(r^4 ho_0 hinspace(\ln ho_0)''\) times the unknown (the label grammar and the profile codes are in utils.decode_label and radial_profiles.proffdir). For the section h row with ThermaD > 0, for example, the diffusion term is

\[ r^2 abla\cdot(\kappa p_0 abla s) = \left[r^2\kappa p_0 hinspace s_l'' + \left(2r\kappa p_0 + r^2(\kappa p_0)' ight)s_l' - \mathcal L hinspace\kappa p_0 hinspace s_l ight] Y. \]

docs.title: Eigenproblem
docs.text:
assemble.py puts the blocks into \(A\mathbf x = \lambda B\mathbf x\). \(B\) holds \(-\)inertia in the momentum rows and entropy in the heat rows. \(A\) holds coriolis \(-\) viscous_diffusion \(-\) buoyancy in the momentum rows and \(-\)thermal_advection \(+\) thermal_diffusion in the heat rows, so each row reads

\[ \lambda hinspace\mathbf u + 2 hinspace\mathrm{Gaspard} hinspace\hat{\mathbf z} imes\mathbf u = \mathrm{ViscosD} hinspace ho_0^{-1} abla\cdot( ho_0 u\mathsf S) + \mathrm{Beyonce} hinspace g hinspace s hinspace\hat{\mathbf r}, \] \[ \lambda hinspace p_0 s = -p_0 u_r rac{dS}{dr} + \mathrm{ThermaD} hinspace abla\cdot(\kappa p_0 abla s), \]

projected as in the table above. The composition enters in the same way: composition in \(B\), \(-\)comp_buoyancy in the momentum rows of \(A\), and \(-\)comp_advection \(+\) comp_diffusion in its own rows. solve.py finds the eigenvalues nearest a target \( au\) by shift-and-invert with SLEPc, factoring \(A - au B\) once with MUMPS (Solver). Forced runs solve \((A - i hinspace\mathrm{wf} hinspace B)\mathbf x = \mathbf b\), with wf the forcing frequency; for the random force of forcing 11, \(\mathbf b\) is derived on Reynolds-stress forcing.

docs.title: Boundary conditions
docs.text:
The conditions (assemble.bc_u_spherical, bc_theta_spherical) are applied at the outer wall (bco) and at the inner one (bci, when ricb > 0); the full sphere has no condition at the centre:

setting condition rows bco = 0 stress-free \(u_r = 0\), and zero tangential stress \(\partial_r(u_\theta/r) = \partial_r(u_\phi/r) = 0\) \(P_l = 0\), \(\thinspace r^2P_l'' + r^2(\ln\rho_0)'P_l' + \left[r^2(\ln\rho_0)'' + \mathcal L - 2 - r(\ln\rho_0)'\right]P_l = 0\), \(\thinspace rT_l' - T_l = 0\) bco = 0 with a drag (kappa_cmb, topo_drag) \(u_r = 0\), and the tangential stress balances the drag of the wall on the slip the stress-free rows plus the terms of the drag (Drag at the outer wall equations) bco 0 or 2 where the background field ends in a current sheet the tangential stress balances the push of the sheet on the fluid the stress-free rows plus the terms of the push (Magnetic field equations) bco = 1 no-slip \(\mathbf u = 0\) \(P_l = 0\), \(\thinspace P_l' + \left[(\ln\rho_0)' + 1/r\right]P_l = 0\), \(\thinspace T_l = 0\) bco_thermal = 0 fixed entropy \(s_l = 0\) bco_thermal = 1 zero diffusive entropy flux \(s_l' = 0\) bco_compositional = 0 fixed composition \(c_l = 0\) bco_compositional = 1 zero diffusive flux of the composition \(c_l' = 0\)

The density enters the stress-free and no-slip rows through \(u_\theta\) and \(u_\phi\). The thermal conditions are used only when ThermaD > 0, those of the composition only when CompoD > 0. Without viscosity only \(P_l = 0\) is imposed at the outer wall, whatever bco. bco = 2 (and bci = 2) replaces \(u_r = 0\) by a zero viscous radial stress, \(\left[r(\ln\rho_0)' - 3\right]P_l + 3rP_l' = 0\), which does not contain the pressure.

docs.title: Regularity at the centre
docs.text:
The centre of a full sphere is not a boundary, but the fields must be smooth there, and kore imposes no condition to make them so. This section says why none is needed, when a solution is still not smooth at the centre, and how to check it.

A field that is smooth at the centre has radial functions that go as \(r^l\) there, for a component of degree \(l\), times a series in \(r^2\). The basis gives \(P_l\), \(T_l\), \(s_l\) (and the \(f_l\), \(g_l\) of a magnetic field) the parity of \(l\), and the equations exclude the lower powers of that parity, as long as the background is smooth at the centre too. Each background profile follows the same rule with its own degree \(n\): the \(f_n\) of a differential rotation, the \(h_n\), \(k_n\) of a magnetic field, the \(\sigma_n\) of a thermal wind and the \(P_n\), \(T_n\), \(\sigma_n\), \(\gamma_n\) of a background flow go as \(r^n\), \(dS/dr\) and \(g\) as \(r\), and \(\ln\rho_0\), \(p_0\), \(\nu\), \(\kappa\) are series in \(r^2\). kore evaluates every profile at \(\lvert r\rvert\) with the parity of its degree, which gives the parity but neither the power nor the smoothness. A profile can fail in two ways:

  • It lacks the power. The \(P_2\) term of 'Y20' and 'conical', and the entropy of thermal_wind 3, keep their value at the centre. The modes converge in N, but to solutions that are not smooth there either.
  • It has a kink or a jump. Its even or odd continuation to \(r < 0\) is not smooth: 'Y20-wall-bounded', 'shellular' unless \(\sigma\) is even and positive, a 'user' expression in \(\lvert r\rvert\), a \(dS/dr\) that changes abruptly near the centre. The modes then converge slowly in N.

With ricb = 0, submatrices.py checks every profile near the centre and prints a WARNING for each failure (background.centre_check).

Spurious modes. Without viscosity (ViscosD = 0) or with ThermaD = 0, the spectrum of a full sphere also holds modes that do not converge when N or lmax is raised: without viscosity some of them grow, with ThermaD = 0 they crowd near zero frequency. Many of them sit at the centre, where they are not smooth; others sit at the wall. Target the frequency of the mode you want, and keep the modes that stay put in N and lmax.

irreg₀. In a full sphere spin_doctor prints irreg₀ for each solution (column 28 of flow.dat): the largest term \(a_p r^p\) with \(p < l\) of the flow and of the field, at \(r = \pi/\mathrm N\) (about the spacing of the Chebyshev points at the centre), relative to their largest value (utils4pp.centre_irregularity). It is at round-off for a resolved smooth mode and near 1 for a spurious mode at the centre. Values in between come from a background that is not smooth at the centre, or from a mode that is not resolved there. After the table spin_doctor counts the solutions above \(10^{-6}\).

docs.title: Checks
docs.text:
spin_doctor.py evaluates the budgets of Energy balance for each solution, from the fields and independently of the matrices. The radial integrals use Gauss–Legendre quadrature with \(3N/2\) nodes, the angular ones the orthogonality of the harmonics (\(\int\lvert Y_l vert^2 hinspace d\Omega = 4\pi/(2l+1)\)). The force of a differential rotation and the dissipation \(D_ u\) are computed on an \((r, \cos heta)\) grid, with Gauss–Legendre quadrature in \(\cos heta\), exact for these polynomials. Each residual is relative to the largest of its terms:

residual budget in spin_doctor's names residσ \(2\sigma K - W_ u - W_b - W_c - W_\Omega - W_p - W_f = 0\) (and the Lorentz work) 2σ KE - Dkin - Wthm - Wcmp - Wdr - Wp - Wf residω its imaginary part, with the Coriolis force 2w KE + Wcor_im - Dkin_im - Wthm_im - Wcmp_im - Wdr_im - Wp_im - Wf_im, \(w = \mathrm{Im} hinspace\lambda\) resid\(s\) \(2\sigma T - W_{ m adv} + D_{ m th} - W_{\Omega, m th} = 0\) 2σ TE - Dthm - Wadv - Wdr_thm (Dthm \(= -D_{ m th}\)) resid\(c\) \(2\sigma C - W_{ m adv,c} + D_{ m c} = 0\) 2σ CE - Dcmp - Wadv_cmp - Wdr_cmp (Dcmp \(= -D_{ m c}\)) residD \(W_ u - W_ u^{ m wall} + D_ u = 0\) Dkin - (Wv_icb + Wv_cmb) + Dvisc resid𝐋 \(\lambda L\) = the torques on the fluid (Rotating solids equations) lam*angmom - (-vtorq - vtorq_ic - mtorq - mtorq_ic [+ i Gaspard angmom])

residσ, resid\(s\) and resid\(c\) judge whether a solution is resolved (Solver gives the thresholds), also for forced runs, where \(\sigma = 0\). Where the walls drive the flow along themselves (the libration, forcing 7 with \(m\) = 0, and the steady rotation of the walls, forcing 12), \(W_ u = W_ u^{ m wall} - D_ u\) is a small difference of two large terms, so residσ, and resid𝐄 with a field, are relative to \(D_ u\) too. A residual whose terms all vanish, such as residω of a steady flow with \(m\) = 0, is 0. \(W_f = 2 hinspace\mathrm{Re}\int ho_0 hinspace\mathbf u^*\cdot\mathbf f hinspace dV\) is the power of a body force that the right-hand side puts in the fluid: that of a known flow \(\mathbf x\) whose equations make it (forcings 1 and 8),

\[ \mathbf f = -\left[\lambda\mathbf x + 2 hinspace\mathrm{Gaspard} hinspace\hat{\mathbf z} imes\mathbf x - rac{ abla\cdot oldsymbol\sigma(\mathbf x)}{ ho_0} - \mathbf F_\Omega(\mathbf x) ight] , \]

with \(\mathbf F_\Omega\) the force of a differential rotation (utils4pp.body_force_terms). Its enstrophy term enters residens, and \(W_f\) is 0 for the other forcings. residD compares two independent computations of the viscous terms: \(W_ u\) from the viscous force of each degree (utils4pp.visforce), and \(D_ u\) from the strain rate on the grid (utils4pp.viscous_dissipation). It is \(10^{-15}\) to \(10^{-12}\).

The work at the walls (utils4pp.wall_powers). kore does not solve for the pressure. spin_doctor recovers it from the momentum equation: \( abla\Pi = \mathbf F - \lambda\mathbf u\), with \(\mathbf F\) every force but the pressure, and the consoidal component of a gradient is \(\Pi_l/r\), so that for each degree \(l\) of \(P\)

\[ \Pi_l = r\left[\mathbf F - \lambda\mathbf u ight]_{s,l} , \]

the consoidal component of the Coriolis, viscous and differential-rotation forces and of \(\lambda\mathbf u\) (utils4pp.pressure_force). The buoyancy is radial and does not enter. With \(q_l = \mathcal L P_l/r\) the radial velocity, \(s_l\) and \(t_l\) the consoidal and toroidal components of \(\mathbf u\),

\[ W_p = -2 hinspace\mathrm{Re}\sum_l rac{4\pi}{2l+1}\Big[ ho_0 hinspace r^2 hinspace q_l^* hinspace\Pi_l\Big]_{ m inner}^{ m outer}, \]

and the stress on a sphere is

\[ oldsymbol\sigma\cdot\hat{\mathbf r} = \mathrm{ViscosD} hinspace ho_0 u\left[\left(2q_l' + frac23(\ln ho_0)'q_l ight)Y\hat{\mathbf r} + \left(s_l' - rac{s_l}{r} + rac{q_l}{r} ight)r abla Y + \left(t_l' - rac{t_l}{r} ight)r abla Y imes\hat{\mathbf r} ight], \]

dotted with \(\mathbf u^*\) and integrated over each wall for \(W_ u^{ m wall}\). flow.dat has these terms for each wall (Output files).

\(\Pi_l\) needs the radial derivatives of \(P_l\) up to the third at the walls. That is where the truncation error of the tau method is largest, and near a surface of low density the \((\ln ho_0)'\) terms of the viscous force amplify it. The wall pressure therefore converges with N more slowly than the volume integrals: residσ of a forced run with moving walls can need two to four times the N at which the kinetic energy and the dissipation have converged. Where \(u_r = 0\) at the walls, \(W_p = 0\) whatever the resolution.

ru_insane.py checks the same pairings on the operators themselves: inertia Hermitian and positive, Coriolis anti-Hermitian, viscous Hermitian and negative, the entropy and diffusion blocks, the buoyancy and the advection against quadratures, and the differential-rotation blocks against an \((r, heta)\) grid. tests/tidal checks the budgets with moving walls, against an exact solution of the forced flow and on runs with a variable density, buoyancy and a differential rotation.

docs.title: Output files
docs.text:
A run writes all its files into the run directory (Getting started). solve.py overwrites its files on every run, while spin_doctor.py appends one row per solution to its own, so that a series of runs builds up a table.

file written by content submatrices.npz submatrices.py the radial operators and the parameters they were built with; later steps stop if the parameters have changed. With write_mtx = 1, also one Matrix Market file per operator A.npz, B.npz assemble.py the matrices of the eigenvalue problem \(A\mathbf x = \lambda B\mathbf x\) B_forced.npz assemble.py, with forcing > 0 the right-hand sides of a forced run, one per column eigenvalues0.dat solve.py the eigenvalues of the last solve, one per row: real and imaginary parts flow.npy solve.py the solutions for the flow, one column per solution (below); also thermal.npy (entropy), composition.npy, magnetic.npy, magnetic_ic.npy, magnetic_mantle.npy and rotdyn.npy when those features are on no_conv_solution solve.py written when no eigenvalue converged, or when a forced solution contains NaN (Solver) rsf_spectrum.dat, rsf_ke.dat solve.py, with forcing = 11 the power spectrum of the forced kinetic energy (Convective forcing) timing.dat solve.py the run time of the solve, appended eigenvalues.dat spin_doctor.py the eigenvalues, appended track_target spin_doctor.py, with track_target 1 or 2 the eigenvalue that the next run aims at (below) params.dat spin_doctor.py the parameters of each solution (below) flow.dat spin_doctor.py the kinetic energy and the checks of each solution (below) thermal.dat spin_doctor.py, with thermal = 1 the entropy budget of each solution (below) composition.dat spin_doctor.py, with compositional = 1 the composition budget of each solution (below) magnetic.dat spin_doctor.py, with magnetic = 1 the magnetic energies and budgets of each solution (below) rotdyn.dat spin_doctor.py, with rotdyn = 1 the rotation of the solids and the torques on them (below) parameters.json parameters.py, when it calls par.export_json every parameter of the run (below)

python3 bin/units.py prints the eigenvalues of eigenvalues0.dat as frequency and growth rate in nHz (Background model). Rows with the same index in params.dat, flow.dat, thermal.dat, composition.dat, magnetic.dat and rotdyn.dat belong to the same solution. Start a new params.dat rather than append to one written by another version of kore, which may have different columns.
