docs.title: Solution files
docs.text:
The solution files hold the spectral coefficients of each field, one column per solution (Numerical method). By default each field is one binary numpy file of complex numbers: flow.npy, thermal.npy, and so on. With field_format = 'text' each field is instead two text files, real_flow.field and imag_flow.field. Text files are much larger and slower to read and write.

spin_doctor.py, the tools and koreviz read either format. In python,

import field_io                            # with kore's bin/ on the path
x = field_io.load('flow', folder='path/to/run')   # all solutions, one per column
x2 = field_io.load('flow', 2)                     # solution 2 alone

returns None when the field has no file. A .npy file can also be read directly with np.load('flow.npy').

docs.title: The parameter file
docs.text:
par.export_json('parameters.json') at the end of parameters.py writes every parameter of the run to one file, exactly. To run the same case again, here or elsewhere, use as parameter file

from params_default import default_params
par = default_params()
par.load_json('parameters.json')

docs.title: Many runs
docs.text:
A parameter study runs one case many times with one parameter changed. The scripts in tools/ run such a series in one folder, one step after the other (ramp.sh), or in one folder per run on a cluster, and collect the results into one table.

script what it does tools/ramp.sh name value1 value2 ... runs the case once per value of par.name (e.g. tools/ramp.sh ViscosD 1e-4 7e-5 5e-5), from kore's top folder. The results accumulate in the .dat files. It stops when a step finds no solution. The environment variables ncpus, ranks (MPI processes), opts (extra solver options) and MPIEXEC can be set tools/setpar.py name value [file] sets par.name = value in bin/parameters.py, so that it takes effect after everything else tools/dodirs.sh prefix name mode start step end creates one folder per value of par.name, each with a copy of kore. With mode e the values are powers of ten, with d they are linear. Edit the paths at the top of the script first tools/dosubs.sh (same arguments) submits a batch job in each folder that runs ramp.sh there. Edit the job header in tools/subramp.sh for your cluster first tools/reap.sh prefix collects the .dat files of the folders prefix* into prefix.par, .flo, .thm, .cmp, .mag, .rot and .eig tools/get_data.py [prefix] reads them (or the .dat files of the current folder) into one pandas table with named columns, and writes it to prefix.csv (or results.csv) tools/getresults.py [prefix] in IPython, %run -i tools/getresults.py prefix gives the same table as df, and its most used columns as arrays

Ramp a parameter that the run actually reads, such as ViscosD, not Ek: Ek, Etherm, Ecomp and Le are only used by set_scales().

docs.title: Following a mode
docs.text: Along a ramp the eigenvalues move, and a fixed target can lose the mode of interest. With track_target = 1 each run aims at the eigenvalue stored in the file track_target (instead of rtau, itau), and spin_doctor.py replaces it with the eigenvalue it found nearest to it, so the next run aims there. Small steps keep the same mode. Before the first run, write the starting eigenvalue to the file (echo "-0.1 1.0" > track_target: real and imaginary parts), or let a first run with track_target = 2 pick its solution with the smallest ratio of poloidal to toroidal kinetic energy, such as the spin-over mode. Tracking works for eigenvalue problems only.

docs.title: Reynolds-stress forcing
docs.text: This page derives the random force of forcing 11: where it comes from, its statistics, why its strength follows from the viscosity, how kore writes it in its variables, and what the resulting spectrum means. How to run it is on Convective forcing. The notation is that of Anelastic equations, in kore's units.

docs.title: Where the force comes from
docs.text:
In a convection zone the velocity is the sum of a large-scale flow \(\mathbf u\), the modes that kore solves for, and the convective eddies \(\mathbf u'\), which are much smaller and faster. The eddies act on \(\mathbf u\) through the divergence of their flux of momentum, the Reynolds stress: the momentum equation of \(\mathbf u\) contains the force

\[ - rac{1}{ ho_0} abla\cdot\left( ho_0 hinspace\mathbf u'\mathbf u' ight). \]

This force has two parts.

  1. The response to the large-scale flow. On average the eddies mix momentum down the gradients of \(\mathbf u\), as a viscosity does: the trace-free part of the mean of \(\mathbf u'\mathbf u'\) changes by \(- u_t hinspace\mathsf S(\mathbf u)\), with \( u_t\) the turbulent (eddy) viscosity and \(\mathsf S\) the trace-free rate of strain. In a convection zone this is kore's viscous force: kore's viscosity \( u\) is the sum of \( u_t\) and a part \( u_f\) that is not turbulent, such as the viscosity of a radiative zone.
  2. The fluctuation. What is left, \(\mathbf u'\mathbf u'\) minus its mean, does not depend on \(\mathbf u\). It is a random stress, and its divergence is a random force that drives the modes,
\[ \mathbf f = rac{1}{ ho_0} abla\cdot\left( ho_0 hinspace\mathsf s ight), \]

with \(\mathsf s\) a random symmetric tensor per unit mass. Its sign does not matter, since \(\mathsf s\) and \(-\mathsf s\) have the same statistics.

The two parts come from the same eddies, so they are not independent. The viscous part alone would damp every mode to zero, and the random part alone would let the modes grow without bound. Together they keep each mode at a finite energy, in a statistically steady state. Brownian motion is the same: the friction on a particle and the random kicks it receives come from the same molecules, and their ratio is set by the temperature (Einstein's relation). For a fluid in thermal equilibrium, Landau and Lifshitz add to the viscous stress a random stress whose variance is the temperature times the viscosity, so that the fluctuations of the flow have the energy that equipartition requires. Forcing 11 applies this construction to the eddies: the viscosity is \( u_t\), and the temperature is a turbulent temperature \(\Theta(r)\), about the kinetic energy of one eddy.

docs.title: The random stress
docs.text:
kore takes \(\mathsf s\) trace-free and white, with the covariance

\[ \mathbb E\left[s_{ij}(\mathbf x, t) hinspace s_{kl}^*(\mathbf x', t') ight] = rac{4 hinspace\Theta hinspace u_t}{ ho_0} hinspace\Pi_{ijkl} hinspace\delta(\mathbf x - \mathbf x') hinspace\delta(t - t'), \] \[ \Pi_{ijkl} = frac12\left(\delta_{ik}\delta_{jl} + \delta_{il}\delta_{jk} ight) - frac13\delta_{ij}\delta_{kl}, \]

where \(\mathbb E\) is the mean over realisations and \(\Pi\) the projector onto symmetric trace-free tensors. With \(\Theta\) replaced by \(k_B T\) and \( ho_0 u_t\) by the dynamic viscosity, this is the random stress of Landau and Lifshitz (divided by \( ho_0^2\), because \(\mathsf s\) is per unit mass).

  • White. The eddies are much smaller than the modes, and their turnover time is shorter than the periods of the modes, so that on the scales of the modes their stress is uncorrelated in space and time. kore can give the eddies a finite size (below).
  • Trace-free. The trace of \(\mathbf u'\mathbf u'\) is the turbulent pressure. Its gradient drops out of the curls that kore takes of the momentum equation, and what is left has no dissipative partner, since kore has no bulk viscosity. Leaving it out keeps the relation of the next section exact.
  • Strength. The factor \(4\Theta u_t/ ho_0\) is what the next section requires. A direct estimate gives the same form. For Gaussian eddies with \(\langle u'_i u'_k angle = frac13 u_c^2\delta_{ik}\), the trace-free part of \(\mathbf u'\mathbf u'\) has the covariance \(2(u_c^2/3)^2 hinspace\Pi\). If it is correlated over a volume \(\ell_c^3\) and a time \( au_c = \ell_c/u_c\), it acts on larger scales as a white noise of strength \(2(u_c^2/3)^2 hinspace\ell_c^3 au_c hinspace\Pi\). Equating this with \(4\Theta u_t\Pi/ ho_0\), with the mixing-length viscosity \( u_t = u_c\ell_c/3\), gives \(\Theta = ho_0 u_c^2\ell_c^3/6\); a time correlation \(e^{-\lvert t vert/ au_c}\), whose integral over all lags is \(2 au_c\), gives
\[ \Theta = frac13 hinspace ho_0 hinspace u_c^2 hinspace\ell_c^3 , \]

the value kore uses. \(\Theta\) is thus the kinetic energy of one eddy, up to a factor of order 1, which rsf_scale absorbs.

docs.title: Energy of a mode
docs.text:
With the inner product \(\langle\mathbf a, \mathbf b angle = \int ho_0 hinspace\mathbf a^*\cdot\mathbf b hinspace dV\), kore normalizes its eigenvectors to \(\langle\mathbf a, \mathbf a angle = 1\), a kinetic energy of 1. The random stress vanishes at the walls (below), so for any velocity field \(\mathbf a\) an integration by parts gives

\[ \langle\mathbf a, \mathbf f angle = -\int ho_0 hinspace abla\mathbf a^* : \mathsf s hinspace dV = - frac12\int ho_0 hinspace\mathsf S(\mathbf a)^* : \mathsf s hinspace dV, \]

because only the symmetric trace-free part of \( abla\mathbf a\), which is \( frac12\mathsf S(\mathbf a)\), meets the symmetric trace-free \(\mathsf s\). With the covariance above,

\[ \mathbb E\left[\langle\mathbf a, \mathbf f angle(t) hinspace\langle\mathbf a, \mathbf f angle^*(t') ight] = \int ho_0 hinspace\Theta hinspace u_t hinspace\lvert\mathsf S(\mathbf a) vert^2 hinspace dV\;\delta(t - t'), \]

with \(\lvert\mathsf S vert^2 = \mathsf S^* : \mathsf S\). The viscous force does on the same field the work \(- frac12\int ho_0 u\lvert\mathsf S(\mathbf a) vert^2 hinspace dV\) (Anelastic equations). The force that a field receives and the energy that it dissipates are the same integral: with a uniform \(\Theta\), the variance of the force is \(2\Theta\) times the dissipation by \( u_t\). This is the fluctuation–dissipation relation.

For a mode \(\mathbf a\) of eigenvalue \(\lambda\), with modes that are orthogonal, the amplitude of the mode obeys \(\dot c = \lambda c + \langle\mathbf a, \mathbf f angle\), with \(-\mathrm{Re} hinspace\lambda = frac12\int ho_0 u\lvert\mathsf S(\mathbf a) vert^2 hinspace dV\). A white force of strength \(Q\) keeps \(\mathbb E\lvert c vert^2 = Q/(2\lvert\mathrm{Re} hinspace\lambda vert)\), so the kinetic energy of the mode is

\[ \mathbb E\lvert c vert^2 = rac{\int ho_0\Theta u_t\lvert\mathsf S vert^2 hinspace dV}{\int ho_0 u\lvert\mathsf S vert^2 hinspace dV} = \Theta_{ m eff} hinspace f_t, \] \[ \Theta_{ m eff} = rac{\int ho_0\Theta u_t\lvert\mathsf S vert^2 hinspace dV}{\int ho_0 u_t\lvert\mathsf S vert^2 hinspace dV}, \qquad f_t = rac{\int ho_0 u_t\lvert\mathsf S vert^2 hinspace dV}{\int ho_0 u\lvert\mathsf S vert^2 hinspace dV}. \]
  • A mode holds the energy of one eddy, \(\Theta_{ m eff}\), averaged with the mode's own dissipation as the weight, times the share \(f_t\) of its damping that the turbulence provides. This is the result of Goldreich & Keeley (1977) for the solar p modes: the energy of a mode is about that of an eddy.
  • For a given \(\Theta\) the energy does not depend on the viscosity: \( u\) sets the width of the resonance, not its area. (With the 'nu' law of rsf_theta, \(\Theta\) itself grows as \( u_t^2\).)
  • A mode that dissipates mostly where the viscosity is not turbulent, in a radiative zone for example, has \(f_t \ll 1\) and receives little energy.
  • The modes are close to orthogonal when they are weakly damped in a uniformly rotating fluid. A differential rotation makes them far from orthogonal: the response to the force then differs from this estimate, and only the forced solve, which kore does, gives it.

docs.title: The force in kore's variables
docs.text:
At degree \(l\), with \(Y = Y_l^m\), \(n_l = \int\lvert Y vert^2 hinspace d\Omega = 4\pi/(2l+1)\), \(\mathcal L = l(l+1)\) and the vector harmonics \(\mathbf B = r abla Y\) and \(\mathbf C = \hat{\mathbf r} imes\mathbf B\), the stress is \(\mathsf s = \sum_k c_k(r) hinspace\mathsf T_k\) with five trace-free tensor harmonics:

\(k\) \(\mathsf T_k\) \(\int\lvert\mathsf T_k vert^2 hinspace d\Omega/n_l\) 1 \(Y hinspace\hat{\mathbf r}\hat{\mathbf r} - frac12 Y(\mathsf I - \hat{\mathbf r}\hat{\mathbf r})\) \(3/2\) 2 \(\hat{\mathbf r}\mathbf B + \mathbf B\hat{\mathbf r}\) \(2\mathcal L\) 3 \(\hat{\mathbf r}\mathbf C + \mathbf C\hat{\mathbf r}\) \(2\mathcal L\) 5 \( abla_1 abla_1 Y + frac12\mathcal L hinspace Y(\mathsf I - \hat{\mathbf r}\hat{\mathbf r})\), the trace-free Hessian of \(Y\) on the unit sphere \(\mathcal L(\mathcal L - 2)/2\) 6 the tensor of components \((-b, a, b)\), where \(\mathsf T_5\) has \((a, b, -a)\) \(\mathcal L(\mathcal L - 2)/2\)

\( abla_1\) is the gradient on the unit sphere, and the components are \(( heta heta, heta\phi, \phi\phi)\). \(\mathsf T_5\) and \(\mathsf T_6\) exist for \(l \geq 2\). The force \(\mathbf f = f^P hinspace Y\hat{\mathbf r} + f^B hinspace\mathbf B + f^C hinspace\mathbf C\) then has, with \(h = d\ln ho_0/dr\) and a prime for \(d/dr\),

\[ f^P = c_1' + \left( rac3r + h ight)c_1 - rac{\mathcal L hinspace c_2}{r}, \] \[ f^B = - rac{c_1}{2r} + c_2' + \left( rac3r + h ight)c_2 - rac{(\mathcal L - 2) hinspace c_5}{2r}, \] \[ f^C = c_3' + \left( rac3r + h ight)c_3 - rac{(\mathcal L - 2) hinspace c_6}{2r}. \]

kore's momentum rows are \(r^5 ho_0 hinspace\hat{\mathbf r}\cdot abla imes abla imes(\cdot)/\mathcal L^3\) and \(r^3 ho_0 hinspace\hat{\mathbf r}\cdot abla imes(\cdot)/\mathcal L^3\) (Numerical method), and the curls of \(\mathbf f\) at degree \(l\) are \((\mathcal L/r^2)[f^P - (rf^B)']\) and \(-(\mathcal L/r)f^C\). The right-hand side in the rows of \(P_l\) and \(T_l\) is therefore

\[ b_u = rac{r^3 ho_0}{\mathcal L^2}\left[f^P - (r f^B)' ight], \qquad b_v = - rac{r^2 ho_0}{\mathcal L^2} hinspace f^C, \]

for the default powers of \(r\) and \( ho_0\) (rpower_u, rhopower_u, rpower_v, rhopower_v in general), and zero in the rows of the heat equation.

  • Only the shear stresses drive the radial vorticity. \(c_3\) is the \(r heta\), \(r\phi\) part of the stress and \(c_6\) its horizontal shear: they force the toroidal rows, and with them the Rossby modes and the other vortical modes. \(c_1\), \(c_2\) and \(c_5\) force the poloidal flow.
  • Statistics. Since \(\delta(\mathbf x - \mathbf x') = \delta(r - r') hinspace\delta(\Omega - \Omega')/r^2\), the \(c_k\) are independent across \(k\), \(l\), \(m\) and frequency, with
\[ \mathbb E\left[c_k(r) hinspace c_k^*(r') ight] = rac{4\Theta u_t}{ ho_0} hinspace rac{\chi_k}{r^2 n_l} hinspace\delta(r - r'), \] \[ \chi_k = rac{n_l}{\int\lvert\mathsf T_k vert^2 hinspace d\Omega} = frac23,\ rac{1}{2\mathcal L},\ rac{1}{2\mathcal L},\ rac{2}{\mathcal L(\mathcal L - 2)},\ rac{2}{\mathcal L(\mathcal L - 2)} . \]

docs.title: Finite eddies and walls
docs.text:
A force that is white in radius cannot be resolved, and real eddies have a finite size. kore therefore smooths the noise over the eddy size \(\ell_c(r)\), and makes it vanish at the walls.

Radial correlation. The white \(\delta(r - r')\) is replaced by a unit-area Gaussian of width \(\ell_c\). kore draws the noise at centres \(r_j\) spaced \(h_j = \sigma_j/2\), with \(\sigma_j = \ell_c(r_j)/\sqrt2\), from below the inner wall (or \(r = 0\)) to above the outer wall, and builds

\[ c_k(r) = au(r) hinspace A_{lk}(r) hinspace S(r)^{-1/2}\sum_j\sqrt{h_j} hinspace\xi_j hinspace g_j(r), \] \[ S(r) = \sum_j h_j hinspace g_j(r), \qquad A_{lk} = \left( rac{4\Theta u_t}{ ho_0} hinspace rac{\chi_k}{r^2 n_l} ight)^{1/2}, \]

with \(g_j\) unit-area Gaussians of width \(\sigma_j\) centred at \(r_j\) and \(\xi_j\) independent complex Gaussian numbers of unit variance. For a uniform \(\ell_c\), \(\mathbb E[c_k(r)c_k^*(r')]\) is \( au(r) au(r')A_{lk}(r)A_{lk}(r')\) times a unit-area Gaussian of width \(\ell_c\) in \(r - r'\). The amplitude \(A_{lk}\) is taken at \(r\), not at the centres, so that the stress vanishes wherever \( u_t\) does: none of it leaks into a radiative zone.

Horizontal size. With rsf_angular = 1 the variance at degree \(l\) is multiplied by \(e^{-\mathcal L\ell_c^2/(2r^2)}\): eddies of size \(\ell_c\) do not force degrees much above \(r/\ell_c\).

Walls. At a stress-free wall the rows carry no surface traction, so the stress must vanish there. The taper \( au\) goes from 1 to 0 over rsf_taper below the outer wall, as \( frac12 hinspace\mathrm{erfc}\) of width rsf_taper/8 centred rsf_taper/2 below it. The same holds above an inner core, over rsf_taper_in above \(r = 0\) in a full sphere, and above rsf_rcut over rsf_rcut_width when a cut is set.

These choices only lower the force: for every field \(\mathbf a\),

\[ \mathbb E\lvert\langle\mathbf a, \mathbf f angle vert^2 \leq \int ho_0 hinspace\Theta u_t hinspace au^2 hinspace e^{-\mathcal L\ell_c^2/(2r^2)} hinspace\lvert\mathsf S(\mathbf a) vert^2 hinspace dV \]

per unit time, with equality in the white limit. A mode receives less energy than \(\Theta_{ m eff}f_t\) when its radial or horizontal scale approaches \(\ell_c\), and when it dissipates near a wall, inside the taper.

docs.title: Eddy size and turbulent temperature
docs.text:
• Turbulent viscosity. \( u_t\) = ViscosD \((\hat u - u_f)\), clipped at 0, with \(\hat u\) the viscosity profile and \( u_f\) = rsf_nu_floor (Convective forcing).
  • Eddy size. \(\ell_c = \left(\ell_{\max}^{-4} + (\alpha H_p)^{-4} ight)^{-1/4}\), a smooth minimum of \(\alpha H_p\) and \(\ell_{\max}\), with \(H_p = -p_0/p_0'\) the pressure scale height (infinite at \(r = 0\)), \(\alpha\) = rsf_alpha and \(\ell_{\max}\) = rsf_lc_max; or the constant rsf_lc.
  • Turbulent temperature, rsf_theta, times rsf_scale:
    • 'nu': eddies of size \(\ell_c\) whose mixing-length viscosity is \( u_t\), \(u_c = 3 u_t/\ell_c\), so that \(\Theta = frac13 ho_0u_c^2\ell_c^3 = 3 ho_0 u_t^2\ell_c\);
    • 'mlt': the mixing-length velocity of the convective flux, \(u_c^3 = \alpha F_c/(10 ho_0)\), with \(F_c = L_\star/(4\pi r^2) hinspace u_t/\max u_t\) and the luminosity \(L_\star\) = rsf_lum, and \(\Theta = frac13 ho_0u_c^2\ell_c^3\);
    • a number: a uniform \(\Theta\).

\(\Theta\) is an energy, in units of \( ho_u L^5/ au^2\), with \( ho_u\) the unit of density and \(L\) and \( au\) the units of length and time.

docs.title: The spectrum
docs.text:
Each realisation is the Fourier amplitude of the force at the frequency \(w\), normalized so that, for any quantity \(y\) that depends linearly on the flow, \(\mathbb E\lvert y(w)\rvert^2\) is the two-sided power spectral density of \(y\): \(\int\mathbb E\lvert y(w)\rvert^2\thinspace dw/2\pi\) is the variance of \(y\). The kinetic energy that kore reports for an azimuthal wavenumber \(m\) is that of the real flow \(\mathbf u\thinspace e^{im\phi}\) + c.c., so that for \(m \neq 0\) the integral of the mean kinetic energy over \(dw/2\pi\) is the mean kinetic energy of the forced flow. For \(m = 0\) the flow is real, its spectrum is even in \(w\), and the halves \(w > 0\) and \(w < 0\) are the same motion: the integral over all \(w\) is twice the energy. A white noise is white in every rotating frame, so the frame of the run does not matter.

Near a mode, the forced flow is \(c(w)\thinspace\mathbf a\) with \(c(w) = \langle\mathbf a, \mathbf f(w)\rangle/(iw - \lambda)\), and its mean kinetic energy is

\[ \mathbb E\lvert c(w)\rvert^2 = \frac{Q}{(\mathrm{Re}\thinspace\lambda)^2 + (w - \mathrm{Im}\thinspace\lambda)^2}, \]

a Lorentzian centred at \(w = \mathrm{Im}\thinspace\lambda\), of half-width \(\lvert\mathrm{Re}\thinspace\lambda\rvert\) and height \(H = Q/(\mathrm{Re}\thinspace\lambda)^2\). Its area, \(\int\mathbb E\lvert c\rvert^2\thinspace dw/2\pi = Q/(2\lvert\mathrm{Re}\thinspace\lambda\rvert)\), is the energy of the mode: \(H\lvert\mathrm{Re}\thinspace\lambda\rvert/2\).

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• The model is linear: it gives the energy that each mode receives, not the nonlinear saturation or the coupling between modes.
  • An unstable mode has no stationary response.
  • The time correlation of the eddies is neglected. Deep in the solar convection zone the turnover time approaches the periods of the inertial modes. The fluctuation–dissipation relation still holds for a viscosity that depends on frequency: read \(\nu_t\) as the eddy viscosity at the frequency of the modes.
  • Left out: the turbulent pressure (the trace of \(\mathbf u'\mathbf u'\)), the fluctuations of the convective heat flux (the heat equation is not forced) and any anisotropy of the eddies.

Philidet & Gizon (2023) model the same source for the solar Rossby modes on a two-dimensional \(\beta\) plane, with a source taken from the observed surface turbulence and a damping set separately. Here the source and the damping are tied by the fluctuation–dissipation relation, and the source has a depth profile.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• Goldreich, P. & Keeley, D. A. 1977, ApJ 212, 243.
  • Landau, L. D. & Lifshitz, E. M. 1987, Fluid Mechanics, 2nd ed., Pergamon, chapter XVII (Fluctuations in fluid dynamics).
  • Löptien, B., Gizon, L., Birch, A. C. et al. 2018, Nature Astronomy 2, 568.
  • Philidet, J. & Gizon, L. 2023, A&A 673, A124.

docs.title: Rotating solids equations
docs.text: This page gives the equations of the rotating solids (rotdyn = 1, Rotating solids), the torques that couple them to the fluid, and the angular momentum balance that spin_doctor checks (resid𝐋). They hold for any density profile and any poloidal background field (bin/rotdyn.py).

docs.title: Equations
docs.text:
The mantle and the inner core turn about the rotation axis at the rates \(\omega_M\) and \(\omega_{IC}\) relative to the frame, and \(\varphi\) is the angle of the inner core relative to the mantle. Each solid's angular momentum changes by the torques on it. For a mode \(e^{\lambda t}\)

\[ \lambda I_M\,\omega_M = \Gamma_M + K\varphi, \qquad \lambda I_{IC}\,\omega_{IC} = \Gamma_{IC} - K\varphi, \qquad \lambda\varphi = \omega_{IC} - \omega_M - c\,\varphi , \]

with \(I_M\), \(I_{IC}\) = MoIZ_M, MoIZ_IC, \(K\) = gTorque Gaspard² and \(c\) = Gaspard/OmgtauIC in the units of the run. \(\Gamma_M\) and \(\Gamma_{IC}\) are the torques of the fluid on the mantle and on the inner core (below): the viscous ones times vtrq, the magnetic ones times mtrq. These are the last three rows of \(A\) and \(B\), after all the fields (utils.offset['rot']).

The walls. The fluid follows the solids through the no-slip walls. A rigid rotation \(\omega\) about the axis is the toroidal flow of degree 1 with \(T = \omega r\) (\(u_\phi = T\sin\theta\), kore's \(Y_1^0\) being \(\cos\theta\)), so the no-slip rows of that degree become

\[ T(1) = \omega_M, \qquad T(r_i) = r_i\,\omega_{IC} , \]

and every other wall condition is unchanged. At a stress-free outer wall (bco = 0) the row of \(T_1\) stays the stress-free one, and a drag acts there on the slip relative to the mantle, \(T_1(1) - \omega_M\) (Drag at the outer wall equations); without a drag only the field couples the fluid to the mantle. A rigid rotation carries an axisymmetric field without changing it, so the rotating solids leave the conditions on the field, and the field of a conducting inner core or mantle, as they are for solids at rest, but for a fluid slipping along a conducting outer wall, whose electric field enters the wall through the slip relative to the mantle (assemble.bc_b_slip).

docs.title: Torques
docs.text:
The torques are the moments of the stresses on each wall. With \(T\) the toroidal flow of degree 1, the axial angular momentum of the fluid is

\[ L = \int ho_0\,s\,u_\phi\,dV = rac{8\pi}{3}\int_{r_i}^{1} ho_0\,r^3\,T\,dr . \]

Viscous. The shear stress on a sphere is \(\sigma_{r\phi} = c_ u\,(T' - T/r)\sin heta\) with \(c_ u = ho_0\, u\,\)ViscosD, so that

\[ \Gamma^ u_M = - rac{8\pi}{3}\,c_ u\,r^2\left(rT' - T ight)\Big|_{r=1}, \qquad \Gamma^ u_{IC} = rac{8\pi}{3}\,c_ u\,r^2\left(rT' - T ight)\Big|_{r=r_i} . \]

Magnetic. The magnetic stress on the fluid's side of each wall, with \(B_{0\phi} = 0\) there:

\[ \Gamma^B_M = -\mathrm{Hendrik}\oint s\,B_{0r}\,b_\phi\,dS\,\Big|_{r=1}, \qquad \Gamma^B_{IC} = \mathrm{Hendrik}\oint s\,B_{0r}\,b_\phi\,dS\,\Big|_{r=r_i} . \]

It acts on everything beyond the wall: a thin conducting layer, a resolved mantle or a conducting inner core (at an insulating wall \(b_\phi = 0\)). With \(b_\phi = -\sum_l g_l\,\partial_ heta Y_l\) and \(B_{0r} = \sum_n n(n+1)\,h_n Y_n/r\) (the degrees \(n\) of the poloidal background, cnorm included),

\[ \oint s\,B_{0r}\,b_\phi\,dS = \sum_l C_l\,g_l, \qquad C_l = 2\pi r^2\sum_n n(n+1)\,h_n\, rac{2l(l+1)}{(2l+1)(2n+1)}\left(\delta_{n,l-1} - \delta_{n,l+1} ight), \]

which is \( frac{16\pi}{5}\,r^2 h_1 g_2\) for a dipole.

Gravitational. \(K\varphi\) on the mantle and \(-K\varphi\) on the inner core, which also relaxes towards alignment at the rate \(c\).

docs.title: The angular momentum balance: resid𝐋
docs.text:
The fluid's angular momentum changes only through the torques on it. spin_doctor computes them from the fields, apart from the matrices, and checks

\[ \lambda L = -\Gamma_M - \Gamma_{IC} , \]

with the viscous torques from \(T\) at the walls and the magnetic ones from the stress \(\mathrm{Hendrik}\,(B_{0r}\,\mathbf b + b_r\,\mathbf B_0)\) on a grid in \(\theta\) at each wall, for any poloidal and toroidal background (rotdyn.viscous_torques, wall_torques), whatever vtrq and mtrq. Both are taken on the fluid's side of the walls: where \(\mathbf B_0\) ends at a wall in a current sheet (Current sheets at slipping walls), the magnetic one holds the torque on the sheet's currents, which the viscous one balances at a slipping wall. The other forces exert no net axial torque: the pressure is normal to the walls, the buoyancy radial, and for \(m = 0\) neither the Coriolis force nor the advection by a differential rotation \(\Delta\Omega\) has one, since \(\int\rho_0\,\mathbf u\cdot\nabla(s^2\Delta\Omega)\,dV = 0\) between impenetrable walls.

Equatorial. For \(m = 1\), symm = -1 the same balance holds for the equatorial angular momentum, with

\[ L = \frac{16\pi}{3}\int_{r_i}^{1}\rho_0\,r^3\,T\,dr = \frac{L_x - iL_y}{N} , \]

\(N = -1/\sqrt2\) the normalisation of kore's \(Y_1^1 = N\sin\theta\,e^{i\phi}\), the torques in the same combination (the viscous ones with \(16\pi/3\) for \(8\pi/3\)), and the Coriolis torque \(-\boldsymbol\Omega\times\mathbf L\), which is \(i\,\mathrm{Gaspard}\,L\):

\[ \lambda L = -\Gamma_M - \Gamma_{IC} + i\,\mathrm{Gaspard}\,L . \]

A differential rotation would add a torque here, so this case needs diff_rot = 0.

Forced runs. In a forced run \(\lambda = i\,w\), \(w\) the forcing frequency, and the axial balance holds as above where the forcing moves the walls only along themselves and puts no force in the fluid: the libration (forcing 7 with \(m\) = 0), the steady rotation of the walls (forcing 12, where \(\lambda = 0\) and the torques on the two solids cancel) and the thermal forcing (forcing 13). A flow through a wall would add the Coriolis torque of the mass it carries across, and a body force its own torque. For the body forces \(\mathbf f\) that spin_doctor knows, the Poincaré force of the libration in the frame of the mantle (forcing 8) and the force of the wave-like tide (forcing 1, axial for \(m\) = 0 and equatorial for \(m\) = 1), the balance includes that torque, the same integral as \(L\) over the toroidal part of \(\mathbf f\) of degree 1 (utils4pp.body_force_terms). resid𝐋 is not computed for the other forcings, nor with a wall of zero radial stress (bco or bci = 2) of a viscous fluid: the fluid crosses it, carrying angular momentum through it.

resid𝐋 is the residual of the balance relative to the largest of \(\lvert\lambda\rvert L_{\rm abs}\), the torques, ViscosD \(L_{\rm abs}\), and Gaspard \(L_{\rm abs}\) for \(m = 1\), with \(L_{\rm abs}\) the same integral of \(\lvert T\rvert\): a mode on which no torque acts (stress-free walls) is then checked to carry no angular momentum, and a steady flow (\(\lambda = 0\)) on which none acts, such as the thermal forcing between stress-free walls with a drag, to feel no torque on the scale of the viscous one.

docs.title: Energy
docs.text:
With a field, resid𝐄 (Magnetic field equations) counts the solids too. In the units of spin_doctor's kinetic energy a rigid rotation \(\omega\) of a body of moment of inertia \(I\) has the energy \(I\lvert\omega\rvert^2\), and the equations above give

\[ 2\sigma\left(I_M\lvert\omega_M\rvert^2 + I_{IC}\lvert\omega_{IC}\rvert^2 + K\lvert\varphi\rvert^2\right) = 2\,\mathrm{Re}\left(\omega_M^*\,\Gamma_M + \omega_{IC}^*\,\Gamma_{IC}\right) - 2Kc\,\lvert\varphi\rvert^2 . \]

The power of the viscous torques is minus the work of the moving walls on the fluid, which the viscous power of the fluid includes; at a stress-free outer wall with a drag the two differ by the power the drag dissipates (Drag at the outer wall equations). The power of the magnetic torques moves energy between the solids and the field: it is minus the flux of \(\mathbf v\times\mathbf B_0\) through the moving walls (\(\mathbf v\) their velocity), which resid𝐄 leaves out of the induction work with the rest of the flux of \(\mathbf u\times\mathbf B_0\) through the walls (utils4pp.INDU_WALLS). So resid𝐄 adds the energy of the solids to the left-hand side, and the power of the viscous torques and the loss \(-2Kc\lvert\varphi\rvert^2\) to the right. It does so when both torques act on the solids (vtrq and mtrq 1).

docs.title: Checks
docs.text: tests/rotdyn checks the rotating solids against exact results (solids coupled only to each other; very heavy solids, which behave as fixed walls), the conservation of total angular momentum and energy with a variable density and a magnetic field, and the equatorial angular momentum balance. tests/couette checks resid𝐋 in the forced runs with turning walls, libration and thermal forcing.

docs.title: Rotating solids
docs.text:
An axisymmetric mode of the fluid pulls on the mantle and on the inner core, and their rotation changes in return. rotdyn = 1 lets both solids turn as rigid bodies about the rotation axis. They are coupled to the fluid by the viscous and magnetic torques at the walls, and to each other by gravity.

setting default meaning rotdyn 0 1: the mantle and the inner core turn under the torques MoIZ_M, MoIZ_IC 11.16, 9.2e-3 axial moments of inertia of the mantle and of the inner core, in units of the density unit times the outer radius of the fluid to the fifth power gTorque 5e-8 gravitational coupling: the torque between inner core and mantle per radian of misalignment (dimensionless) OmgtauIC 2.3e3 the time over which the inner core relaxes viscously back into alignment, times the rotation rate; np.inf for no relaxation vtrq, mtrq 1, 1 0 switches off the viscous or the magnetic torque on the solids

The defaults are Earth-like (2.3e3 corresponds to a relaxation time of one year). A run needs an axisymmetric, equatorially symmetric eigenvalue problem with an inner core and a no-slip inner wall. The outer wall is no-slip, or stress-free with or without a drag (Drag at the outer wall):

par.m = 0
par.symm = 1
par.bci = 1
par.bco = 1
par.rotdyn = 1

docs.title: How the solids are coupled
docs.text:
Three unknowns join the fields: the rotation rates of the mantle and of the inner core relative to the frame, and the angle of the inner core relative to the mantle.

  • The walls move with the solids. The fluid at each no-slip wall turns with the solid beyond it. At a stress-free outer wall the fluid slips along the mantle, and a drag (if any) pulls it towards the mantle's rotation.
  • Viscous torque. The stress of the fluid on each wall (at a stress-free outer wall, only that of the drag).
  • Magnetic torque. The magnetic stress on whatever conducts beyond each wall: a thin conducting layer, a resolved mantle or a conducting inner core. An insulating solid feels none.
  • Gravitational torque. It pulls the inner core and the mantle back into alignment, while the inner core relaxes viscously towards alignment over OmgtauIC.

No torque comes from outside, so fluid and solids together conserve their angular momentum. The eigenvalue 0 is the rigid rotation of everything; ignore its residuals.

The equations: Rotating solids equations.

docs.title: Output
docs.text:
• rotdyn.npy: the two rotation rates and the angle, one column per solution, normalized as the eigenvector.
  • rotdyn.dat: one row per solution with the same three quantities, the gravitational torque, and the viscous and magnetic torques on the mantle and on the inner core (Output files).
  • With a field, resid𝐄 also counts the energy of the solids (Magnetic field).

docs.title: The angular momentum check: resid𝐋
docs.text:
The angular momentum of the fluid changes only through the torques on it. spin_doctor computes both from the solution and prints resid𝐋, the relative mismatch of this balance. Like residσ, it should be small for a resolved mode. It is computed:

  • for eigenvalue problems with m = 0, symm = 1 (axial angular momentum) or m = 1, symm = -1 (equatorial angular momentum, which includes the spin-over mode), with or without the rotating solids;
  • for forced runs with m = 0, symm = 1 whose force on the fluid is known: libration (forcings 7 and 8), rotating walls (forcing 12), thermal forcing (forcing 13), and the wave-like tide (forcing 1).

It is not computed with centrifugal = 1, for m = 1 with differential rotation, or with walls of zero radial stress. flow.dat holds the angular momentum, the torques and resid𝐋 (Output files).

docs.title: What is supported
docs.text:
Supported: any structure; with or without buoyancy; a no-slip or a stress-free outer wall, with or without a drag; with or without a magnetic field (with any poloidal B0, and a toroidal B0_tor that vanishes at both walls); insulating walls, a thin conducting layer, a resolved mantle or a conducting inner core ('conducting, Chebys').

Not supported (kore stops with a message):

  • m other than 0, symm other than 1, a full sphere, forced runs, or no flow (hydro = 0);
  • an inviscid fluid, an inner wall that is not no-slip, or an outer wall with zero radial stress (bco = 2);
  • a non-rotating frame (Gaspard = 0);
  • differential rotation, a background flow or the centrifugal deformation;
  • a toroidal B0_tor that does not vanish at both walls.

docs.title: Solver: bad solutions and memory
docs.text:
solve.py finds the eigenvalues nearest a target τ = rtau + i itau. At each iteration it solves a linear system with the matrix \(A - \tau B\), which the MUMPS library factors once (a sparse LU factorization). This factorization uses almost all the memory, and causes most numerical trouble. This page lists what to try when a solution looks wrong or a run runs out of memory.

Solver options go in par.petsc_opts in parameters.py, for example

par.petsc_opts['st_mat_mumps_cntl_1'] = 0.1

Eigenvalue runs read the options that start with eps_ and st_, forced runs (forcing > 0) those that start with ksp_, pc_ and mat_. So the same MUMPS option is st_mat_mumps_... in an eigenvalue run and mat_mumps_... in a forced run. An option given on the command line (mpiexec -n 4 ./bin/solve.py -st_mat_mumps_icntl_14 100) overrides parameters.py. The defaults, with comments, are in bin/params_default.py.

docs.title: First, check the solution
docs.text:
Judge each solution with spin_doctor.py, not with the residual that solve.py prints (which refers to a rescaled problem). Accept a mode when:

  • its energy residual residσ (and the entropy residual resid𝑠, with thermal = 1) is below 1e-5;
  • its ℓ-convergence is below 1e-4;
  • in a full sphere, irreg₀ is below 1e-6 (Regularity at the centre).

The same checks apply to forced runs. A forced flow that is a rigid rotation has no budget to judge: its residuals compare round-off errors and can be ignored (Spherical Couette flow).

A failure is one of two kinds:

  • Resolution. It fails every time, and the eigenvalue moves when N or lmax is raised. Raise N for the residuals and lmax for the ℓ-convergence. A full sphere needs about twice the N of a shell. N must be even.
  • Solver. It comes and goes between identical runs, or between runs with nearly the same parameters. See below.

docs.title: Bad solutions
docs.text:
symptom what to try the mode you want is not among the solutions put the target on it (in nHz: units.set_target(par, omega=..., sigma=...)) and raise nev; to look for growing modes, put the target at a positive growth rate along a series of runs, the mode drifts away from a fixed target, or the solver jumps to another mode let each run aim at the eigenvalue the previous run found: track_target = 1 (Following a mode) in a full sphere without viscosity or without thermal diffusion, modes that move when N or lmax is raised, many with irreg₀ near 1 spurious modes (Regularity at the centre): target the mode you want and keep only the modes that stay put the run stops with INFOG(1)=-9 or -20 MUMPS's workspace is too small: set st_mat_mumps_icntl_14 to 50, then 100–200 or more (extra workspace, in %). A run near the limit can fail once and pass the next time a forced run returns NaN the same problem: set mat_mumps_icntl_14 = 100, or turn on BLR (below); mat_mumps_icntl_4 = 1 prints MUMPS's error codes the run stops with INFOG(1)=-13, or is killed out of memory: see below in a cluster of nearly equal modes, some fail spin_doctor or move slightly between identical runs round-off in MUMPS on several processes is amplified for nearly parallel eigenvectors. st_mat_mumps_cntl_1 = 0.1 (default 0.01) makes this less frequent. Repeat the run and compare each mode with the repeat or with nearby parameters two modes at an avoided crossing split differently from run to run their sum is stable: quote the sum, or a trend over several runs

Runs on a single process are exactly reproducible, so a small case can be debugged on one process.

Leave MUMPS's own scaling on, and do not lower the pivot threshold cntl_1 below its default. par.prescale = None (the default) chooses the matrix rescaling automatically.

docs.title: Out of memory
docs.text:
The memory grows roughly as \(N^2\) times lmax to a power somewhat above 1, and with the width of the couplings (differential rotation, the thermal wind, the magnetic field). As a reference, the smooth Sun example (examples/smooth_sun) needs about 21 GB.

What to try, cheapest first:

  1. Resolution. Use the smallest N and lmax that pass the checks above. The eigenvalue usually converges at a lower N than the residuals need.
  2. drop_tol = 1e-14 removes negligible matrix entries: about 30 % less memory, with essentially unchanged eigenvalues.
  3. Block low-rank factors (BLR): st_mat_mumps_icntl_35 = 2 (for forced runs mat_mumps_icntl_35 = 2), with the tolerance st_mat_mumps_cntl_7 = 1e-14 (the default). Somewhat less memory, and often faster. Check the residuals: a larger tolerance can spoil the eigenvectors.
  4. Out of core: st_mat_mumps_icntl_22 = 1 writes the factors to disk, for about half the memory and a slower run. Point st_mat_mumps_ooc_tmpdir to a real disk, not to a /tmp held in memory.
  5. More processes spread the factors: less memory per process, a little more in total. lmax − m + 1 must be a multiple of twice ncpus.

Set icntl_14 only as high as INFOG(1)=-9 requires, since it adds memory.

docs.title: The cost of a differential rotation
docs.text:
A rotation profile with Legendre terms up to degree n couples each harmonic degree of the solution to its neighbours up to n away. With the heat equation the thermal wind reaches further (about twice as far with thermal_wind = 2). The matrices get wider, and the factorization needs more memory and time. The memory grows roughly linearly with n: at degree 32 it can be ten times that of the same run without differential rotation.

To plan a large run, measure the cost at your resolution with

python3 tests/diff_rot/dr_cost.py WORKDIR N LMAX NCPUS [LIMIT_GB]

It runs a test problem for increasing degrees n, stops any step above LIMIT_GB (default 30) and skips the larger degrees.

docs.title: Thermal forcing
docs.text: Forcing 13 heats the inner wall unevenly in latitude, the way the Sun heats the ground of a planet more at the equator than at the poles. kore returns the flow that this heating drives: an overturning circulation in the meridional plane, like the Hadley cells of the Earth's atmosphere, together with the zonal winds that the Coriolis force makes of it.

docs.title: What it imposes
docs.text:
The entropy at the inner wall varies with latitude as

\[ s(r_i, \theta) = A\thinspace P_2(\cos\theta), \qquad P_2(\cos\theta) = \tfrac12 (3\cos^2\theta - 1), \]

with \(A\) = forcing_amplitude_icb. With bci_thermal = 1 the same pattern is imposed on the heat flux instead. \(P_2\) is \(-\tfrac12\) at the equator and 1 at the poles, so a negative \(A\) makes the equator warmer. The flow is proportional to \(A\).

Requirements:

  • m = 0 and symm = 1 (the pattern is axisymmetric and symmetric about the equator);
  • an inner core (ricb > 0), thermal = 1 and ThermaD > 0.

With forcing_frequency = 0 the solution is the steady flow. It then needs at least one no-slip wall (bci = 1 or bco = 1) or a drag at the outer wall (Drag at the outer wall); otherwise a rigid rotation could be added to any solution. Both walls must also stay in place (bci and bco 0 or 1). A non-zero forcing_frequency gives the response to a heating that oscillates in time.

The forcing also works with a magnetic field (Magnetic field). Combining features lists what else it combines with.

docs.title: Example: a Hadley cell
docs.text:
Write in bin/parameters.py

from params_default import default_params

par = default_params()

par.timescale = 'rotation'
par.Ek = 1e-3
par.Etherm = 1e-3
par.set_scales()                  # Gaspard = 1, ViscosD = Ek, ThermaD = Etherm

# Boussinesq fluid in a thin rotating shell, stably stratified
par.structure = 'Boussinesq'
par.stratification = 'inverse square'
par.thermal = 1
par.Beyonce = 10.0
par.ricb = 0.9
par.bci = 1                       # no-slip ground
par.bco = 0                       # stress-free top
par.bci_thermal = 0               # the entropy of the ground is imposed
par.bco_thermal = 0

# axisymmetric and equatorially symmetric
par.m = 0
par.symm = 1

par.N = 48
par.lmax = 47
par.ncpus = 2

# steady heating of the ground, the equator warmer than the poles
par.forcing = 13
par.forcing_frequency = 0.0
par.forcing_amplitude_icb = -1.0

and run

./bin/submatrices.py 2
mpiexec -n 2 ./bin/assemble.py
mpiexec -n 2 ./bin/solve.py

It takes a few seconds. The solution is in flow.npy and thermal.npy (Output files).

The figure shows the northern hemisphere. The fluid rises over the warm equator, moves poleward aloft, sinks at high latitudes and returns to the equator along the ground: one cell per hemisphere. The Coriolis force turns the poleward flow aloft into a prograde (westerly) jet, and the return flow near the ground into retrograde (easterly) winds at low latitudes. At higher latitudes the winds near the ground are prograde, because a steady flow exerts no net torque on the ground.

A linear, axisymmetric flow has no eddies, so the cell reaches from the equator to the pole and there are no Ferrel cells. At lower Ekman numbers the circulation retreats into the boundary layer at the ground and towards the equator.

docs.title: Reading the output
docs.text:
For m = 0, each field is a sum over Legendre polynomials \(P_l(\cos\theta)\). With the poloidal and toroidal coefficients \(P_l(r)\), \(T_l(r)\) and the entropy coefficients \(s_l(r)\) of the solution (Output files), and uniform density as in the example, the meridional streamfunction \(\psi\), the zonal velocity and the entropy are

\[ \psi = -2\thinspace\mathrm{Re} \sum_l r\thinspace P_l(r) \sin\theta\thinspace \partial_\theta P_l(\cos\theta), \qquad u_\phi = -2\thinspace\mathrm{Re} \sum_l T_l(r)\thinspace \partial_\theta P_l(\cos\theta), \qquad s = 2\thinspace\mathrm{Re} \sum_l s_l(r)\thinspace P_l(\cos\theta). \]

The streamfunction gives the meridional velocity, \(u_r = \partial_\theta\psi/(r^2\sin\theta)\) and \(u_\theta = -\partial_r\psi/(r\sin\theta)\). In the northern hemisphere, negative \(\psi\) is a cell that rises at the equator.

docs.title: Tidal forcing
docs.text:
Forcing 14 moves the walls radially in the pattern of a degree-2 tide, the way the tidal bulge raised by a companion moves the surface of a star or a planet. kore returns the flow this drives inside: tidally forced inertial and gravito-inertial waves, their dissipation, and the power that the tide puts in. Repeating the run over a range of forcing_frequency gives the frequency spectrum of the response.

Two related tides are described at the end of this page:

  • Forcing 1 solves for the wave-like tide of an incompressible fluid, the part of the tide excited by rotation (The wave-like tide).
  • Forcing 2 moves the walls of the ocean of Enceladus with its eccentricity tide (The eccentricity tide of Enceladus).

docs.title: What it imposes
docs.text:
At each wall the radial velocity is

\[ u_r = A\thinspace Y_2^m(\theta)\thinspace e^{i(m\phi + wt)} + \text{c.c.}, \]

with amplitude \(A\) = forcing_amplitude_cmb at the outer wall and forcing_amplitude_icb at the inner wall, and frequency \(w\) = forcing_frequency. Three tides are possible:

tide m symm eccentricity tide, \((l, m) = (2, 0)\) 0 1 obliquity tide, \((2, 1)\) 1 −1 eccentricity and asynchronous tide, \((2, 2)\) 2 1

The pattern rotates at the angular velocity \(-w/m\) in the rotating frame, so a negative \(w\) is prograde, as everywhere in kore. For a body spinning at the frame rate \(\Omega\) with a companion on a circular orbit of angular velocity \(n\), the (2, 2) tide has \(w = 2(\Omega - n)/\Omega\) with timescale = 'rotation'. If you know the tidal displacement of the wall rather than its velocity, set the amplitude to \(w\) times the displacement. The flow is proportional to the amplitude, and every power to its square.

Requirements:

  • no-slip walls (bco = 1, and bci = 1 with an inner core), or an inviscid fluid in a full sphere;
  • one of the three (m, symm) pairs above.

In a full sphere (ricb = 0) only the outer wall moves. The forcing works with any structure, with buoyancy, differential rotation, a background flow and a magnetic field (Magnetic field). Combining features lists what else it combines with.

docs.title: Example: the (2, 2) tide in a rotating shell
docs.text:
Write in bin/parameters.py

from params_default import default_params

par = default_params()

par.timescale = 'rotation'
par.Ek = 1e-3
par.set_scales()                  # Gaspard = 1, ViscosD = Ek

# incompressible fluid in a rotating shell, no-slip walls
par.structure = 'Boussinesq'
par.thermal = 0
par.ricb = 0.35
par.bci = 1
par.bco = 1

# the (2, 2) tide: m = 2, equatorially symmetric
par.m = 2
par.symm = 1

par.N = 96
par.lmax = 49
par.ncpus = 2

# radial velocity Y_2^2 at the outer wall, at the frequency w = 1 (retrograde in the frame)
par.forcing = 14
par.forcing_frequency = 1.0
par.forcing_amplitude_cmb = 1.0
par.forcing_amplitude_icb = 0.0

and run

./bin/submatrices.py 2
mpiexec -n 2 ./bin/assemble.py
mpiexec -n 2 ./bin/solve.py
./bin/spin_doctor.py 2

It takes a few seconds. spin_doctor prints the power the walls put in (P_in) and the viscous dissipation (Dν), and writes the whole energy budget to flow.dat (Output files):

import numpy as np
f = np.loadtxt('flow.dat', ndmin=2)[-1]
P_in  = f[20] + f[21] + f[23] + f[24]   # work of the pressure and of the viscous stress at both walls
D_nu  = f[25]                           # viscous dissipation
print(P_in, D_nu)                       # 0.1416912 0.1416912

With uniform rotation and no buoyancy, all the power that the tide puts in is dissipated by viscosity, so the two numbers agree.

To compute a spectrum, loop over forcing_frequency. submatrices.py does not depend on it, but assemble.py and solve.py must be run again for each frequency.

docs.title: The energy of the response
docs.text:
For a forced, periodic response, spin_doctor evaluates the energy budget of Energy balance:

\[ P_{ m in} = W_p + W_ u^{ m wall} = D_ u - W_b - W_\Omega , \] quantity columns meaning \(P_{ m in}\) flow.dat 21 + 22 + 24 + 25 the power the moving walls put into the fluid: the tidal power \(W_p\) flow.dat 21 (inner wall), 22 (outer wall) the part done by pressure \(W_ u^{ m wall}\) flow.dat 24, 25 the part done by viscous stress \(D_ u\) flow.dat 26 the viscous dissipation, the heat released \(-W_b\) thermal.dat 5 (with the opposite sign) the power given to the entropy perturbation, released by thermal diffusion \(W_\Omega\) flow.dat 18 the power taken from the differential rotation

Which one to report depends on the question:

  • Orbital and spin evolution depend on the tidal power \(P_{ m in}\). It equals the viscous dissipation \(D_ u\) only with uniform rotation and no buoyancy.
  • Tidal heating is \(D_ u\), plus the thermal diffusion of the entropy perturbation with thermal = 1.
  • Exchange with the differential rotation, \(W_\Omega\), can have either sign. The waves can draw energy from the shear, so that the fluid dissipates more than the tide puts in, or give energy to it. kore keeps the background rotation fixed, so report \(W_\Omega\) together with the others.

All powers are averages over one period of the oscillation.

docs.title: Interpreting the response
docs.text:
• Unstable modes. The forced solve gives an answer even when the background has growing modes. The answer is the part of the flow at the forcing frequency, which is meaningful only if those instabilities are saturated by something else. It is not meaningful near a growing mode: run an eigenvalue solve (forcing = 0, itau = forcing_frequency) and check that no growing mode has a frequency close to the forcing.
  • Critical layers. With differential rotation, waves can meet critical layers, where the forcing frequency matches the local rotation. Only viscosity resolves them; check that the response converges with N and lmax.
  • No-slip walls. Forcing 14 imposes zero tangential velocity at the moving walls, which creates viscous boundary layers there. On the solid surface of a core this is physical. At the free surface of a star or a giant planet it is not. Compare runs at several Ekman numbers to tell the dissipation in the wall layers from that of the waves inside.
  • Resolution. The pressure work \(W_p\) converges more slowly with N than the kinetic energy, especially when the density varies strongly. Accept a response only when spin_doctor's residσ is below \(10^{-5}\).

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: parameter meaning forcing 14 forcing_frequency \(w\), in the rotating frame; negative is prograde forcing_amplitude_cmb amplitude of the radial velocity at the outer wall forcing_amplitude_icb amplitude at the inner wall (not used in a full sphere) m, symm (0, 1), (1, −1) or (2, 1) bci, bco bco = 1, and bci = 1 with an inner core

docs.title: The wave-like tide (forcing 1)
docs.text:
In a fluid body the tide has two parts. The equilibrium tide is the large-scale flow that follows the tidal bulge as it moves. The wave-like tide is the response that the Coriolis force on that flow excites: inertial waves, whose dissipation depends strongly on frequency. Forcing 1 solves for the wave-like part alone, as Lin & Ogilvie (2018) do.

The equilibrium tide of degree 2 in a shell is

\[ \mathbf u_e = \nabla\big[X(r)\thinspace Y_2^m(\theta)\thinspace e^{i(m\phi + wt)}\big] + \text{c.c.}, \qquad X(r) = -\frac{3a}{4}\thinspace\frac{r^2 + \tfrac23 r_i^5 r^{-3}}{1 - r_i^5} , \]

with \(a\) = forcing_amplitude_cmb, \(w\) = forcing_frequency and \(r_i\) = ricb. The Coriolis force on this flow acts as a body force on the wave-like tide, which kore solves for with walls at rest. The solution in flow.npy is the wave-like tide; add \(\mathbf u_e\) to get the whole tide.

Requirements:

  • a uniform fluid without stratification or field: structure = 'Boussinesq', thermal = 0, compositional = 0, magnetic = 0;
  • (m, symm) = (0, 1), (1, −1) or (2, 1);
  • bco 0 or 1, and bci 0 or 1 with an inner core;
  • no drag at the outer wall;
  • with m = 2, an inner core (in a full sphere this tide drives nothing). With m = 0 or 1 a full sphere works, and the fluid may then be inviscid.

Differential rotation and a background flow work.

Example. In the example of forcing 14 above, set

par.forcing = 1
par.forcing_frequency = 1.0
par.forcing_amplitude_cmb = 1.0

and run the same four steps. The walls now do no work: the power comes from the body force (flow.dat column 42), and the viscosity dissipates it.

docs.title: The eccentricity tide of Enceladus (forcing 2)
docs.text:
Enceladus has an ocean between an icy shell and a rocky core. On its eccentric orbit the tide stretches and squeezes both, so the walls of the ocean move, radially and along themselves. Forcing 2 moves the walls with the fits of Rekier et al. (2019, appendix A.1), which depend on the radius ratio ricb, and kore returns the flow in the ocean, with its inertial waves and their dissipation.

forcing_amplitude_cmb scales the motion at both walls (1: the fits as they are). The tide of a moon in synchronous rotation has three parts, each a separate run whose powers add: m = 0, and m = 2 with forcing_frequency equal to −Gaspard (prograde) and to Gaspard (retrograde).

Requirements:

  • ricb between 16/21 and 1, where the fits hold (Enceladus has about 0.88);
  • (m, symm) = (0, 1) or (2, 1);
  • no-slip walls (bci = bco = 1) and a viscous fluid.

Any structure, buoyancy, differential rotation and a background flow work, as does a magnetic field with insulating walls. kore stops with a conducting solid behind a wall (Magnetic field). The power is read as for forcing 14 (The energy of the response).
